metadata.speaker: Arese Ugwu
metadata.title: Personal Finance and Wealth Management

content:
Welcome to the Smart Money Tribe podcast. I'm your host, Arese. I'm the founder of smartmoneyafrica.org, a financial education platform tailored to the African millennial woman, but I'm probably best known as the author of two best-selling personal finance books: The Smart Money Woman and The Smart Money Tribe. I love having money conversations that encourage African women to think bigger and become the chief financial officers of their own personal economies. This podcast is a weekly show that will focus on powerful conversations, stories, and practical lessons that teach African millennial women how to make money, keep money, and grow money.  

Hello, hello, hello! I'm so excited because I've been obsessed with podcasts for the longest time, and I've always wanted to start my own podcast, but I've always told myself, "Ugh, I don't have enough time" or "I need to come up with the right format first" or "There's too much on my plate right now to start." But after the COVID-19 pandemic hit, it felt like we were all playing musical chairs, and the music stopped suddenly, leaving us all confused and with plenty of questions around our finances. So I thought, why not start now? Create a platform where we can have all these conversations.  

So COVID hits, and a lot of questions I kept hearing around money were like: What does earning look like in the face of a lockdown? Do I still have a job? Can my business survive? How will my investments fare in this crisis? Do I even have any investments to speak of? What is the value of my assets? Do I have an emergency fund? Blah, blah, blah, blah, blah. Seeing, I don't know which table you are on, but in one way or the other, everyone was forced to confront the realities of their financial positions or at least the short-term consequences of their long-term financial habits.

So for the first episode of the broadcast, I thought a great topic would be to begin with overcoming money mistakes, because we've all made them, and I find that learning from your mistakes is always a great place to begin when you want to revamp your personal finances. As the saying goes, you learn more from your failures than you do from your success.

Now, I'll start with myself, because people often assume that because I create personal finance content, I'm perfect when it comes to my money. This is not true. My goal is not perfection. My goal has always been and will always be to teach others what I've learned the hard way and share the strategies that I've used to take control of my own personal finances over the years. So I've made a lot of money and I've lost a lot of money as well, but I've learned a lot of important lessons along the way.

So yes, I have a financial background. I've worked in financial services. My superpower is how to break down the financial jargon in a way that the everyday person can understand, right? So I'm not perfect. It's a journey for me as well, but I have a lot of strategies that I've learned that other people have also imbibed from reading my books, and it's made a huge impact on their personal finances.

So smart money is not necessarily about being the richest person in the room. It is about learning how to optimize your limited resources. It's about learning how to master skill sets that you can monetize. It's about learning how to cut expenses ruthlessly on the things you don't care about and spending intentionally on your goals. Smart money is basically a concept that encourages you to find strategies that help you cope in times of difficulty and help you leverage on what you have to get what you want.

So we're not all going to go from extreme poverty to extreme wealth. We're not all going to have magical stories, but a lot of us when it comes to money, we just want to learn how to cope. How do I get from point A to point B based off of what I have now? How do I realize, you know, my vision or reach my goals starting from my own starting point, right? So my books, this podcast, hopefully give you like the framework that you need in order to learn how to manage your personal finances. So I'm not your financial advisor. My job is to break down the financial jargon in a way that's relatable and fun and give you the financial education and tools that you need to have productive conversations with your financial advisors or whoever handles your money.

I've made a lot of financial mistakes on my journey, but I've also learned from them. And I find that there's often a powerful shift in perspective when one is forced to face the consequences of their mistakes. And I've probably learned my biggest money lessons from the three mistakes I'm about to share.

So the first financial mistake or money mistake that I used to make was saving to spend instead of saving to build. Ding ding ding! How many people can relate? How many people have found themselves in situations where they realize, "Wow, I've been saving all along, but I've been saving to spend it on something. I've been saving towards financial obligations, but I haven't been saving to build. So I haven't necessarily been building assets that can protect me in the future."

Now, I learned this the hard way. So the first time it really hit me that I was saving to spend instead of saving to build was when my marriage fell apart. I was 27 years old. I had to find a new apartment, buy new furniture, pay two years' rent upfront, pay service charge for one year in advance—all with a one-year-old child in tow. So to say the least, it was a financial struggle because it depleted my savings significantly. And I found myself thinking, "Wow, wow, wow. How did this happen? You work in finance, so you know better. You have a decent job, so you don't have the excuse of saying you're a low-income earner. And you save and invest very regularly. So how did you find yourself here, please?"

But it was my first aha moment and one of the biggest lessons I would learn about managing my personal finances, because it was the first time I realized I had been saving, but I had not been saving enough in proportion to the income that I was earning. So I was saving and investing, but I wasn't saving and investing enough in proportion to the income I was earning.

So I've always been a regular saver since I was a child; my parents insisted on it. I worked in finance and I knew the ins and outs of financial instruments, so I also invested regularly. But it was always an afterthought. It was something that I did after I had finished paying my bills or covering my lifestyle expenses. So when I took a deep dive into my finances to figure out exactly what I had done with money that I made, I was shook. I was shook because it hit me that I've been really good at saving towards important financial obligations like rent, and even better saving towards lifestyle expenses like buying a Chanel bag or paying for a holiday, but I wasn't saving enough towards assets that could protect my financial future.

Now, the thing with things like rent and holidays is that they're great—it shows you that you're disciplined enough to save. But once that money is paid, it's gone forever. It improves your lifestyle, but it doesn't improve your net worth, right? So I had been saving and investing, but I was not saving and investing intentionally to improve my net worth. So I was saving to spend, but I wasn't saving to build.

It was such a huge aha moment for me because it's funny how we measure financial success of wealthy people by quoting their net worth. So we'll say, "Dangote is on the Forbes list; he's worth approximately 8.3 billion dollars." But when we're measuring the financial success of our peers, we tend to look at their spending patterns. So we'll say, "Does he drive a Range Rover? Does she have a Birkin? Does she go on various holidays every year?" Because unfortunately, as a society, we've become obsessed with status symbols, and as a result, it's become more important for people to look like they have money as opposed to actually having it.

But can you blame us? In my opinion, if you're born in Africa, because of our long history with poverty, the focus is primarily on earning: get a good job, start a business so you can make money. But we're not taught in any formal framework how to keep money or grow money. They don't teach us in primary school, secondary school, or even university. We're just supposed to magically figure out what to do with our money when we get our first job out of uni.

But wealthy people know that financial success is not about how much you earn, but about how much of what you earn you are able to convert into assets that can provide you with an income in the future. So it became important to me to calculate my net worth, to know what my net worth is, and intentionally save and invest towards improving my net worth.

And I know for a lot of people, it's really scary because they're like, "These are big... How much money do I have? Do I want to start finding out that's a minus 5 million or minus 100 million, whatever the case may be?" But I found that the figure is not as important as the trends in net worth. So as long as you make a commitment to keep growing, you'll be fine, right? And it's an important measure of financial success. We can no longer afford to say that we don't know, right?

It was so interesting to me that I think a few weeks ago there was this argument online and all this outrage around Kylie Jenner's net worth not being a billion dollars, right? And I found it funny because, you know, there were so many valid points, but I found it even more interesting that a lot of people didn't understand how to calculate their net worth. So they were out in these social media streets arguing about Kylie Jenner's net worth when they don't know their own, or more importantly, when they don't know how to calculate their own.

So don't find yourself in these streets arguing about whether somebody has 900 million dollars or a billion dollars when you don't know how to calculate your net worth. So your net worth is your assets minus your liabilities, right? So make a list of everything you own and its value, minus a list of everything you owe and its value. This is what will show your true financial position, right? So what is your value? What is your net worth?

This episode is brought to you by wealth.ng. Wealth.ng is a self-service investment marketplace based in Nigeria. It acts as a one-stop shop for all your investment needs. From the convenience of your phone or laptop, they give you access to a bouquet of investments that range from treasury bills, stocks, and bonds to agri-products. Download the wealth.ng app to find out more.

So the second financial mistake that is now fortunately in my past is that I used to have global savings goals, right? So I'm sure most people relate to this, right? You say, "Yes, I'm saving. I have savings," right? And you're saving into one account. So you're not intentional about what your savings targets are. You're just putting everything—whether it's for your car, whether it's for emergencies, whether it's saving towards your retirement, whether it is money you're saving towards your next trip—it's all in one account.

And I find that what happens, guys, is that when we see money in one global savings account, we don't know or we don't have a clear idea of what we can afford and what we cannot afford, right? So the money in the bank does not always equal spending. Let me explain.

Hi, my name is Arese, and I am naturally an impulsive spender. Which means if there is money in my account, I will find a way to spend it. So a long time ago, I found a way to curb this. So I had to learn how to create systems around my money that removed me from the equation. So I created savings buckets for different goals: so an account for emergencies, an account for rent, an account to save towards travel, an account to save towards my short-term frivolous goals like shopping, eating out with my friends, that kind of thing.

But by organizing my money, I now had clarity around where the money I was earning was going, and it helped me save more efficiently. And more importantly, I had a clearer understanding of what I could afford and what I could not afford at any given point in time.

A lot of people make the mistake of saving for everything underneath one savings umbrella. Which means that when they call you from your village, "Ah, Mama is sick," it comes from that savings account. When your car breaks down, the money comes from the same savings account. You want to buy a house, the money comes from that savings account. You'd like to go on holiday, same savings account. The problem with this is that you never have a clear picture of what you can afford to do, and it makes it difficult for you to measure your progress with your savings goals, right?

So if your money is efficiently allocated to all your different goals in different accounts, you can say, "Oh, okay, I'm halfway to my goal to buy land. I've reached 20% of my goal to buy a new car," right? And instantly, when money needs to come out from somewhere, you can see very clearly whether you can afford it or you can't afford it. So create savings buckets so that you can save more efficiently and you're not just taking out of one account and not clear about what you can afford and what you can't afford.

The third money mistake I struggle with, right, is underestimating the importance of an emergency fund. So I've always had an emergency fund; I always have one. But the part I struggle with is prioritizing and replenishing it instead of investing in assets or in my business, because like most people, I prefer not to think about the possibility of bad things happening to me.

Growing up, my parents would say things like, "Keep quiet. Don't use your mouth to say negative things. God forbid it's what happens to you," because we live in a superstitious society. So even when we see bad things happening to other people, we tell ourselves, "God forbid, it's not going to happen to me." But the truth is bad things happen to good people all the time, and it can happen to you too. So it's better to be prepared, because the opportunity cost of not having cash to cover your expenses because something sudden happened can be very expensive.

Nobody ever plans to lose their jobs, nobody ever plans to have financial difficulties in their businesses or have medical emergencies, but emergencies happen. COVID happens, and it can be expensive to not be prepared for financial surprises. So your emergency fund is typically three to six months of your living expenses, and is designed to protect your long-term investments from your short-term unexpected expenses.

But honestly, in Africa, it's more like 9 to 12 months, because there are more uncertainties in this part of the world, and we pay more lump sums for living expenses. Like in other places, you pay maybe a month at a time. In Nigeria, you pay minimum of a year ahead or two years ahead. So it's better to have at least 9 to 12 months of living expenses saved up, right? And usually you have to see it as a revolving fund. So as money goes out to say fix your car, money needs to go back in to replace that money.

And that's part of what I struggle with a lot, because when I want to put money back in my emergency fund, I start to think, "I can put this money back in my business and make X amount of money," or "If I invested it in another financial instrument, it would make me more money." Because your emergency fund is not there to make you money, so you're not putting it in risky asset classes. You're putting it—even if you earn an interest on it, it's like a nominal interest rate—but you're putting it in an instrument that preserves the capital. It's not necessarily there for money making; it's there to protect your long-term investments from short-term unexpected expenses.

So I hope by sharing some of my own money mistakes, you've learned some strategies to help you recover from some of yours. I can't wait to hear some of the money mistakes that you've made, some of the personal finance strategies that you've learned on your own journeys. So I'm looking forward to your feedback.

Three key takeaways from this episode:

Your net worth is the most important measure of financial success. So it's not about how much you earn, but about how much you can keep and grow.

There's a big difference between saving to spend and saving to build. Be intentional about both.

Your emergency fund is the foundation of your financial life. It's designed to protect your long-term investments from short-term unexpected expenses.

If you still feel confused about your money, if you're seeking financial clarity and need a framework and strategies to help take control of your personal finances, then book a one-on-one coaching session with me by visiting smartmoneyafrica.org.

Thank you for listening to this episode of the Smart Money Tribe podcast. I hope you enjoyed it. I'm super excited about creating financial content for African millennial women who want to live a fabulous life, but also want to learn how to find the balance between spending on their lifestyle needs and building assets that could protect their financial futures.

metadata.speaker: Folorunsho Alakija
metadata.title: Fashion, Printing, Energy and Enterprise Development

content:
Forum participation in the Nigerian petroleum industry dates back to the early 20th century when European authorities recognize oil as the fuel of the future and encourage private businesses to undertake aggressive exploration all over the world. Since then economic challenges have been mounting in Nigeria forcing the central bank to introduce currency restrictions to conserve foreign exchange reserves which have fallen to more than an 11year low. My name is Peace Hyde and this is My Worst Day today on Forbes Africa TV.

The attainment of Independence in the 1960s led to intense exploration activities as the nation put in place policies that would lead to Major economic and political changes in the oil sector. Deep water fields that first begun production 10 years ago now account for more than half of Nigeria's production. Among the patriarchal owners of these wealthy Fields, an unlikely Titan emerged. Let's find out who she is.

Born in 1951 to the family of Chief L A Ogbara in Lagos State, Mrs Folorunsho Alakija is a Nigerian businesswoman who is the second richest African woman and also the third richest woman of African descent in the world. She is worth an estimated $1.61 billion according to Forbes. She is a business tycoon involved in fashion, oil, and the printing Industries. Mrs Alakija is the Vice Chair of Famfa Oil, a Nigerian exploration and production company that has a 60% participating interest in Block OML 127, part of the larger Agbami field, one of Nigeria's largest deep water discoveries with its Partners Chevron and Petrobras.

Her first company was a fashion label that catered to Nigeria's Elite women. Mrs Alakija is the Group Managing Director of the Rose of Sharon Group which consists of the Rose of Sharon Prints and Promotions Limited and Digital Reality Prints Limited. She is also the founder of the Rose of Sharon Foundation which has a focus on empowering widows and their families as well as orphans to be successful through educational programs and scholarships. Mrs Alakija and her husband also founded the Christian Ministry, the Rose of Sharon Glorious Ministry International. Mrs Alakija is also a renowned author, having written University of Marriage, Alone with God, her autobiography Growing with the Hand that Gives, The Rose, and The Cry of Widows and Orphans, to name a few. In conjunction with her Partners, her company is also a major sponsor of the Agbami Medical and Engineering scholarship scheme, one of the most reliable scholarship schemes in Nigeria with over a thousand people yearly as beneficiaries.

Thank you for joining me on My Worst Day on Forbes Africa TV. And today we are joined by an exceptional woman, the iconic Mrs Folorunsho Alakija. Thank you very much for joining me on My Worst Day.

You're most welcome. It's a pleasure to be here.

Now first of all, we want to start by finding out: Who is Mrs Folorunsho Alakija?

Folorunsho Alakija is a mother, a grandmother, and a wife to my husband of almost 40 years. And God has blessed us with four sons and two grandchildren. Folorunsho Alakija is a businesswoman. She's a philanthropist. And the success story that one can talk about now has not been overnight. It's taken well over 30 years in business to get to this point. But I give God the glory.

You've had quite a diverse career, from banking to fashion, oil, and then also your printing industry. Can you talk us through that Journey, please?

In fact, I started out as a confidential secretary when I came back from England and I worked with Sijuade Enterprises for about a year and a half. And then I moved to a bank that was just starting out in Nigeria at the time and I was there for almost 12 years. But then shortly after that, I realized that more people were being hired and some were being taken above me. And I decided that it was time to move on. So I decided that I needed to go and set up my own business.

I decided I was going to go and study fashion design. I believe in doing things properly. I don't like half measures. Anything worth doing at all for a Folorunsho is worth doing well. So I decided to go back to England to study fashion design properly and set up my own fashion house, which was called Supreme Stitches at the time. Immediately when I launched my label, I was invited to take part in a fashion competition. And that fashion competition brought me out into the limelight because I won the competition.

Somewhere along the line, on an occasion when I traveled to England to go and see my children who were schooling abroad at the time, I met a friend of mine on board who had invited me, who had told me that she was involved with a business group that wanted to lift crude in Nigeria. And from that point, that was the point where anything about oil came into my life. She wanted me to see whether I could get the company that she was involved with an opportunity to lift crude—Nigerian crude. It was an American company.  

And I went knocking on a few doors to be able to get me an appointment with the oil Minister. And the petroleum Minister told me that the government of the day was not really interested in doing that anymore, but that they preferred to get companies to invest in the Nigeria oil industry. I took the message back and they said they didn't want to invest in Nigeria, so they left.  

And then I thought to myself after that that well, now that I have a foot in the door, why don't I go back to the oil Minister and find out what I can do in that industry? Basically, all that was in my mind was to try and get any kind of contract just to earn a little bit more than what I was making in my fashion business. So I went back, went to see some relatives of mine in NNPC, and they suggested that why don't you go and try for transportation of crude? So I did my homework in that area. I went back to the Minister and he said, "Well, by the time we start connecting more pipelines, we won't be needing the trucks as much as before."  

So I felt a bit disappointed again. I went back and I was wondering what else I could do. On another visit, he then suggested to me that because the current government at that time was more interested in getting Nigerians involved in exploiting its oil industry rather than having the multinationals continue to cart away the wealth of Nigeria, that why don't I look at oil exploration and production?  

So I felt rather depressed, dejected, and it seemed as if the final door had been shut in my face. I decided to not give up. Folorunsho Alakija is not the type of person that gives up easily. I decided to do some more homework. I started looking for technical partners, which I found, and we applied for an oil license. It took 3 years to get that oil license, and oil Ministers changed hands a couple of times, and each time I had to reapply all over again.  

Then the license eventually came in August 1993, to my delight. And it was funny that it took another 3 years to be able to get a new set of technical partners, because the first set of technical partners that we had did not want to have anything to do with the kind of block that we were allocated. It was deep offshore. Technology had not reached the water depth of the oil block that we had been allocated, which was about 5,000 feet.

So we were going around looking for technical partners that would team up with us and that would be able to not only provide the technical know-how, but also provide the funds for us to be able to explore and exploit it. After 3 years, we did get an invitation by Texaco for a meeting, and we negotiated for 3 months backwards and forwards. And I can say, to the glory of God, the rest has been history.

When you were given that deep offshore oil block and the general consensus was that it was one of the worst, what was going through your mind? How did you feel about acquiring it and taking the risk to actually work on it, not knowing if it would bear fruit or not?  

During the period that I was trying to get the oil license, I became born again. And in becoming born again, I had entered into a covenant with God, and I had said, "If You will bless me, I'll work for You all the days of my life." So I knew that God would not disappoint me.  

Following that Journey, what would you say has been your worst day in business so far?

Hm, how can I ever forget that day? The worst day of my life in business. This was in, I think it was 1999, when the government of the day decided to back into our oil block by taking 40% of our 60% shareholding, which is two-thirds of our ownership. Two-thirds of our ownership of something that we had suffered over the years!

When we initially got into making inquiries in the oil industry from January 1991 to 1999, 8 years of our lifetime had passed. All our life savings had been put into it. We had taken a sole risk, meaning that if we did not strike oil and strike it in commercial quantity, we could have been wiped out. We decided to take that risk. And it was after we had discovered oil in commercial quantity that the government decided to back into our block and say, "Okay, now that it's looking juicy, we want a part of that."

It wasn't fair. We felt cheated. We went calling and knocking on doors of friends who might be able to help us to salvage the situation. Nobody helped. It seemed as if we had suddenly become the plague. Nobody wanted to have anything to do with us, to the extent that I had friends in high places who, when they bumped into me, would look the other way or would hold a newspaper to cover their faces. It was as bad as that.

Wow. So now you were here with the government essentially taking away everything you had worked hard for. What was going through your mind? What did you want to do? How did you feel?

We felt that we had nothing to lose by fighting back, but we had everything to gain if we won. So we decided to take the government of the day to court. People thought we were crazy, but there was nowhere else to go. Every door had been shut in our face. We were depressed, dejected, upset, angry. But who do you want to punch? Nobody to punch. It seemed as if it was the end of the world and everything had collapsed in our faces.  

I mean, this was a family business that had become a family business. We were all working in it—my husband, my children, myself. And short of throwing in the towel and giving up, we decided we would not do that, that we would take the matter to court.  

People were saying, "But you can never win against the government. When you go to court, government always wins." We said, "It's going to be fight to finish. We are going to go all the way, whatever it takes."  

So we started from the lower courts. It took 12 years to get to the point of the final judgment at the Supreme Court. It was bittersweet. There were times we would win on some motions, there were times we would lose on some motions in court. And my husband played a fantastic role. He's a lawyer. Throughout that 12-year period, he was in court all the time. And we were paying huge sums to be represented by other lawyers and chambers in various courts. And there were sleepless nights. We were fasting, praying, and it was like we were on our own.  

Friends, relatives were abusing us, and they were saying things like, "Oh, so the government took 40%, came back, took another 10%, leaving us with just 10% from our 60% shareholding of the entire partnership. So is 10% not enough for them? What are they looking for?" So abuses everywhere.

So that first day, that one day in retrospect, when we look back, we thank God for taking that bold step to decide to fight back. And why did we eventually win? We had signed a contract at the beginning with the government that they could back into the oil block, but there were steps and processes that needed to be followed which the government did not do. They were supposed to sit us down and negotiate with us before they could do anything with our block. They were supposed to give us compensation for whatever percentage they wanted to take from us. But where they went wrong was they didn't do any of that. And what they did is, "We gave the license, we had the right to come into any block at any time that we please, and we can take what we want."  

Meaning they wanted to reap where they didn't really sow, because we had paid for the block—all the government dues we had paid right from the start. Nigeria has a constitution, and nobody, even the government itself, is not above the Constitution. So it was those arguments that we built on that got us the opportunity to win the case.  

12 years is a very long time. Was there any point in that process that you felt like just throwing in the towel and giving up or doubting even whether you would come out successful?

Giving up was not an option. Folorunsho does not give up. My husband does not give up. My children do not give up. We were a force that had to be reckoned with.

When you think of the worst day when you found out what the government was trying to do, and you contrast it to the moment you found out that you had actually won the legal battle, how did you feel?

On top of the world. Elated. Closer to God. I decided I was going to develop an even deeper relationship with Him. Within that 12-year period, we had learned that man will deceive you, man will disappoint you, man will reject you, man would turn their backs on you, but God would always be standing.

And also there's a lot of young entrepreneurs, young business people that are looking up to you. Your story is extremely inspiring. What would be your advice to them? And for young people who are looking to venture into uncharted territories and see how successful they can become, what would be your advice to them?

What I would say is: there's no industry or sector that's the exclusive preserve of any gender. Make sure that you do your homework. Make sure that you look for mentors. Make sure that you acquire the requisite skills to enable you to succeed in your chosen venture. Never take no for an answer. I didn't take no for an answer; I never will take no for an answer. And for me, there's no such word as "can't."

One of the very first things that one should do is always to ask God first, to ask God where He wants you to be, what He has planned for your destiny. And I believe that if you do that, against all odds, no matter what may be thrown at you, you will still be standing the way I'm standing today, to God's glory.

Absolutely phenomenal. Thank you so very much for joining us on My Worst Day, Mrs Alakija. You've been absolutely amazing.  

Thank you very much. It's been my pleasure.  

Well, there you have it. You've heard from the Visionary herself about her journey through her worst day as an entrepreneur. Now let's find out what her closest allies had to say about this phenomenal woman.  

My name is Mrs Toin Uwa. I'm the Secretary to the Rose of Sharon Glorious Ministries International, and I'm also a member of the Board of Trustees for the Rose of Sharon Foundation.  

My name is Elsa. I'm the Chief Operating Officer at Digital Reality Print Limited.  

Hi, my name is Dayo Alakija. I'm Folorunsho Alakija's son.  

I've known Mrs Alakija for over 10 years... 26 years... Mrs Alakija, my mom, she's... Mrs Alakija is very passionate. Mrs Alakija is the ultimate woman—focused and very enterprising. She's energetic. She's very, very business-focused. When she sets her sight on something, she does not allow anything to distract her until she achieves her goal.

But I think one of the things that surprises me the most is how much of a workaholic she is. She's really passionate and she's driven. She never considers anything as impossible. I mean, she literally spends all her time on one form of product or another. I find it... I don't know where she finds the time, you know?

Someone who is always very focused on everything that she does. She's a go-getter. So if she has to move mountains to get to her objective, trust me, she would. You know, even sometimes when you come up with ideas or reasons why things can't work, she doesn't agree with you. She sees how things can work. I guess that's why she's achieved so much.

Passion is a thing of the heart. If she feels something is right, either from an ethical, social, or spiritual point of view, she fights for it. And she's forgiving and she's very prayerful, and she's someone I see as who genuinely tries to follow what she believes Christ is all about. Those are the qualities that I see in her and that I really admire in her and I try to follow.

She's really a lovely person, but she's also my mother at the end of the day. It's actually kind of amazing. We really are proud of her in this position, and we hope that it inspires others, not just in Nigeria, but throughout Africa, to try to emulate the type of person that she is—to give and to help others, and to touch people's lives.

It is often said failure is hard, but success is far more dangerous. Everything you want as an entrepreneur is on the other side of fear. Those who achieve success are those who venture into uncharted waters, often with no life jacket, ready to sink or swim. Which one of these entrepreneurs are you? My name is Peace Hyde, and this is My Worst Day on Forbes Africa TV.

metadata.title: Banking, Venture Capital, Africapitalism and Entrepreneurship

content:
Hi Tony, it's so great to have you here. Thank you for being with us today. You are one of the most celebrated and most decorated business leaders in Africa, and I would posit the world, so it's truly an honor to be able to host you at Stanford this afternoon. Thank you very much.

We watched a video earlier where we learned a little bit about the Foundation, which we'll speak about towards the later half of the interview. But we saw there that you're such a supporter and such an advocate of entrepreneurship, which isn't really a surprise because your parents were entrepreneurs. I'm curious to know how seeing them build businesses at a young age influenced you and impacted your journey.  

So I'm pleased and honored to be with you all today. Stanford, a great university, and a team from this great university visited the Tony Elumelu Foundation before the pandemic, I think. And I was quite impressed—they were on time in spite of the chaotic traffic situation in Lagos, and the research work was also very, very impressive. So for me, coming back here is such an honor. I have a great impression of your school.  

Entrepreneurship is in my DNA. I preach entrepreneurship, I encourage entrepreneurship. I also try to catalyze more entrepreneurs in Africa, because in my own life journey, I've come to appreciate the significance and importance of entrepreneurship in transforming families, in transforming self, in transforming communities, in transforming countries, societies, and humanity entirely.  

And when we founded the Tony Elumelu Foundation, it was driven by the need and urgency to help catalyze development in Africa at a scale that's sustainable, realizing further that entrepreneurship is the way to that. I was privileged, lucky, blessed to have been mentored in this journey of entrepreneurship first by my parents, especially my mom, who was an entrepreneur on a small scale. But the lessons I imbibed watching her, supporting her, continue to help me to date.  

And it's also critical in the message and advice I give to young entrepreneurs. I learned from her about hard work. She was extremely, extremely hard-working. At the time to date, she's just turned 94, and she's still very hard on me! She will cook for me, and I driver to come apologize, pick food, and I'm like, "Mom, I have somebody to cook for me." But that spirit in her remains ever so strong.  

She was disciplined, and I have come to realize that this journey of entrepreneurship—they say before I know entrepreneurship, everything in life—discipline is critical for success. She was extremely tenacious, and I've come to see, and I preach too, that the journey of entrepreneurship is not a linear journey. It's up and down. But if you're tenacious, if you are resilient, you cross the finishing line. So those are part of the early learnings from my parents, my mom.  

My dad long ago told us, and the reason is in my brain today: that if you earn a dollar and you're unable to save, if you earn a billion dollars, you will not save anything. So that for me is the first lesson in capital formation. Capital formation starts from savings. If you do not save, you don't have money to invest. If you don't invest, you remain where you are. And so these lessons have helped me in this journey of entrepreneurship.  

So let's fast forward a few years. You graduate from university with a bachelor's and master's degree in economics. You then proceed to become one of the youngest bank branch managers in Nigeria, typically a job reserved for people who are in their 50s or 60s. You become the managing director of one of the biggest banks in Nigeria. And then 2005 comes around, and you are being asked to help lead what becomes like the biggest merger in Nigeria's corporate history. What were some of the challenges that you faced during that time, and which leadership principles did you stay rooted in as you were guiding this process?  

At the time, quite a lot of challenges, but just to contextualize to understand it: we took over a distressed bank called Standard Trust Bank in 1997, and in 2005, we merged Standard Trust Bank and United Bank for Africa. But before the merger, there was an acquisition. Standard was acquiring significant interest in United Bank for Africa, then we merged, and I emerged the CEO.  

So first, you saw United Bank for Africa as almost 70 years old as an institution, and set in its ways of doing things. Then digital adoption was not so strong, and so at times it took people months to read emails. And in terms of service delivery, those days the old-generation banks were not so strong on service delivery. And we were coming from a bank that was so strong in service delivery and technology, young people, etc.  

So a bank the size of less than 1,800 people and United Bank for Africa had about 12,000 staff. This 1,800 younger, technologically advanced, and this other one older and a very big bank. So it's not easy integrating, because as you see in corporate mergers, the legal combination is not the issue. The difficult part is the people integration, the cultural integration—that is the tough part.

And so, and if you can see from history, most corporate institutions, it takes so many years to integrate people and culture. And if you do not integrate people and culture properly, you lose the major value levers. And so we were mindful of this. I wanted to make sure we were able to merge, integrate. And this is a financial institution that was like... you merge today, customers don't care whether they want to be served by the same institutions, they move them.  

There was a tough part integrating our people, merging our people, merging cultures—an old culture set in their ways and a vibrant younger culture. But therein lies the interesting aspect of the combination of the job. I say to people: my elder brother, who is seven years older than me, he doesn't have grey hair. I have grey hair! My grey hairs are there from the corporate merger, because making it work, serving your customers, making sure that everyone in the universe of the institution—which was 428 branches at the time—that it was the same level of service across the board. Customers at Standard Trust Bank that were used to a certain level of service delivery, you would not want them to come to the new institution and have a drop.  

So we just had to make sure that service... we put our customers first. And that's why today United Bank for Africa, which interestingly has grown from a one-country bank to a bank that operates in 20 African countries, with presence also in Paris, London, recently Dubai, and the only African bank that operates in the U.S. with a deposit-taking license... it started small, it's gone that big. And that experience during the merger continues to guide what we do, especially how we prioritize our customers and how we prioritize our people.  

So I would say the biggest lesson from that combination was our people—integrating our people and culture. It was realizing that, especially in the service sector where you sell intangibles, so to speak, it is very important that your core army, your workforce, that they are fully aligned, totally integrated, and positively mobilized and motivated. If you have this, you can make progress. And those lessons from the early days—resilience, hard work, discipline, staying focused, prioritizing people—have all helped us in creating today's United Bank for Africa.

And as you mentioned, you all were able to do that very successfully. You expanded from being a single-country bank to one that operates in more than 20 countries in Africa, and then has an impact and influence and reach in other countries as well. Many of us are interested in working in emerging markets or building, developing products or services for emerging markets, or one emerging market to begin with. I'm curious to know: how do you evaluate which markets to enter when you are expanding United Bank for Africa, and how do you determine when's the right time to do so?  

So first, most times people see the empty part of a glass. At times, we see also the full part of the glass. You would always have difficulties and challenges in almost every sector, especially countries you want to go into. So when we decided to expand into Africa, the story was... first, we thought that we had mastered how to serve customers, because that's what banking is about: it's about serving your customers, all about customers, customers, customers. And realizing that to serve your customers, you must have a mobilized workforce that's aligned with the mission and vision that you see for the group.

So we felt, looking at the African landscape, that we had opportunities. We thought Nigeria was, and remains, the largest economy in Africa, and we thought that the level of banking or service support was very high, and now we should leverage this and spread across the continent. And we had to decide: which country should we go to? How do we decide the country? Macroeconomic stability, policies, foreign policies, ease of doing business in countries, taxation policies in countries, and the demographics of countries. Because we were quite set to support small and medium-scale enterprises—that is the bedrock of United Bank for Africa.

So based on that, we came up with 30 countries that met the internal criteria. We settled... at UBA, we developed what we called the UBA Redwood, which explained Africa issues to consider, etc. But in all of those issues, the ease of doing business in countries was very critical to us. The population was also important. The GDP of countries, income per capita was important. Ease of finding the right human capital to work with, because again, human capital is a people business, so that was very important to us.

And we came up with all of this. We now cleared it into what we developed and called the three-tier strategic intent. Tier 1 was we wanted to be strong in Nigeria. Tier 2: be a leading pan-African bank. And Tier 3: being global, having presence in global financial centers, which is why we talk about London, Paris, New York, Dubai—it's all part of our three-tier strategic intent.

The second one therefore, orchestrating our expansion in Africa, and under that was: what strategy do we do? A country strategy or not? Pass-through or have presence in countries? And we decided that we needed to have presence in countries. And next was: okay, how do we tier the countries again? We used GDP, so we tiered the countries and we said, rolling out: greenfield, brownfield, acquisition, mergers—how do you want to grow? We decided that we'd do a combination of both.

So in the countries we went to, some countries we acquired banks, some were merged, and some we started greenfield. And the journey is, so far, so good. Today, United Bank for Africa serves over 35 million customers in Africa and is still growing. We're helping to simplify payments on the continent, we're helping to orchestrate trade transactions, intra-Africa trade transactions.  

Prior to this time, Africa did not trade with and amongst itself. Or we believe the reason Africa didn't do this is because of payment issues, because of even infrastructure, transactional infrastructure, and also making sure we support capacity for small and medium-scale businesses to grow. So UBA has done quite a bit in this space.  

And most importantly, financial inclusion: trying to make sure that everyone... on a continent with about 1 billion people, the banked population is not so high. So to us, it's not just about banking or offering banking services; it's about what we call the democratization of access to financial services. It's about financial inclusion. So making sure that almost everyone in markets where we operate has access to banking facilities and banking services.  

And that's why in some countries we spear-headed and pioneered the opening of bank accounts with zero balances, because what's important to us is to be able to attract people. We believe that Africa has an informal economy that is very large, and all of us should be involved in trying to formalize the informal economy. And this is one of the ways we are doing so through our banking services.  

In other areas of our operations as a group, we're trying to do the same thing. What we do at the Tony Elumelu Foundation is all, again, about helping to develop the continent: financial empowerment, taking opportunities to people irrespective of your level in society, where you live, whether in urban or rural areas. So those are things we need to keep doing to create a more inclusive society, especially in Africa.  

You alluded to this a little bit earlier: there's a lot of innovation happening in the financial services industry, a lot of tech disruptors, many of which are working towards that goal of democratizing access to financial services. From your position as CEO and now Chairman of United Bank for Africa, how do you see the company collaborating or even competing with some of these disruptors, particularly thinking about new technologies like cryptocurrencies, peer-to-peer payments, etc.?  

First, I was CEO of UBA about 12 years ago, so today I don't see myself as a banker per se. I'm an investor that invests in banking, in helping to improve access to electricity on the continent—a critical resource deficit on the continent that's important to breach if Africa must leapfrog and move the continent to where it should be. We're investors in the healthcare sector, having realized that indeed health is wealth. If the pandemic taught us one thing, it is about prioritizing health and realizing that what war couldn't do, health or lack of it can do! Who would have thought that the entire world would go into a lockdown mode? I didn't know or think that could happen in my lifetime!

So we're investing in that sector. We're investing in energy, the full energy chain, because again, for a continent like Africa, it's critical.

So for us, or for me at this point, I'm not so much of a banker. However, as a group, we realize the importance of technology. These digital disruptions that we see in the world are real, and in Africa in particular, thanks to the youth population of our continent, we know that we have to catch up. If we don't catch up, we're going to be left behind.

And for businesses we are associated with, like United Bank for Africa and other businesses, digital adoption is critical for service delivery, for everything that we do. So in the payment space, we lead in the payment space through digitization, through adoption, partnership with fintechs and all kinds, just to make sure that we're able to serve our customers. Today's customers, they don't need a bank—they need a facilitator for payments, they need a facility that fits their lifestyle.  

And banking is changing. It's changing from the way we used to know banking so many years ago. Today, I tell you, at United Bank for Africa... earlier I told you that we have 35 million customers. A few years ago, in 2005 when we did the merger between Standard Trust and United Bank for Africa, all of 2004 UBA celebrated that it was the first bank in Nigeria to have 32 ATMs—32 ATMs! It was a big marketing tool that we had 32 ATMs, and then the first bank also to pay out 1 billion Naira in cash.

And then 97% of our customer transactions occurred in the banking hall. Today, UBA opens about 500,000 accounts every month, and these accounts—95% are opened online, not in the banking hall! Number two: transaction count. We have over 98% of our customer transactions now occurring online, not in the banking hall.

Again, in terms of ATMs, UBA alone has close to 4,000 ATMs in Nigeria—all from that early picture! And of course, POS machines uncountable. There were no POS machines before! So things have changed, and they will change further. Technology is disrupting a lot of things, not just in the U.S. or in the West, but everywhere—even healthcare. In our healthcare sector today, healthcare can be delivered digitally online. So we live in a new world, and every one of us is adopting and adapting faster to the new world we are living in.

You mentioned energy a little earlier, which makes me nervous because it seems as though you're reading my mind, because that's where I want to go next. Last year, the Africa Energy Chamber recognized you as one of the 25 most influential individuals in shaping Africa's energy sector. I'm curious to know, especially knowing that sustainability and renewable energy is a really important subject that gets studied here and talked about a lot: what are the most pressing issues and solutions being discussed right now as it relates to energy in Africa, and also, I would love to know a little bit more about the work that you're doing through Transcorp to address this?  

So access to electricity is extremely poor in Africa. Less than 35% of our people have access to reliable electricity on the continent. This is a continent of young people—over 700 million people are young on the continent, under the age of 30, and yet access to electricity is almost impossible. These young ones are in a very competitive world. They are going to compete with children who are used to 24/7 uninterrupted electricity supply.  

So the world we see ahead is actually frightening, because the divide we want to bridge is not just happening in the digital space, it's happening because of lack of access to reliable energy on the continent. And from the work we do at the Tony Elumelu Foundation, from our close interaction with young Africans, male and female, we know, we can tell, we see, we hear, listen to them that access to electricity is a major hindrance and constraint on their ability to succeed.  

This is why most—I'm sure at Stanford you must have seen this in your business research studies—most small and medium-scale enterprises on the continent die. They don't succeed. And the single most important factor for this is poor access to electricity.

So to us as a group, we believe in the concept and philosophy of Africapitalism, which is a call on the private sector to play a role in developing the continent. It's a realization that the private sector has a role to play in developing the continent. And in practicalizing this and not just speaking to it, we decided that the power sector was critical for us to invest in. And so we mobilized resources and invested in this space.  

Today, we have capacity to generate about 2,000 megawatts of electricity, but we have some other hindrances like gas supply and grid connectivity, so we're able to generate about 700 megawatts out of the capacity of 2,000. But we're happy that we're playing a key role in this area.  

But my message always has been to investors: we've started on this trip, we started from Washington, we've been to New York... Our message, my message has been consistent: we have opportunities in Africa. There's huge opportunity in Africa. A huge population, income per capita has improved and is improving, and we lack access to electricity on the continent.

So as the world mobilizes towards a more inclusive society, as the world mobilizes to a more prosperous world, I always like to remind people that we cannot have that prosperity across the world if we do not deal with the issue of access to electricity on the African continent.

The reason we have youth unemployment in Africa is attributable to this. The reason we have youth restiveness in Africa is attributable to this. The reason some embrace extremism is attributable to this. In fact, government's ability to fight extremism is also limited by this. So at times you see communities and large spaces that do not feel any impact of government or society because there is no access to electricity.  

So for me, it's not just a commercial investment; it's what we should be doing in the 21st century to help improve access to electricity. And I can never shout or say enough, and I want to have more people in this crusade: that all of us, those who have capital, should look at investing in Africa. There are opportunities there. And those who have voices, let's keep shouting to attract attention. So that collectively, all of us can make a difference in Africa.

I want to spend some time on what you mentioned earlier: Africapitalism, which you are known across Nigeria and other countries as being a strong proponent of. I'm curious to know why you believe that Africa needs to take a unique approach to capitalism?

Well, it's not a unique approach to capitalism per se; it's, for me, a realization. At times, there's this entitlement mentality that people have: "Okay, we should be helped, we should be supported, we should be developed." But for goodness' sake, it can't be like that forever! We need to help ourselves too.

So it's a realization that the private sector has also grown, is growing. We need government to prioritize, we need government to create the right environment for the private sector to keep doing well, but the private sector also must be sensible and reasonable and conscientious in how we do things. We should invest in a manner that helps to catalyze prosperity. We should invest in a manner that helps to create social equity, social wealth. We should invest in a manner that helps to create inclusiveness.  

So this is not just about a new form of capitalism or the other; it's more about the fact that the private sector should play a role in helping to develop the continent. Let's stop blaming others for our woes. Let me stop blaming others for everything. Let's lead, and hopefully they follow.  

And I've seen it happen. Some of the investments we made, we did not invest all the capital ourselves. We reached out, and we see that the world we live in is becoming highly interdependent, and people also begin to listen, especially when we show good examples.  

So it's a call on all of us in the private sector—whether in Africa or outside the world—that we have a role to play in advancing society. Again, the meeting I attended in L.A., it all had different names today: patient capital, impact investing, shared prosperity, mutual destinies. We just need to invest in a manner that's not just about profits for the investors; we should invest in a manner that creates mutual benefits for everyone: for the investors, for communities where you do business, for society at large.  

The fact that we do what we do at the Tony Elumelu Foundation—committing 100 million U.S. dollars to supporting African entrepreneurs—it's not because we have so much money, but we also know that some of the basic needs we want to have are provided. So it's not about what we have in the bank accounts; it's about how can we take a part of it and share. But for me, not even sharing in a manner that creates a dependency, perpetual dependency—no! In a manner that makes you stand on your own, it makes you self-reliant.  

And so when we say we'll give non-refundable seed capital of $5,000, and when we do so... to date, over 16,000 Africans have benefited from that program. It is not to encourage laziness—no! But we know, in San Francisco, we're in a tech environment, we know some started with less than $5,000, but today they've grown big. So we just want to give young Africans access, opportunity—opportunity to prove their concept, and then let others see them as good and come and invest in them.

So we need all the private sector playing a role. We need everyone. We need the private sector looking at critical sectors. Today we just spoke about electricity: instead of people keeping their money in bank accounts abroad, why don't you bring your money to invest in the power sector on the continent? You make more money, but you also impact society in a more positive way. That is the entire essence of it.

So we need more private sector leaders showing the way, but we need also our public sector leaders creating the right environment that will enable the private sector to do so. And we need friends of Africa, development partners, to also begin to look at how they intervene, how they engage, and how they give in the 21st century, with the aim to create self-reliance and independence rather than perpetuating the syndrome of dependency.  

Now Tony, typically when people retire from very high-stress jobs such as being the CEO of one of the largest banks in Africa, they take a vacation! You instead decided to found a company, Heirs Holdings, and also the Foundation that you've alluded to. I'm curious... this was a few years ago, I'm curious about what you saw happening in Nigeria or beyond at that time that drove, that was the impetus for you to develop this foundation?  

We did two things when I retired in 2010, 12 years ago. We decided to create a family office, which was to some extent novel in our part of the world. And we said the family office will be quite catholic in the kind of investment that we make, hence this philosophy of Africapitalism. So Heirs Holdings is the epitome and the home of our overall group, anchored on the philosophy of Africapitalism.

And we decided the sectors that we considered very important that we have to move the needle: power. Nigeria and Africa are endowed with a lot of resources, yet we do not have the ability to process all of this and convert them to the state that they can become valuable to our people. So we said energy, from an integrated point of view, across the credit value chains. We looked at the healthcare sector, and we said health is important, that we need to invest in the healthcare sector. So these were the key. Of course, real estate in urban Africa, and hospitality. Hospitality—if you want to grow a country, an economy, transportation and hospitality are critical for this. So those are the things we decided to do at the time. The motivation was to help drive our philosophy of capitalism further, but equally important, to help manage the investments, and wanted Heirs Holdings to be the go-to investment partner on the continent, to help attract investment to the continent. And so far, so good on that.  

On the other hand, the second thing we did was the Foundation. I thought that my story has been one of... this element of luck in my story, this element of being at the right place at the right time. And I wasn't the most intelligent in my class, you know, and also I wasn't the most hard-working of certain people I knew. And therefore, there must be luck in it that I am who I am, what I became.

And I thought... you know, I had risen very rapidly, done quite a lot, and I thought it was time to commit the second phase of my life to helping to impact humanity, to helping to democratize that luck that I had growing up, to help expand access to opportunities, to help people. I mean, you spoke about parents; I said my mother was a small-scale entrepreneur, not the kind of vigor I see. And so I was not like a son of any known family, so to speak—just a regular family person.

And I've been inspired by what I see around the world. Look at Steve Jobs, for instance, and his background. And I asked myself: Steve Jobs, if he were in Africa, if he were an African in Nigeria, would he have been able to succeed at the scale and magnitude he succeeded? I mean, long after his death, a company he founded crossed $1 trillion in market cap, and just recently $3 trillion!

So it's all of these that drove me to say: no, it would be unfortunate... I don't know what I would say to God if I do not create... I'll have to create more Tony Elumelus on the continent of Africa, for instance! And that was what drove my wife and I at the time to decide that we should commit 100 million U.S. dollars to helping to identify, support, and empower the new generation of African business leaders, and to do it at a scale and magnitude that's never been done before.

Given that we do business in many African countries, we decided not to make it a Nigerian issue, but an African issue. Given that we know that poverty anywhere is a threat to all of us everywhere, we decided to make sure that it's broader. And so that is why we started the Tony Elumelu Foundation.

So the motivation for starting the Tony Elumelu Foundation is to help democratize luck, create access to people whether or not you are a rich man's child or a prominent person's child. If you have ideas, you're enthusiastic, you're committed, ambitious, applied, and sector-agnostic, we will give you the opportunity.  

And so when I look back today, I see that as a major, major achievement. What we have done, the happiness I see on the faces of these young Africans, keeps me going.

My final question for you: You seem to be a nation in and of yourself! Through the foundation, you've worked with local governments, international governing bodies to help move capital where it's most needed. And so I'm sure you've heard it asked many times before: Nigeria is now in its election season. I will join the chorus: Why aren't you running for president?  

I didn't see that coming! I think first is, when I look around, I know the potential that we have as a continent and as a people. I see opportunities. I know that life can be a lot better for people, and oftentimes you feel the urge to show interest in how we are governed and how things happen.  

But I soon also realized that because I've never been selfish, because I've never been self-centered, because it's never been to me that it must be Tony, I say to myself: if there are other good people, capable people who are in the race, who are showing interest, why don't you support them and share with them what you think should be the right thing in terms of leadership, in terms of governance in 21st century Africa, where people have suffered and continue to suffer so much?  

You know, I realized also that all of us cannot be in the political space, but I know that evil succeeds or thrives in the world when good people keep quiet. So I said to myself, just the way I'm committed to entrepreneurship, committed to helping to empower young Africans, we should support the emergence and orchestration of good governance across the continent, because I think that is what has held us back as Africans.

So for me, it's not just Nigeria, it's about many countries on the continent. So I am interested in good governance, and I know that what we preach and advocacy and everything we do trying to encourage young people will not succeed if in the political space our leadership is not good. So mine is to continue to encourage the evolution of the political process that will bring about good leadership, and to ensure that our leaders stay accountable.

That process is not there yet, but we are working together. When I was in Washington, I said to political leadership here too that it should be a concerted effort: you should encourage people on the continent to do what is right, even as we also from the continent continue to speak and harp on good governance and accountability.

Thank you so much, Tony. That was amazing. And typically, we like to close with a lightning round of questions, so I have four for you, and I'm going to say them and you have to answer as quickly as possible—hence the lightning part!  

So aside from Palo Alto, California, what's your favorite place to visit? What's your favorite place to travel to?  

Oh, I just came from L.A., Los Angeles. I love Los Angeles!  

Now, with Nigeria out of the World Cup, who are you rooting for?

Wow, even my boys, they were like crying when Nigeria dropped! I think... I think Nigeria!

What is your favorite Wizkid song?

I don't know that... You have to play it!

And last question: What are you most grateful for?

I'm grateful to God for my wife and family and children. I think, you know, you can't do well in life if you don't have a home that's at peace. I do have a very peaceful home, and my children are reinforcing too, so I'm grateful to God for that.  

Thank you so much!

Personality #8: Google Hustle Academy Speakers
Speaker Full Name: Adenike Ogunlesi

Video Title (Exact): Adenike Ogunlesi I Children’s Clothing  for Africa I Hustle Academy Brings You Speaker Series

YouTube URL: http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h3Ms32pUvOY

Channel Name: Google Africa

Approximate Duration: 30 minutes 21 seconds

Relevance to Informal Sector African Entrepreneurs: Adenike Ogunlesi shares her practical journey of growing a Nigerian garment enterprise from trunk sales into a national manufacturing brand, delivering crucial strategies on maintaining quality standards, building operational structure, accessing business credit, and scaling informal craft ventures.

Full Transcript Text:

Transcript Metadata
Speaker: Adenike Ogunlesi

Video Title: Adenike Ogunlesi I Children’s Clothing  for Africa I Hustle Academy Brings You Speaker Series

URL: http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h3Ms32pUvOY

Channel: Google Africa

Publish Date: February 20, 2025

Country: Nigeria

Sector: Fashion Manufacturing, Retail & SME Growth

Full Transcript Text
Hey.

Thank you so much for making it. Thank you.

I remember driving by one of your stores in the early 2000s, I think it must have been 2005. And when we drove by, I remember thinking: that's such a beautiful place. I like beautiful spaces.

Good afternoon, everyone. I always say that excellence is in my DNA. And as a woman, my DNA and my stamp must not only be felt, it's supposed to be seen. And it's also a way of showing people what standards can look like. Beautiful.

And you'd be shocked at the number of people who will stop to say they want to take pictures because the garden looks so nice. So for me, that makes it worth it, because you train your eye to see what is beautiful in an environment where the standards have been so watered down that it's a fight to keep your standards. And as a business owner, you know it's all about standards. It's all about excellence. I'm not talking about perfection; I'm talking about standards. I'm talking about excellence—living the values of excellence through everything that you do, not just in the product, in the packaging, in the way you treat people, in the way you treat your customers, in the environment in which you're operating your business. It's a way of life. So it's part of what I call my values- and principles-based living.

Yeah, we would like to understand a bit more of how did this journey begin for you.

I needed pajamas for my children, and I literally just made pajamas for my kids because I already had a background in manufacturing clothing for women. And I just told all my friends that I made these pajamas, and everybody said, "Make for me." I said, "Make for you? Okay." I made them. Somebody said, "Make me seven pairs." My sister-in-law, seven. So who else is looking for pajamas in Lagos, please?

So I drove up and down Allen Avenue, Opebi, Awolowo Road—the places where you could shop in Lagos at the time. I mean, we're talking 30 years ago almost, you know. And it turns out that there weren't really good quality pajamas. So I made these pajamas and put them in my car. And as I dropped my children off at school, I stood by the gate and said, "Hello, I've got these really nice pajamas."

And some people would walk right past me. Some people would say, "Oh, let me see." So I mean, from that very early age, you understand that rejection is like throwing water on a duck's back. Absolutely. It should just roll off, because you know where you're going and you know what you want to achieve at the end of the day.

So some people would then say they want it right there and then, and I would sell it to them. So I decided to go up and down and look at what's really in this children's clothing market, because my husband then said to me, "Don't just make pajamas. Try your hand on shorts and shirts and this." So I took all my children's clothes and took them all apart to see how the block of a child's pattern is made, because I was used to making grown-ups' patterns. The principles are the same; the scale is smaller.

So that was it. And really, the next thing I knew was my neighbor was having a festival—she said Teddy Bear Festival. She said she's looking for somebody to make children's clothes in Ankara. I said, "You're looking at the person!" Am I going to recommend somebody else when I already started this? But she didn't know that, but I knew that.

And sometimes, you know, opportunities are right in front of us, but we're so caught up in something else that we don't hear, we don't see, and we don't have the feelers out, you know, for it. So it's very important to pay attention and be present in some of these conversations—in a lot of conversations. Absolutely.

And she said, "Okay, you can do it then. But what name are we going to write on the canopy?" You know, the typical bazaar-type of thing in the heat. So I said, "I really don't know," because I hadn't thought about the name.

Not rocket science! What kind of clothes do you want to make? What is this? What is this? I'm telling you this granular level just for you to see that the simplest things in life can give you such a huge impact. But if you dismiss it as "it's not important" or "what does this know," you don't know where learning, prosperity, abundance, anything... you don't know where it will come from.

And she simply said she would draw a drum with children tumbling out of it. And I said I want to make clothes that children can rough around in. There, just in that split second outside her kitchen door, I said the name is Ruff 'n' Tumble. Write that on it.

My children were the first models. I put them in the clothes, I tried the clothes on them, I took pictures of them. Born in Nigeria, made for Nigerians, made for the world, but has its roots deeply embedded in Nigeria. Beautiful.

For me, it's shaped everything that I do. Always be open to conversations. Always be open to continuous learning. Believe in yourself, trust yourself, be clear on what it is that you want. Know your industry. Know what happens on a global scale in your industry. Know the kind of money that can be made in your industry at a global level so you know that when you're bringing it to Nigeria, so long as it can transform into the culture and be accepted by the culture... Nobody said... nobody was going to buy children's clothes that are locally made. And what, 20-something years, almost 30 years later, we've got 17 branches, 300 people working, a factory that manufactures clothing.

How did you structure this passion of yours to become a proper business?

There's like a billion steps in between! For me, setting up a business or setting up a business for growth will rest on a couple of pillars.

So the first pillar would be your product. What is your product? Who does it serve? Why should people buy your product and not somebody else's product? What is special? So what is your USP? What is your unique selling point, and what is the use of that product? How functional is it? So product is one.

The second is people. If you really want to grow your business, you have to build a team. And that can be one of the most challenging things that a small business can do. So you prioritize it over every other thing that you want to do, because you can't do this alone. You need to build that team. With that team, you need to build alignment. You need to be able to delegate to the team.

And this is another thing: letting go for business owners, small business owners. I mean, for me to let go, I was almost blue in the face! It's tough, it is, because this is your... you're awake at night, you're thinking about this business. It's almost like a human being that is attached to you, that you're trying to groom, you're trying to grow. Despite everything everybody is saying to you, you're committed to it. Yes, you bring babies, you carry babies, you do everything to make this thing work.

Almost tempted to micromanage, but you do micromanage when you start. Now, the important thing is that you go on what I call a personal journey of knowing what your own strengths and weaknesses are, because you cannot multiply your one physical body in a million and one places. But more importantly, you must put in structure, systems, processes, standard operating procedures which tell people the how-to to do the things that need to be done in the business. You must be able to manage their performance, so you must have some kind of performance management system in place. If you don't know how to do it, you need to prioritize it and work with a consultant that knows how to do this.

Number one, what it will do for you is it will free you. When it frees you, you become a more strategic thinker, and you don't get stuck in operational things. So you're spending most of your time doing things that are seeing a clearer vision for the business and the potential the business has, and where it has the potential to go. So you have everybody else working at a very operational level. Yes, you like to pack the cakes, but please don't pack the cakes! Let somebody else pack the cakes. You go and look for market, you go look for business, you think of creative ways to sell those cakes, to market those cakes. That's more important.

You need to deploy technology. "Oh, I don't know how to..." You don't need to know! Just hire the people that know how to use it. You know, it's not a case of you knowing everything. As we said, you can't know everything. So you've got to understand that you need to bring in, as your business grows and if you want it to grow, you need to bring in subject matter experts—people who are good at finance, technology that allows you to pay for simple HR systems that can help you. Every little bump on the road is going to be a distraction. You collaborate with people who can support you, people who have expertise in technology, accounting. You know, let the man come in once a week to do your books, pay him. But make sure you get somebody who knows what they're doing, otherwise even you won't find your money!

So for us at Ruff 'n' Tumble, we deploy ERP systems that give us a single point of truth about the business. We can see all the different aspects of the business. We have dashboards that show us daily sales. We can see the sales by the minute, in fact—which location, which part of the country. You have to use technology, you can't get away from it.

You're going to take a risk. Everything is a risk. To invest in yourself is a risk. To invest in people is a risk. You will invest in people, and they will leave you. Yes, they will leave you! So get used to it, and don't get so emotional about your baby!

So know about regulatory laws, know the rules and regulations around taxation, know about withholding tax, know who you should be charging.

Right. And I think as you've grown your business, at different points in time you would have required access to financing. I mean, scaling requires a lot of money.

Trying to raise money for a children's clothing brand in the year 2000 was like drawing stone from blood... the banking system had not... no, not drawing stone from blood, but drawing blood from stone! At the time, it seemed like it was going to be an impossible task. And trying to get a loan from the bank that you're selling children's clothes, it's almost like the man wanted to ask me, "Did you smoke marijuana to come here today?" You know, and it's like, I know what I'm doing.

And I remember I met two banking officers who then said to me that they wanted my account. So I said, "Let's have a conversation." And they said, what did I want, to give me their account? You know, they were all canvassing for accounts at the time. I said, "This is what I want: I want to acquire a piece of collateral. I've saved 50% of the money; I need you to give me 50% of the money so that the next bank that asks me for collateral, I can fling it in their face and they can give me what it is that I want."

So they said, "Okay, oh, all right. Where are your accounts?"

You see, structure! If I didn't have detailed accounts, nobody's going to give you a loan, nobody. So I very happily brought it out.

"Okay, where are your assets?"

I said, "Is it not the asset I want to acquire?"

"Okay, you have all these machines in your factory. How much are they? Okay, take an inventory of the machines. Okay, you have all this fabric in your warehouse. Take an inventory of all the fabric."

Anyway, by the time they finished... How much was I asking for? 20 million Naira. But 20 million Naira in 2000, in the year 2000, was a lot of money. Yeah, was a lot of money. Six banks rejected me.
