Six banks! But with every single rejection, as far as I'm concerned, it was a redirection—that's the first thing. The second thing was, it was empowering me in the places where I had a gap. So in all the areas where I did not do the things correctly, or I was not aligned with what the bank wanted to see, I learned it, refined it, and showed up in another bank.

This time, I had a financial consultant who had gotten somebody from the bank that had stressed all the numbers, and then I focused on the branding, the strategic direction, and growth of the business, and the plan for the business over the next 5 years. And it was the fastest "yes" I ever got in my life! In fact, I had to sort of do a double take, but I got a "yes."

So it's a combination of being attentive, being obsessed with your own vision and the things you want to do, the people you surround yourself with, believing in you and trusting yourself to be disciplined enough to use that money for what it was meant for. And that's where a lot of people lose and get lost. It's not a lifestyle loan! It's a business loan that you're supposed to inject into your business to grow it, to generate wealth. You need to know how to make it, you need to know how to keep it, then you need to know how to grow it. So you have to hold it long enough to be able to grow it into wealth. It's not that you cannot do it; you can do it.

I think one of the most important ways to learn is learning from mistakes. We'd love to learn from some of the mistakes that you've made.

My biggest mistakes were always with people. I hired the wrong people. Sometimes it's also because there's a lot of pressure on you—you're running the business, the business is growing, you need people in the business to do things, you don't put systems in place to test for character, competence, and capacity. You need to test for those three things.

Now character is about your values. Your competencies are two: you are testing for technical competencies, and you're testing for soft skills. Your technical competencies are those things that you know how to do. But those technical competencies are useless unless you know how to communicate, unless you know how to get a team to align to work with you to be able to deliver an outcome. Learning to cooperate with all the different types of people that exist on your team, because you are one individual from a background that is different from the diverse people that are in your team. So how are they thinking? What's important to them? Understanding those things. And as a business leader, those are things that you have to learn; those are the kinds of things you have to prioritize. Get an HR company to help you with the hiring process, so that when you are tired, you are not looking at somebody just as "let him just come and help me because me, I'm tired." You are actually seeing that the person is the right fit.

Now capacity, which is the third C, is ability to do. There are people who can talk, and their CV... oh my god, if you hire based on CV, you're in trouble! You're in deep trouble. But to do, they cannot do. They cannot move this water from here to here; they can't do it. But they can talk! And sometimes you need those kind of people on your team—they've got ideas. So you have to identify if that's what they have, then put them with somebody who can then do it.

The second thing sometimes is that I didn't have the right systems. I didn't have clearly defined OKRs or KPIs or performance management systems, and those things are important.

Another question I would love to ask relates to change. When you think back to Ruff 'n' Tumble the brand then versus now, what have you intentionally changed, or what have you kept?

I had to first begin on myself and define who I wanted to be. Right in front of me, I see a lot of women... we are multifaceted human beings. We are sisters, we are mothers, we're wives, we're daughters, we're friends, we're mentors—we're so many things all wrapped in this beautiful one package of who we are. And sometimes society sends conflicting signals as to who society says we should be or who we ought to be.

And what I want to say to you today as a woman is: you define you. You define the boundaries, you define whatever it is, whoever it is, and however it is you want to show up anywhere through the different seasons of your life. Work on yourself, and don't be afraid to have money conversations. Because when a woman talks about money, she likes money too much. When a man talks about money, "Oh, he's super ambitious." I'm super ambitious! I want to own the skyscraper, I want to own the yacht. I don't own one before the tax people come after me, you know, but I want to own! I want to look in the mirror and say, "You did well, girl. Your life made a difference, it made an impact. You created wealth, you generated wealth—you generated wealth for communities to grow, not just for yourself."

You will always be afraid, but do it anyway. Your business will evolve. Don't become outdated, is basically what I'm trying to say to you. The whole world is going to evolve. The one thing that's constant is change, and if you don't have a growth mindset, you will be left behind and you will become obsolete. So, and that's why I'm saying you need to do a lot of work on yourself. You need to quiet the voice of "you're not good enough, you're not fine enough, your hair is this" to the voice of "you got this, girl, you can do this, girl," and reaffirming that to yourself all the time.

Yeah, so the things that have remained constant in the business are the values and principles that gave birth to the business when it started. And those values for me was I wanted to do something different. So we call them I-STEER. So it's Innovation: so we're constantly trying to do things differently. Then Service: we are all called to live a life of service. You're not just here by accident, so how are you going to use your gifts and your talents in the service of humanity, in the service of the world, in the service of people? Teamwork: as we said, you can't go alone, you got to do it, it's a strong value for us.

Integrity: a couple of weeks ago, a customer returned a pair of trousers that split. This is the second time that was going to happen to us. I don't know how we missed the research and development unit, but we recalled 400 pairs of trousers and gave the customers back their money. That's the values and principles by which we live at Ruff 'n' Tumble. Respect: Nigeria is such a diverse country. There's different cultures all working together in the same place. The way we show respect... Yoruba people are very respect-conscious, and some other tribes are not so respect-conscious. A regard for who you are, where you come from, and understanding that we may be different, but you know, at the end of the day, we're all human beings, you know. Cut us any which way, we all have organs—same, same, same, same, same! So we're all human, so this is important.

And this Spirit of Excellence: the spirit of excellence must permeate everything that you do. You owe it to the generations that are coming behind you to uphold a standard that makes us all proud to be Nigerians. Yeah, of course. Now we have e-commerce as well, so now we're in your face, in your bedrooms, in your living rooms, on your phones, and we're with you 24 hours.

What's your vision for small business in Africa, and based on that vision, what changes would you love to see?

My vision for Africa... let's ask another question: What is the potential of the African continent? We are so used to being programmed to believe that Africa is the Dark Continent. There's nothing dark about the African continent! The sun shines, it rains, it's a beautiful place, birds sing, beautiful blue oceans, sandy beaches, beautiful people, smart, intelligent people. There's a lot of opportunity in Africa, so much energy!

And energy, thank you. So when I look at the potential of Africa, I see potential in the youth. It's a youthful population. I see potential in the youth taking that energy, being curious, and adopting technology that helps us leapfrog all the mistakes that were made by everybody else. We can leapfrog, and it can help us in education, in the healthcare industry, in farming.

So I want to see an Africa that believes in itself, an Africa that is not waiting for a savior. So why don't we take what we have, begin first by appreciating it, loving it, celebrating it? But it's time to look at the potential that Africa has, and you are a representation of the potential that is Africa. So you have to build Africa. So that's the Africa I want to see: self-sufficient, good infrastructure, trading with each other. There's huge opportunities for investment in Africa, huge, you know.

So I believe in Africa, I believe in the potential of Africa, I believe in Nigeria, in the potential of Nigeria. Yes, I know there's a lot going on, but you know, the Great Book of Life in Job says that "that thing that I feared most happened to me." So what you fear will happen, but if you reframe it and restructure your thinking to see opportunities, I can bet you opportunities will start showing up for you, and that is a fact of life.

So that's what I want to see. I want to see the young people. We can already see that music... you're in a store in London, and they're playing Burna Boy or Wizkid or my favorite... what's his name? Asake! How did you know? Asake is the guy! Asake is the dude, you know. So I mean, they're all symbols of hope, they're all symbols of potential. So for me, they are symbols of an Africa that has so much potential. And I want you to focus on what is possible, and not focus on what is not possible. Focus on solutions, focus on service, focus on what you can offer, how you can help. That's the Africa I want to see.

So let's end it this way: One of the things about this series is we have people from all over Africa watching, especially small business owners who either are alumni of the Hustle Academy program or want to join the Hustle Academy program, or just generally people who are small business owners who are looking up to inspiring business leaders like yourself. Leave them with a nugget, just one thing that you think will inspire them.

So what I would say to you, wherever you are, whatever time it is that you see this, is that know that you are the potential that represents the potential of the African continent. Know that nobody's going to build this continent except you. So we all have to become obsessed with building the African continent. And I chose the word "obsessed" because it needs to become an obsession. We need to move from talking to doing.

It's not going to be easy, it's going to be hard. So get ready for hard, because the mistake is to think that as an entrepreneur it's easy, it's easier than a 9-to-5 job. No, it's not! It's not easy. But what's important is that you can do it. You have the potential, you have the capacity. Remain focused, be disciplined, be committed, be consistent, because sometimes people try a little and then drop off. Remain consistent.

I can't remember who it was was asked... I think it was the guy who runs... the Jamaican guy who runs, Usain Bolt. He said he practiced three years for a 10-second run. Can you even begin to fathom the amount of work that he must have done in 3 years to run for 10 seconds and win a gold medal? It takes that long. And what we have to do is commit the time, the energy, resources, the ideas, and the belief in ourselves, the trust in ourselves—because nobody can give those things, they have to come from within us, and we have to want to do it.

Thank you so very much, ladies and gentlemen. I give you Mrs. Adenike Ogunlesi.

Thank you. Thank you. Thank you so much. Thank you.

metadata.speaker: Aliko Dangote
metadata.title: Manufacturing, Industrial Conglomerate, Agriculture and Commodities

content:
Would you like to be President of Nigeria?

Some of us, we need to lead in terms of the trajectory of the growth in Africa through business, not through political leadership.

Are there good investment opportunities for non-Africans in Africa?

Well, there are good opportunities for everybody, you know, and I think that's protection also for everybody.

So the Arsenal team, is that a team that you would like to buy someday?

It is a team that, yes, you might like to buy, you know, someday.

Would you fix your tie, please?

Well, people wouldn't recognize me if my tie was fixed. Just leave it this way. All right.

I don't consider myself a journalist, and nobody else would consider myself a journalist. I began to take on the life of being an interviewer even though I have a day job running a private equity firm. How do you define leadership? What is it that makes somebody tick?

Aliko Dangote is widely known to be the wealthiest man in Africa. So is that a title you're proud to have, or is that one where you get so many people calling you for money, you wish you weren't the wealthiest man in Africa?

Well, first of all, thank you very much, David. It's great to be here, you know, and also seeing you today. Well, you know, when they call you... I mean, wealthiest person in Africa, you know, it comes with a lot of baggage. Of course, there are so many demands, yeah, and white people now come up with so many different, you know, demands. But it is good, because I'd like to give back to the society.

So right now, you are involved in many philanthropic endeavors in Africa and elsewhere. Let's go through some of them before we go to how you actually made all of this money. So recently, you had an event in New York, where we are now, with Mo Ibrahim, also a wealthy African businessperson, and Bill Gates, in which you provided a fair amount of money for the Africa Center in New York, in Harlem. What is the Africa Center, and why did you do that?

Well, we did... the Africa Center idea started... was, you know, Chelsea Clinton had, you know, Mo Ibrahim and my daughter, Halima. My daughter Halima joined them later, and we realized that, look, we need to set up this Africa Center. We need to make it a... you know, a reality, first of all, you know, for us to be able to project Africa in a better light, you know, bringing Africa to the rest of the world, you know, especially when you look at, you know, the fabric of every September, we have the United Nations General Assembly where the entire world converges in New York. And what we want to do is to tell the real narrative of Africa, and tell the rest of the world what Africa is all about. So this has now to do with policy, business, and culture, you know, because sometimes, you know, the... I mean, especially, you know, Americans, literally understand not much about Africa, you know. Somebody will say, "Okay, well, both you Africans, you know, what kind of language do you speak?" For example, in Africa, we speak about 2,000 different languages. That's a lot, that's a lot.

So right now, one of the big problems in Africa is health, and you've been very involved in trying to eradicate polio in Nigeria along with Bill Gates and his foundation. What is the progress that you've made today?

I think we've done quite a lot. The... you know, the progress has been very, very tremendous. In the last three years, we haven't really had any wild, you know, virus of polio, and hopefully, when we work hard between the next six months by April, we'll be certified to be a polio-free country, which means the entire African continent will be polio-free.

Now, one of the things you're doing in the philanthropic world is building a hospital in Nigeria. Why do you feel a need to build a new hospital?

I think we need to build a world-class hospital, because when you look at it, in Nigeria, we spend quite a lot of money where a lot of people go abroad for medical checkup, for medical operations. Then what we are trying to do is to give the hope to the population and say that, look, you don't need to travel abroad; we'll be able to treat you.

Now, for those who may not be familiar with Africa, Nigeria is the most populous country in Africa, is that right?

It is, and it's growing at a very large rate in terms of its population.

Is that now about 200 plus million people? So at the current rate, at some point, more people will be in Nigeria than in the United States?

Well, by 2050, we'll be at about 450 million population, and I'm sure we will be way ahead of the US. We'll be about number three after China, India, and then it'll be Nigeria in terms of... By 2050, we could be the third biggest country at the current population growth rate.

So does that make you nervous about whether Nigeria can house and feed all these people?

Uh, it doesn't really make me nervous. We have massive arable land, we have a lot of water, we have, you know, the right climate. So when you look at it, the major contributor to our GDP in Nigeria is agriculture. So I think we just need to tilt a bit and change from the normal oil, you know, reliant economy to agriculture and manufacturing.

So Nigeria is known as well for having large oil deposits. Is that the major contributor to the Nigerian economy? Is that the major source of wealth in Nigeria?

It's not the major source, but it is... it continues to be 90 percent of the foreign exchange, you know, that, you know, we have, and also 60 percent of the government's revenue is also coming from oil. But I think the government is doing quite a lot to try and diversify the economy by trying to structure their own taxes, because we need to make more money from the taxes. Tax generation in Nigeria is a bit low, so I think government is working very hard to make sure that, yes, they adjust all these.

Now, the wealthiest man in Africa and the wealthiest man in Nigeria, do you get pressure to run for political office yourself? Would you like to be President of Nigeria?

I think I'm doing a great job where I am right now, so I don't think I need to be in a political space. Some of us, we need to lead in terms of the trajectory of the growth in Africa through the business, not through the political leadership.

Let's talk about how you made this amount of money, which is by far the largest amount of money that any individual has in Africa. So, did you come from a wealthy family, or not a wealthy family?

I came from a wealthy family. My late great-grandfather in the 1940s was actually the richest in West Africa. My late grandfather was one of the wealthiest Nigerians. The family name is Dantata, that's from my maternal side. My father, too, you know, was fairly rich, you know, but he was both in business and also in politics. But you know, David, one thing that I'm very, very proud of is that I did not inherit any money from my father. I built everything from scratch.

Your father died when you were relatively young?

Yeah, he died when I was 8 years old.

So he didn't leave in his will a large amount of money for you?

Well, he left in the will, but, you know, I mean, whatever that I inherited from him, which means in assets, I gave that... went to charity since then.

Okay. So did you go to college in Nigeria?

No, I went to Egypt.

Egypt, all right. And what did you study?

Business.

All right. So you graduated at what age?

I graduated at about 20 years old.

All right. So you went back from Egypt to Nigeria?

Yes.

And then what, did you get a job? What did you do?

I started work with my uncle for a few months, and then I went to Lagos and now I started my own business, but just, you know, buying cement and selling. You know, it was just a very low-key business.

All right. So you're 20, 21 years old, you're buying cement, you're a trader.

You know, trading, yes. You're making sure that you're trading it, and I was trading at that time.

Now, cement is your main business, we'll talk about it in a moment, but why is cement such a big part of Africa's, you know, wealth?

Well, you know, the issue is that when you look at cement, cement is what builds infrastructure, and we have a lot of infrastructure deficit. In Nigeria alone, we have about 17,000 deficit of housing, and it is all over in, you know, Africa. So when we started cement in Nigeria, we realized that majority of it was actually imported, and that is why we went in there. We started, and it's a long story.

So you ultimately were trading cement, and then was it hard to get the money to keep that business going?

No, it wasn't really hard at that time. I was buying cement locally. We started importation in 1980, because I started business in '78. So by 1980, we started importing sugar, rice, you know, commodities generally, and then we stopped the cement business because the cement, I was actually doing local trading; it wasn't really import business. We started import of cement in 2000.

Okay, so you had a cement trading business. Somebody thought Lafarge maybe buying it, you decided not to sell because they wanted control, and yet you then decided to build your own cement manufacturing business, is that right?

Yes, I decided in 2003 to build my own cement factory. At that time, Nigeria was only producing about 1.8, 1.9 million tons, but we went ahead and started with 5 million tons of cement capacity.

So what year was that?  

This was 2000... and we started building end of 2003, and we finished in 2007.  

So now you're the largest cement manufacturer in Nigeria?  

Well, the largest cement manufacturer in Sub-Saharan Africa.  

So you're building a refinery in Nigeria. Why does Nigeria need another refinery?  

Well, you know, David, let me give you a little bit of history, you know. What we do as Dangote Group, we use businesses like... now, using our current businesses to build the future of the business. Like when we were in sugar, it was the sugar profits that we used in building the cement. Now with the cement, we're building so many things, you know: refinery, fertilizer, you know, petroleum products, and then we're doing also petrochemicals with the refinery. Your question is, okay, why are we building a refinery? When you look at the entire Sub-Saharan Africa, you know, we have only two working refineries: one is in Côte d'Ivoire, which has only 75,000 capacity; the other one is by Sasol in South Africa. But majority of all these countries, almost all the Sub-Saharan African countries, they don't have refining capacity. So all of them, they export the oil, but they import product. So we realized that majority of the foreign exchange spendings of Nigeria was to petroleum products inputs.  

So Nigeria is exporting its oil and then it has to buy refined oil products back, import it, right?

Yes.

And what you're doing is you're building one of the largest refineries in the world?  

It is the largest single-line in the world. It's 650,000 capacity, 650,000 barrels a day of refining capacity.  

So to do that, do you have to borrow some money, or where did the money come from to build that?  

Well, what we are doing right now, we are borrowing from the commercial banks, we're also borrowing some money from, you know, financial... some financial institutions like the African Development Bank, the development banks, financial development, you know, banks. We're borrowing from African Exim Bank.  

So many companies outside the United States would like to invest in Africa. Where do you recommend that they invest? In Nigeria, South Africa, Kenya? Obviously, you're probably partial to Nigeria, but are there good investment opportunities for non-Africans in Africa?  

Well, there are good opportunities for everybody, you know, and I think that's protection also for everybody. You know, as we speak today, you know, even for university, let me give you an example. In Nigeria, if I have a partnership with you that I'm investing, I don't even... I won't have what you call minimum taxation. But if the company is owned by myself alone as a Nigerian, an indigenous entity, we have a minimum taxation. So there's quite a lot in terms of inviting foreigners to come and invest in Africa. But countries that I can suggest for you to invest: one of them, of course, you know, Nigeria; Ghana is a very good place to invest; Côte d'Ivoire, you know; Kenya, Kenya is also a very good place to invest.  

Now, I first met you a number of years ago when I was raising my firm's African investment fund, and you invested in it. And today, the bloom seems to be off the rose in African private equity investing. It was very attractive to many people 4, 5, 6 years ago; today, it seems to be less attractive. Is that because the economies in Africa have gone down a bit, or what would you say is the reason?

Well, I think most of that reason has to do with, first of all, lack of understanding of what you invest. You know, I mean, look at the investment that we made. Would you... I think I can say that 90 percent of what we invested in were doing very well. So I think it is where you should invest. You... myself as an African, I cannot invest in every single sector, so I have to be very choosy where I invest. And, you know, there's a lot of, you know, wrong perception, you know. People read stories from newspapers and they believe what they are reading. But I think, you know, as we go along, you know, quite a lot of changes in most African countries try and change in terms of, you know, focus on the economy.

Now, you live principally in Lagos, is that right?

Yes.

And how many people are there in Lagos?  

In Lagos today, we have about 25 million—25 million people in terms of population. I know it's very...  

So getting around in Lagos, which I've tried to do, is not that easy. Well, getting around New York's not that easy either. But for example, when you get around, do you have like special police cars that take you around? How do you get around Lagos?  

Well, I get around in Lagos, yeah, sometimes I have, you know, police escort, but not all the time. Normally, weekend I drive myself.

You drive yourself?

Yes, I do.

Do people stare at you and say, "There's the wealthiest man in Africa driving himself"?  

They do, sometimes, when they recognize, you know, the person driving, yes.  

Do you go to a restaurant by yourself? Do people come up for selfies, or do they ask you for money?  

They don't really ask me for money, but even here, anytime when I go to places, you know, to either eat or to, you know, I get a lot of requests for selfies. Well, yes, you know, it's normal.  

Now, you have some outside interests. One of them, I think, you're interested in what we call in the United States soccer, but other people call football: so the Arsenal team. And is that a team that you would like to buy someday?

It is a team that, yes, you know, I would like to buy, you know, someday. What I keep saying today, we have twenty billion dollars' worth of projects, and I think that's really what I want to concentrate on, you know. I'm trying to finish building the company, and then after we finish, maybe sometime 2021, you know, we can...

You're not buying the team right now?

I'm not buying Arsenal right now. I'm buying Arsenal when I finish all this, all right, because I'm trying to take the company to the next level.

What are the attributes that you think you have brought to the table which make you successful?

I think the most important one, number one: if you are going into any business, you must understand the business A to Z. You must know that business.

Okay. So in terms of Africa itself generally, are you bullish on Africa's prospects as a place in which people can invest—private equity firms or industrial companies to invest?

I think I'm very, very bullish when it comes to Africa, and it is the main reason, David, today why we have twenty billion dollars that we invest in, you know, our group, which we'll finish by end of next year, first quarter of, you know, I mean in the next two years. That's in the next two years. I'm very, very bullish, you know, in Africa. We have done very, very well in, you know, Africa, and, you know, I can tell you, if we continue with what we are doing today, based on our own projections, we'll be able to be, you know, within the next five years, in the Fortune 500.

Now, from time to time on some television networks, I see advertisements for Dangote, yes sir, for your companies. Was that general brand building? Why do you advertise that, say, in the United States, the Dangote brand, because most of your businesses are not in the United States?

Well, you know, it's a brand building, and like what we have planned to do, we are not going to remain dominant only in Africa. You know, I also invest... why wouldn't I invest outside Africa? Because what we are doing right now, you know, we were investing, yes, mainly in Sub-Saharan Africa. But if you look at what we are building today, we have a company that has revenues of four billion dollars. In the next two years, we'll have a company that will have a revenue of thirty billion dollars. So with that, we'll have quite a lot of money. What we are trying to do is to use major part of that money and invest outside Africa, and maybe 40 percent of it to continue to invest in Africa, because we are invested very, very heavily now.  

So you're in your early 60s, you're 62 now?  

Well, that's pretty early 60s! So do you intend to keep doing this for 10 more years, 20 more years, 30 more years?  

Ah, let me not commit, but I think I will... I will maybe work for the next at least, you know, very active in the next 15.  

Let's suppose somebody's watching this and says, "I want to be like Mr. Dangote. I want to be a successful businessman in Africa." What are the attributes, or anywhere, what are the attributes that you think you have brought to the table which make you so successful? Is it intelligence, hard work, persistence, all of those things? What would you say are the most important attributes?  

I think the most important one, number one: if you are going into any business, you must understand the business A to Z. You must know that business. You shouldn't just want to invest because somebody now says, "Okay, you know, there's good money in cement," then you want to jump into cement. You have to understand the business in and out, and that's the difference with me: I know my business. You know, now you can wake me up anytime and ask me about fertilizer, ask me anything that we are doing. And the other one is really to work very hard, and you have to have the tenacity of continuing. You'll have some hiccups here and there, but you have to be... you have to be focused in terms of what you do.

You know, I've known you for a while, and I never seem to get you to yell or scream or... You seem very low-key, you know, use this technique of yelling and screaming at people, or just very low-key and even-keeled. So to what do you attribute that, or am I wrong?

I think, no, yeah, no, you're not wrong. That's my nature. I'm always... I'm very quiet and I'm very, very calm. I get upset sometimes when people try to be, you know, either to outsmart me, or I don't like people who will not tell me the truth. I always like people to look at me, too, you know, and tell me the truth.

So will you invest any in the United States?

We are going to start investing, you know, in the United States. Just after this project, we want to open a family office both in New York and in London. We already have an office in London which has been operating for the last 30 years, so we want to turn part of that, you know, as an office so that we can diversify the wealth, as you know, you know, I've discussed this one with you before, where, you know, sometimes in Africa you have issues of devaluation, you know, you know. So we want to really preserve some of the family's wealth.

Right now, sometimes wealthy people, they collect art, they collect cars, they collect other things. What, some of your wealth that you're not using for philanthropy, what do you do with it? Do you collect art, are you a collector of things, or...?  

I'm not really a collector of art, you know. Any time when I have excess money, I like to put more in terms of charity. I don't really have a very expensive lifestyle.  

And the great pleasure of your life is just building your company and then giving away extra money, that's your greatest pleasure in life, okay?  

Yes.

Well, it's a very good success story, and I know a lot of people wanted to hear how you've done it, and I guess you're saying it's hard work and persistence, a little luck maybe from time to time?

Definitely, luck must be there. You know, if there's no luck, you can't be able to make it, of course.

Well, thank you very much for coming today, and I appreciate your giving us your insights. Thank you.

Thank you so much, David.

metadata.speaker: Deola Sagoe
metadata.title: Fashion Design, Textile Innovation and Luxury Retail

content:
The legacy that I would like to leave behind is one who went back into a heritage, into our history, and made us to be recognized once again that we are indeed people who add value.

The fashion industry in Nigeria has come a long way since pre-colonial times. Fashion design has changed from being a trade for the uneducated young person who needed a skill to get by, to today where even the most accomplished academics are involved, all vying for the opportunity to showcase their talent on some of the world's most exclusive fashion destinations.

Our next guest is one who has managed to break the consistent boundaries that the fashion industry holds up, both locally and internationally: Mrs. Deola Sagoe. Deola Sagoe has entrepreneurship in her blood, coming from a prominent family in Nigeria—entrepreneurs and owners of the Odua Group. She studied Business Administration at the University of Miami and returned to Nigeria to get a Master's degree in Finance Management from the University of Lagos.

Deola's mother had been running a small tailoring house called Odua Creations and was known for producing meticulously embroidered traditional Nigerian menswear. In 1989, Deola joined her mother with a view of expanding the label's repertoire to encompass more contemporary designs for the ever-developing, cosmopolitan Nigerian society. The following year, Deola began designing under her own name.

My brand is called Deola, or rather the House of Deola. The House of Deola carries two labels at the moment that are very well-known: that is the Deola label, that used to be known as the Deola Sagoe label, which is the high-end luxury, the bespoke line; and we've got Clan.

Basically, what I've done or what I keep doing and will keep doing long into the future is to reach back into our heritage in terms of our fabrics and in terms of our crafts and our skills, and contemporize them, make them relevant in today's world, and in that way continue to sustain them well into the future.

It can be said that in pre-colonial times, the traditional Nigerian fashion industry was already well-developed. There were designers and producers who made royal clothing, who were members of the King's court. The trade was exclusively for the King's important members and himself—the haute couture category. Deola is a haute couture fashion designer from Ondo State, Nigeria. She is a fashion visionary with a unique approach to her craft that has endeared her to followers and critics all over the world. For the past 25 years, Deola has left a global footprint across the various continents.

I have seen myself foremost as a businesswoman who happens to be very creative—or should I say the other way around? I have seen myself as a creative who can actually not only survive, but actually make something huge out of what I do. So yes, I know that the constraints are there as a woman in terms of you're not taken seriously, and they're still looking for the man who's behind you, you know, stuff like that. But I do not concentrate on such things. I have no time; I cannot afford the luxury to keep thinking first, "Oh, I'm a woman," then... If I do that, I might as well say, "Oh, I'm a woman, I'm Black, I'm Nigerian," and then what happens? It paralyzes me! But I choose to look at the positive sides of things: that African women are very, very strong women.

Well, the vision for the House of Deola is to be the African brand of choice when it comes to luxury, when it comes to premium ready-to-wear, when it comes to any products that can be or needs be traced back to Africa.

Well, the Nigerian fashion industry has grown in leaps and bounds. The awareness is there; it's all over Nigeria. And it's obvious—just go on social media, go on Instagram, and you'll see that a lot more people are getting into fashion in many different ways.

There are those people who consume fashion, and I think that for every African—it's not just Nigerians, Africans—fashion is intrinsically woven into our culture. So we love to be fashionable, we love to look good, and we love to wear the best. Even the Maasai tribesmen, even though most of what they wear is beads and the rest of their bodies are mostly left uncovered, but you can see that sense of fashion—they love fashion.

So coming back to Nigeria and to this day, as I said, you have the consumers of fashion, you have the suppliers of fashion—those are the tailors, the fashion designers, the people who sell fashion as well, you know, the retailers. So we have all that. But unfortunately, we do not have structure yet.

The challenges range from not having a structure through to a serious issue with infrastructure. You know, and of course, embedded in the problem with structure that we have is the fact that distribution is a big problem. However, when you talk in terms of we are aware of what is going on about fashion, we're very much aware, even sometimes more than our counterparts in Europe and in the Americas.

Using hand-woven materials which she brings to life in a range of distinct cultures, contemporizing almost lost traditional African techniques, Deola's designs present a unique vision and attitude for the well-rounded modern woman.

Deola uniquely showcases contemporary fashion utilizing authentic African fabrics of antiquity, bringing together contemporary and traditional in a unique and fresh way. Deola is well known for uncanny attention to detail, her expert handling of a diverse range of fabrics, as well as her exemplary understanding of the African woman's body. Amongst her many innovations is Komole, her own authentic answer to every African's yearning: the original interpretation and crafting of lace.

The creation of Komole... for the first time in Africa, we've been able to come up with a fabric that is our beloved lace, but is made from our own African authentic fabric, which in many parts of Africa, like Nigeria, Ghana, Ethiopia, even Madagascar, there is a lot of weaving that goes on on ancient looms. So it's a great breakthrough for us to be the first to actually make this fabric out of our own hand-woven fabric.

Young fashion designers need to know exactly what they want. Do they want the drama behind just being recognized as a fashion designer, as a celebrity, or are they looking out to actually make a business of it? Of course, if they want it to be sustainable well into the future, they would say, "Well, I love to design, but I can't starve. I've got a nation or nations to prove, and even if I am going to clothe them beautifully and creatively, I still need to make money." Because at the end of the day, the bottom line is that you're able to not just survive, but to actually make it work, make profits from it. At the end of the day, it's a business, it's not a show.

Deola Sagoe has gained international notoriety for her lively and colorful designs. Her fashion design credentials took a huge leap forward when she won the M-Net AngloGold African Design Award. She's been nominated by the legendary US Vogue editor André Leon Talley as one of the four designers from Africa to show their work at the New York Fashion Week in 2000. She later on went to be the first Nigerian who had her own stand-alone show at the New York Fashion Week in September 2014. Deola became the first Black woman to present a collection at Alta Roma, Rome's celebrated Fashion Week back in 2004. Her globally appealing style has earned her an enviable clientele that ranges from Africa's First Ladies to society ladies like Lydia Hearst, top model Alek Wek, and famous personalities such as Oprah Winfrey and Will Smith.

My life revolves mostly around the brand. I find that most days, it's always from home to work, and then back home. And I think that it's chiefly because I enjoy what I do so much that it is not a chore; it's not something that I wake up to each morning not wanting to do. It's become a part of me, but I do realize that I have to have time for leisure.

Well, as a designer, it's all about, "My goodness, she's outdone herself this time! What is she going to do next time?" Most of the time with every collection—and I would say especially with the Komole collection—it's been, "You've outdone yourself! I don't know what else you're going to do for the next 20 years, you don't have to design a thing!" But it's good pressure for me, and I like it because it keeps driving me to do more, to keep on being the best that I can be. And in that way, I get even much more innovative. There's still so much that is in the pipeline that has not come into manifestation yet.

She was appointed to represent Nigeria in an international campaign organized by the United Nations World Food Programme. The campaign, titled "Catwalk the World: Fashion for Food," began in Nigeria in April 2006 and recently staged an event in Ghana which brought celebrities like Damon Dash, his wife designer Rachel Roy, and Ghanaian-born, London-based designer Ozwald Boateng. The campaign's goal is to raise money towards halving the number of hungry people in the world, particularly children, by 2015.  

Sagoe frequently exhibits her couture collection at Cape Town Fashion Week, and she continues to lead the way in carving a space for Nigeria on the global fashion map.  

Deola's story is that of an iconic woman who has over the years put Nigeria's fashion industry on the world's global map—a feat she achieved against all odds.

Success to me means being able to impact upon the lives of other people in such a way that it's a win-win.

metadata.speaker: Kenneth Ize
metadata.title: Fashion Design, Textile Preservation, Artisanal Craft and Global Luxury Retail

content:
Welcome back to The Morning Show here on Arise News. There is a strong belief that in exploring and nurturing existing cultures, one opens up an exciting territory for creating and inspiring future cultures. Joining us today is fashion designer Kenneth Ize, who believes strongly in this idea.

Welcome to The Morning Show, Kenneth.

Straight off the runway of Arise Fashion Week 2018. Now, can we just say your collection was absolutely amazing! It really did stand out, and your vibe is really about heritage and Nigeria and Africa. Why did you decide to take this approach?

I believe that there are so many things that have been done, and in my own country and my own continent being developed now, I think it's just something to focus on. Reinterpreting cultures and identity matters a lot, because this is who we are and this is what I understand.

What do you see when foreign designers use African fabric? Do you feel it's flattery, should we be excited, or do you think it's cultural appropriation?

Honestly speaking, I think I only think more about my work. So I try not to... because it's work, so I know where I'm going to. So I try to then do it the way I would want to do it.

They like to use our fabric and prints and things like that, and then mark up the price. And then when a Nigerian decides to put a price, the equivalent becomes a problem. Do you think that's due to the "abroad syndrome"?

No, because I feel like fashion itself is not... Fashion is a business, right? So there's a way people should go about it. Education is very important. As a fashion designer, I feel like that will actually make you understand the work ethic on how to grow a brand, I would say.

In terms of like... there's a pattern cutter, there's a tailor, there's a showroom also. So before... during the process of making a collection, there is so much that is needed to be done. So it's not just like, "Oh yeah, I'm going to my tailor and making this, and that's just it." So there's a process, actually.

What's the process like to make a scarf like this?

Okay, so I'm going to tell you my overall process before I actually ended up at this state. This is like starting... So I researched a lot. I research a lot, I travel a lot, I start getting involved. I look at people. I'm very curious about things, so I'll just walk up to someone and ask them questions: "Okay, so how do you get this?"

So that was my research for about three years, and I failed a lot of times. But there was a time where I had to then revisit my research from day one, and then go back to it. So it's a journey; it didn't just start now.

Now, the fashion industry, like everyone knows, is a multi-billion dollar industry, but it's almost like Nigerians haven't really keyed into it. They haven't really harnessed the full potential of the industry. What would you say is missing, or do you see areas designers can do better?

High-quality check production could be done better here. Understanding that everyone is not a designer—we have to understand that also. It's about understanding the process of design, that's very important, like I said before. And knowing where something is coming from, not just making something, you know? You have to be realistic in anything you do.

So I believe that designers that are good then intend to work this way, because they think about the future and they think about the present time now. So it's not just like, "Oh yeah, I'm only designing for this Nigerian market." I don't want to design for just one market—I want my clothes to be seen around the world. I want it to be worn by a lot of people.

And it's not just about me being selfish, but it's also about promoting my own culture and my own country. When I started making these scarves, it was so sad because a lady in Paris told me, "Oh yeah, you're from Nigeria? Wow, like Boko Haram, for example."

Then I said, "You know what? This is exactly why I'm coming to your country, to Paris, to show you my work—something that could make you happy. So I'm making this fabric, I'm telling a different story entirely, completely different about what people know about Nigeria."

And she was quite amazed. I said, "Yeah, this is why I want to show you the things we could do." And it's a developing country. I feel like we need so many things as well, definitely in terms of production skills, people skills.

The weavers making this fabric, they have no formal education. They have no idea... After she's done with this fabric, I don't think she's going to pass it on to the next person, because there's nobody to hold it back, to own this treasure. So it's not anymore. And I feel like... she has a job to offer people, only if people knew there was a job there. So I feel like a lot of people don't know there are actually jobs that this could provide.

It's so unique, and that's the beauty. What you were saying about the Parisian lady that was talking about Boko Haram, when you're now changing the conversation to your print and what you're doing with the fabric in your collection, your designs obviously tell another story about Nigeria. So whenever she wants to have a conversation again about Nigeria, she's more likely to discuss Kenneth Ize.

Now, that brings us to the Arise Fashion Week that recently concluded. How important are fashion shows like that to the fashion industry here in Nigeria?

Arise is very professional. I would say it's so far my best show I've had in my career. It's very exciting to just work with so many experts in the industry to actually understand, you know... Making a collection took me about four to five months. I've cried in those nights, you know. I've gone through a lot during this process, being down on the street trying to get my work done, but nobody knows about this thing. So it's just that five to ten minutes that you have the time and the chance to show your work, and working with people that understand it makes so much more sense.

Will we be expecting to see more showcases, or was this a one-off for this Arise Fashion Week collection?

I don't know. To me, design is about feeling, and it's just like what I'm feeling right now, I just would love to share it more. I want people to look sexy, you know. I want people to look very rich. I'm into a Black man looking super, super rich—I'm into that a lot! Because this thing you're wearing, it's really not super expensive, but at the same time, the idea and where it's coming from makes it a luxury.

I would love to see a lot of people just wearing my clothes, and it's money, you know? It's fresh, it's swag.

Will there be stores across the country?

Right now, we stock in Vienna, in a store called Park Vienna, and we stock in Switzerland in a shop called Cabinet Zurich. Yeah, just those stores for now.

Do you see yourself training upcoming designers, skills you may want to pass on? Do you see that as something you will take on?

Definitely, definitely. Two years ago, I used to have an assistant that graduated from UNILAG, and at that point, finished UNILAG with nothing else to do. That really touched me a lot, because at the end of the day, I have had chances because I've gone to school abroad. Probably this person doesn't know the next step to take.

Then I told her, "Okay, this is Nigeria right now, why don't you be a tour guide, for example?" Because I have lots of friends I would like to visit, but Nigeria is not like a tourist place; they don't intend to actually come unless they have someone on board that could take them around.

So, long story short, I'm always into helping younger people. It's not just even with my qualification; my job is about my ideas that I can give.

How do you rock these scarves? And tell me your social media platforms where people can reach you.

Yeah, it's @kennethize on Instagram. It's K-E-N-N-E-T-H I-Z-E.

That's amazing. Thank you so much for joining us!

Thank you so much! Thank you.

Well, that brings us to the end of The Morning Show today. Thank you so much for watching. Enjoy the rest of your day. Goodbye!

metadata.speaker: Iyinoluwa E. Aboyeji
metadata.title: Technology, FinTech, Venture Capital and Talent Acceleration

content:
Hey guys, so I was thinking this morning that one of my favorite things on Founders Connect now is I have the opportunity to actually have a sit down with people that I really admire. I'm just like, oh my god, is this my life now? Anyway, on today's episode, we're going to be having a conversation and interview with famous E. I'm just going to learn all about his journey from Andela to Flutterwave to Future Africa, and all the many, many companies that he's a board of director or non-executive director at.

So hey guys, this is Iyin.

Hi, it's good to have you here.

Thank you very much for having me, I'm so excited.

Thanks for stopping to watch this video. My name is Peace Itimi and I'm very passionate about growing people and growing businesses. On this channel, I create videos on marketing, branding, business, and life. Sometimes I share my life lessons, like on this series where I interview leading African entrepreneurs. If this is your first time on this channel, thank you so much for being here! Make sure you click on the subscribe button down below, and the bell notification button so every time I release a new video, you'll be one of the first people to know. And if this is not your first time, you know how I feel about you—I really love you, thank you so much for being here. Now let's get right into the video.

Welcome to my YouTube channel! I am Peace Itimi—a changemaker, professional, and creative who is passionate about growing people and growing businesses. Like, comment, subscribe to my channel, and please always share my videos. It promises to always be impactful and insightful.

So, first question right: beyond entrepreneurship and venture capital, who are you? Like what three phrases most accurately describe who you are?

Huh, that's a great question. Before entrepreneurship, beyond entrepreneurship and venture capital, I think of myself as a changemaker, right? Somebody who really loves to inspire change. I'm an optimist—I really do believe in working towards a better future for myself and for my country. And then I would say I'm a Christian.

So he's a changemaker, an optimist, and a Christian.

Yeah, I wish I could squeeze Nigerian in there somewhere... I don't know, can I?

Awesome! What was growing up like for you?

Well, that's a great question. I grew up in Lagos, I was born in Lagos actually, in Yaba, and I grew up in the Yaba community area. When I was growing up, my father had just finished his MBA at the University of Lagos and he was looking to get a job. And so it was somewhat a tumultuous childhood, not too bad, but I had to go stay with my grandmother, my mom's mother. I remember very fondly we used to hawk wara.

Hawking wara?

Yeah, very fondly! And then when my father got a job first at Mobil and then Shell, he came back to Lagos and then we started a typical middle-class upbringing in the '90s. I went to primary school at St. Saviour's in Ebute Metta. And then when I was in Primary 4, my parents had to move to Warri, so I spent a bit of my childhood in Warri where my father was working community relations for Shell, trying to manage hostage-taking and stuff like that.

So I grew up a little bit in Warri, and then I went to boarding school at Loyola Jesuit College in Abuja—still the best secondary school! I mean, I'm sorry, it's not about bragging, the record speaks for itself. So I went to boarding school, made a lot of great friends till this day at Loyola, and the education was excellent—Jesuit education full of values.

So that was really my path all the way up to that point. I think for me, I always had a strange kind of ambition growing up, because I wasn't one of those kids who was like, "Oh, I'm going to be an entrepreneur from day one." I didn't think that. I oscillated a little bit; I was good at a lot of things, whatever I wanted to be good at. That made my life very difficult because it was like: do science, do arts, do this...

When I started out seeing my father, he was a cab driver, so I would follow him. I'd be in the front seat—people were nicer about that then, like "today is school day, why is your child in your front seat?" But people were nice. So I would sit with him in the front while he picked people up and dropped people off doing kabu-kabu. My mother used to sell fish, so I also watched her do some entrepreneurship. Education was one of those things where we did it to survive, so I never really thought about business as a career path, because I thought business people were poor!

So I thought I would go and be an engineer or a doctor or something like that, until I got into secondary school SS1 where you have to pick your subjects. My parents really, really wanted me to study science. I said, "Let me give it a try," but with chemistry and physics, there was nothing for me there! So I remember my mother flew all the way to Abuja like, "How did you change your subjects without telling us?" I said, "See ma, literature, English, and government—that's my thing, that's how I like it."

So I switched over. When I went to Canada, I went to the University of Waterloo. I spent a year in Ibadan, which was very formative for me because I learned how to fend for myself in the outside world. I spent some time at UI, and some time at a school called Lead City, one of those A-level schools. And then we left for Canada in January.

The whole family?

No, just myself and my brother. Actually, you know the funny story about that? This honestly is one of the things that defined my time in Canada. My father was only going to send my brother because my brother studied science. He was like, "It's a waste of money for you to study arts, what's my business?" So my father was like, "I don't want to spend the money," but being a Nigerian parent, he couldn't resist a good deal! They told him, "If you send two people, we'll give you a 25% discount." He sort of did the math and was like, "25% off is something!" So he said, "Okay, if I'm only paying half fees for this one, let his brother follow him so it won't be as if I was wicked."

But I always imagined that one day my father would just call me and be like, "Don't waste my money, just pack your bags." So you know what I did? The first semester in Canada, I went to this prep school called Columbia International College. First semester, I took ten courses—ten! I was like, I must enter university with scholarships! You're supposed to be there for one year before you go to university. I got there in January; my fear was if I stayed till next January, my father would pull the plug in September. So I just took all ten courses, and I got into school in September with a partial scholarship.

I went to Waterloo, and one of the good things about Waterloo is they have cooperative education (co-op). So out of four years, you have to have two and a half years of work experience to graduate. So I worked—I actually went to New York and worked for my school fees. It didn't come easy; I had to work for it.

After doing legal studies, how did you find tech?

That's an interesting story. I have a very close friend, his name is Pierre. The way we met was very random: I walked into the first day of school, I couldn't afford to live on campus because it was too expensive, so I lived off-campus. I was with all the other people for orientation, and this guy with long hair walks up to me and says, "Hey, my name is Pierre." I'm like, "Yeah, my name is E." He's like, "Yeah, my accommodation on campus isn't ready, can I stay at yours tonight?"

Just straight asking for a place to stay! But I was like, "I need friends, so okay, come inside the house." We became very close friends from that day.

What happened was, because of co-op, we lost touch. He went off to co-op in Silicon Valley, and I went to the UN in New York for an NGO. So we lost touch. I was running the school newspaper, and I was coming out of the student life center basement office, went to get my pizza and Coke, and I saw Pierre coding on his computer.

I said, "Guy, what's up? What are you up to?" He said, "I went to work for this guy called Peter Thiel, he's a member of the PayPal Mafia." He started telling me all these stories, romanticizing things: "I used to sleep under the desk, San Francisco is a beautiful city, working for Peter Thiel..."

I got roped into this thing, and he kept pulling me. Two things happened on campus around 2010 that were defining: The Social Network movie came out, and there was this wave of entrepreneurship from Y Combinator that had just started. A number of founders were starting to get real attention. The most famous founders from Waterloo were all dropouts—like Mike Lazaridis who built the BlackBerry, he never finished.

So the school, being very smart, said, "If we allow this, everyone will drop out. Let's create a lab for people in residence." So they created a new residence. Pierre was living in that residence with a lot of very interesting people: Vitalik (founder of Ethereum), Ted Livingston (founder of Kik), Eric Migicovsky (founder of Pebble). Today I look at these guys like, "Billionaires!" But then we were together eating pizza without money.

So that was the circle the school brought together. I went with Pierre to found a startup. That was how we started our first company. I got the seed capital from the former Ologbotsere of Warri—I just went to visit and collected money! I took the money, used it for my startup called 1000ml (or The Network).

How long did you spend on it?

Three years. It was easy because we were in school, but the day I got involved in that startup, I stopped going to classes and spent all my time on it. One of the companies, Kik, backed by Fred Wilson, became super big. The founder sold secondary shares, made maybe $2-$3 million, and took $1 million of his money and gave it to the school to set up Velocity! That's literally how the school started funding velocity labs. Without that $1 million, none of us would be here.

What ended up happening with our product? We had eight co-founders—we were inexperienced, immature, and the product didn't make sense. We tried to build an LMS to replace Blackboard. Blackboard was $500,000, and schools give tenders. Why would they give a tender to students still in school? So that failed.

Then, as sharp guys, we started downloading past question papers from the Chinese Students Association and charged people to access them. We made small money, but Waterloo is a research school, and professors reuse their exam questions. When students started paying us for past questions, professors said, "Wait, these questions are my IP, you're using them without permission and making money!" They threatened to sue us and expel me!

So I went to meet the professors, begged them, and asked, "What can I do to help you?" A professor said he wanted to teach his courses outside the university online, but there was no Udemy then. He asked if we could build websites for that. So we built that for him and sold the technology to Professor Andrew. We didn't make money; we just paid off debt, and I came back to Nigeria straight.

When I was coming back to Nigeria, I had ideas. I had two options: stay in Canada and get a job, or come back to Nigeria. Canada was too cold for my mental health! I couldn't find a job in America or Canada, so I looked at home and said, "There's no money there, let me look for money as I'm coming back."

My co-founders and I built Fora. The big idea was: Covenant University has a professor in AI, Babcock has a professor in psychology. Babcock doesn't offer AI because they lack a professor, Covenant doesn't offer psychology. What if students could watch lectures from other universities and get cross-credits?

When I landed in Nigeria, I landed in Abuja—big mistake! I went to the NUC (National Universities Commission) to get permission for credit exchanges. I went every day for 4-5 weeks, sitting outside waiting for the official. One day he saw me and said, "I'm tired of seeing you. What you want to do, I don't agree. That's it."

So I carried my bag and went to Warri. My parents were like, "This startup thing didn't work, come and do an LNG or Shell interview." But I wasn't cut out for oil and gas. I missed the interview, my father was angry. I told them, "God said I should go to Lagos, and God will provide!" I used my remaining N40,000 as a seed on the altar, begged my mother for bus fare to Lagos, and stayed with my uncle.

We tweaked the idea for Fora. Since NUC blocked credit exchanges, we targeted online MBAs—selling online MBA programs from University of Liverpool and Walden University. We helped executives apply, do paperwork, get bank loans, and pay from their salaries. We made 20% commissions. It was hustle work, but it kept us afloat.

When I wanted to raise money again, I reached out to a Canadian VC who offered $50,000, but I had to come to New York for a program. I went to New York, met my team (who I hadn't seen in 3 years), and we won the pitch competition!

An older gentleman, Lee Rubinstein, connected me to Jeremy Johnson. Jeremy had previously co-founded 2U, which did online degree enablement. I badgered him for a meeting. He invited me to his office in New York at 9:00 AM. I took a 12-hour $100 Greyhound bus overnight from Toronto to New York, arrived at 8:00 AM, bought him coffee, and we had a great discussion.

Later, when we met again, I explained how Fora's model was struggling with regulatory friction. Jeremy broke it down for me: "Online MBAs in Africa can't scale easily at high price points. But Africans have the grit to work. Instead of credentials, what if we train them in software engineering skills for free, and connect them to global tech jobs where they earn money?"

I said, "Do you want to try this in Nigeria?" He said, "I'll back you if you run it."

I called my team: "Look, I've been suffering, let's try this!" Coding was where the money was, and that's how Andela was born out of Fora.

I carried my Fora investors over to Andela at a $5 million valuation so they wouldn't lose their money. That built immense trust with my investors.

We started Andela in 2014. At first, it was extremely hard. We moved offices six times in the first year! Myself, Nad, Iyin, Christina, and Bangkoli all lived in one 3-bedroom apartment in Palm Grove. Every morning, we'd take a bus from Palmgrove to Yaba, then to Golden Gate in Ikoyi where Mrs. Adelaiye gave us her BQ to use.

When she got full-time tenants, we got scammed by a fake landlord who took our rent money to fund his wedding! Then we squatted at CC Hub for a while. We did digital marketing on the streets—handing out flyers at churches, mosques, and bus stops: "Come for free coding training!"

That's how we grew the program. When Jeremy and Christina saw the first class—people going from earning N40,000 a month (or nothing) to gaining skills and landing remote engineering jobs paying $2,000-$3,000 a month—it was incredible. Jeremy came on as CEO, and I served as co-founder and Director of Recruitment, driving talent sourcing and evangelism.

I stayed at Andela for two and a half years, from 2014 to May 2016.

Why did you leave Andela after all that hustle?

It boiled down to two things: First, the company grew very fast. Because it grew so fast, there were things I didn't understand about managing a company at that scale. Success is a much better teacher than failure, but I had never worked at a scaled startup before. I felt I needed to go to business school to learn management frameworks. I applied and got accepted into two business schools.

Second, around that same time, I met the founding team of Flutterwave—GB (Olugbenga Agboola) and others. The problem they were solving was massive: payments in Africa were completely broken. Even at Andela, we struggled to process payments locally.

So instead of business school, I applied to Y Combinator with the Flutterwave team. I said, "If YC accepts Flutterwave, I'll forgo business school and build Flutterwave." YC accepted us!

I became founding CEO of Flutterwave because I had more startup experience in the African terrain. My job was handling regulatory approvals, pitch narrative, banking partnerships, and government relations. I was flying every week between Lagos, San Francisco, and Abuja—educating bank CEOs and regulators about digital payment rails.

What lessons from Andela did you bring to Flutterwave?

The biggest lesson was that mission is everything. Everyone underestimates the power of a company mission. Andela was world-class at defining mission—you knew why your work mattered. At Flutterwave, our mission was connecting Africa to the global economy through payments. That mission made prioritization clear and helped us attract world-class talent and investment.

Why did you eventually leave Flutterwave?

Flutterwave was GB's vision and company—I came in to help get it off the ground, build early momentum, structure the team, and establish regulatory trust. Once the foundation was rock-solid, it was time to hand over total executive leadership to GB.

Additionally, I had just gotten married and had a child. I was on back-to-back long-haul flights every single week. I wanted to spend time with my newborn child and take paternity leave. So in 2018, I stepped down as CEO.

Both Andela and Flutterwave became tech unicorns. What makes you most proud about them?

It's the ripple effects and the people. The companies themselves are just vehicles. What makes me proud is seeing engineers who earned N40,000 now leading engineering teams globally, or small African businesses accepting payments from anywhere in the world. They proved that world-class technology companies can be built from Africa.

How did Future Africa start?

After taking time off, I moved to Silicon Valley, intending to angel invest. But I faced two major frustrations: First, Silicon Valley investors wanted me to scout deals for them, but weren't willing to back an African-led fund investing directly in African founders on the ground. Second, I experienced casual racism and banking friction despite having legitimate exit proceeds.

Then COVID-19 happened, and I moved back to Nigeria permanently. My co-founders and I started writing online articles about African tech, and when we surveyed our readers on what they needed most, the overwhelming answer was: "Capital!"

Founders were struggling to raise $25,000 or $50,000 pre-seed rounds. So we built Future Africa as a syndicate platform using AngelList. I wrote detailed investment memos on promising African startups and shared them with global investors.

We grew from zero to hundreds of syndicate members funding dozens of African startups at the earliest stages. Future Africa evolved into an asset management firm and venture studio that doesn't just write checks, but actively helps early-stage founders with talent hiring, regulatory navigation, marketing, and go-to-market execution.

What is the biggest lesson you've learned over your journey?

My biggest lesson is that the biggest challenges are actually the biggest opportunities. The moment you put on glasses that view infrastructural friction, lack of systems, or market gaps as business opportunities, the entire world looks different. In a country like Nigeria, everywhere you turn there are problems—and every single problem is a multi-million dollar business waiting to be built.

What is your advice for young Africans thinking about leaving the country ("japa")?

Go get global experience if you can! See how world-class systems operate, build skills, and learn best practices. But ultimately realize that Africa is the frontier where you can make the greatest impact and build true legacy. You can't build the next Flutterwave or Andela in markets that are already saturated and mature. Greatness is built on the frontier.

Thank you so much, Iyin, for sharing your story!

Thank you for having me!
