So I can hear my thoughts. I can hear the silent one's voice more clearly because there are no interruptions and I often come back so refreshed. One time I came back and my husband says he felt like locking me up in a room just so that he could just keep enjoying the way I looked after coming back from that experience because like Jesus Christ it's quite an experience. It's quite an experience. If you spend five days by yourself, not talking to any human and just spend time in prayer and in silence, you'll be surprised the kind of ideas, the kind of thoughts, the kind of strongholds that fought as a result. So those are some of the routines that I have cultivated. So that is the secret behind the glue. That's a good place to end. I like that. Thank you so much, TMD. Really grateful for making our time for this. Thank you. Oh, thank you. I thoroughly enjoyed.

metadata.speaker: Fred Swaniker
metadata.title: Education, Leadership Development, Human Capital and Tech Talent Acceleration

content:
Wow, I think I need to pinch myself, because I never imagined that we would be here today, ten years into the journey of establishing the African Leadership Academy.

I stand before you here today as a mere servant of a vision that is bigger than any one of us, and as a servant of a journey that many of us have been on through thick and thin for the last decade. We're celebrating today not just ten years of ALA's journey, but really we're here to celebrate the very future of our continent. And I'm overjoyed with the tremendous belief that all of you are showing by coming from all over the world to be with us today.

Now, before we get started, I think I need to clarify something: ALA has been in operation for ten full years, and that's what we're celebrating today. We have admitted 10 classes and we've trained almost a thousand young leaders. However, if we want to be completely accurate, the journey of establishing ALA actually started 14 years ago when Chris and I graduated from Stanford. We began working on this in 2004, so it's actually 14 years since the whole project started.

Today, I want to share with you three stories about this journey that we've been on—just three stories.

The first story is about Opportunity.

In 2008, I was invited to give a keynote address at Harvard Business School's Africa Business Conference. At the end of this conference, I announced that we were selecting the first class to join us at the African Leadership Academy. At the end of the conference, there was a closing party—an invitation-only event for speakers and special guests. In the middle of the event, this young, scrawny white man came up to me, and he was shaking as he was talking to me. He introduced himself; he said his name was Eric Ljungstrom, and he was with an organization called Educate!. He had traveled all the way from New York to see me because he heard I was going to be at this conference. He didn't have an invitation, but he had someone sneak him in because he wanted to tell me about a young man called Joseph Munyambanza.

He told me this young man was a refugee from the Congo living in a refugee camp in Uganda, and he had built an amazing organization in his refugee camp to help educate other young people, providing healthcare services and all these things. He said, "We have to admit this guy; he's applied to your first class." So I said, "Okay, fine," and I took his name.

I then went back home and looked through our admissions files, and unfortunately, this young man was set to be rejected because his grades were not good enough. But then I thought further: if this person had so inspired someone to come and sneak into a party to tell me about him, there must be something special about this kid.

And so we admitted him. Today, ten years on, Joseph Munyambanza is serving on the UN Secretary-General's Advisory Council for Youth. He has expanded his organization, built schools in his refugee camp, trained thousands of young people, and he recently told me that he was working on a project with the Minister of Education from the Congo to get a million young children back into school in the DRC. On WhatsApp, he is in contact with Nobel Prize winners like Malala Yousafzai.

I tell you this story because it illustrates three things:
First, it illustrates what happens when you give young people with talent and depth an opportunity. This is really what we do at ALA: we find young people with potential, give them opportunities to develop, and then plug them into powerful networks so that they can take their impact and expand it at a much larger scale.

Second, it's a powerful reminder to me about just how much talent there is on this continent that unfortunately doesn't get these opportunities. I believe that talent is evenly distributed throughout the world, but opportunity is not. It is our job to try and find young people and give them that opportunity.

Third, the story reminds me of just how far we've come as ALA as an institution—from a refugee camp to advising the UN Secretary-General, being on a first-name basis with Nobel Prize winners, running his own organization, and sponsoring young people to go to school and get opportunities like he had, all in just 10 years. This to me is a real sign of the progress that we have made as an institution.

The second story I'd like to tell is about Faith.

You may have heard earlier today about how things got so bad in the early days financially that we were constantly running out of money. When I graduated from Stanford Business School, I had to come up with $120,000 to pay back McKinsey, and I had to borrow money from my mother. In those days, I had no salary, so for two years what I would do was schedule a meeting at breakfast, one at lunch, and one at dinner. Because I was a poor, starving entrepreneur, the people who took me out would typically cover the bill!

The other people on the team had also not been paid. I remember one particular day when I was in New York and I took a train from New York to New Jersey to go and see a donor to ask them for money. As it would have it, I didn't get the money that day. Unfortunately, I was so broke that I didn't even have money to get the train back to New York! Here I was in New Jersey, looking at the skyscrapers on the other side of the river, remembering how my classmates from Stanford Business School were all sitting in those skyscrapers earning hundreds of thousands of dollars, and I didn't have train fare to get back to the other side.

Things got so bad that the founders called a meeting and said, "We're going to shut down this project. Everyone has to go home, the team has to get other jobs." We agreed that in two months, everything would stop if we didn't get any support.

A month later, we were looking for sites that could potentially be the campus for the Academy. We went to a building in the Cradle of Humankind where there was a conference center, and we asked to rent it. They said, "We don't have space here, but why don't you go next door? There's a property that maybe you can use."

So we went next door, and we said, "Why did they send us here? This is just a farm, there's nothing here that we can use for the Academy." But the person who managed the farm said, "The person who owns this property is very interested in education, so why don't you send us a little write-up about what you're doing?"

So we put together a one-pager—literally one sentence about the vision for the Academy, and the rest listing our needs for rooms and beds—and we sent it off. It turned out that land was owned by an angel called Rebecca Oppenheimer.

She saw this note and said, "Well, I don't have a property that you can use for your Academy, but I'm willing to build it for you!"

We said, "Well, does she know how much it's going to cost to build this?" Chris and I flew up to Seattle to see her, and we met her. She didn't know who we were, but she committed $5 million!

Two months before the whole project was to be shut down, Rebecca came into our lives. She has since continued to support us and has become the single largest individual donor to the African Leadership Academy, and we honestly would not be here without her.

What that really tells me is that in the pursuit of a big goal, there will be many times when it will appear completely impossible. None of it was logical. Why were we sent to an empty farm when there was no place to use for a campus? And why did she trust two young guys that she had never met? It's completely unexplainable, but what this really tells me is the importance of having faith, and that sometimes when things are meant to happen, they just do.

The third story I want to tell is about Partnership.

I really believe that great accomplishments are never achieved alone, and ALA is no different. It has drawn on the strengths and energies of people from all over the world. Thousands of people have given blood, sweat, and tears to get us to this point. ALA really shows me the power of humanity and collaboration.

About 5,000 schools across Africa have over the years become our partners, feeding us talented young people to become part of our community; 200 staff members have worked with us over the years; over 100 university partners take our graduates after they leave us and give them opportunities; corporate partners give them internships; guest speakers come to campus to inspire them; host families and parents, especially that first class of parents... when 1,700 young people applied to a school with no track record, what were those parents thinking to let their children apply to a school with no track record? We owe deep gratitude to this group.

Since inception, this project has attracted about $150 million USD from donors all around the world—foundations and individuals. In Rand terms, that's about 2 billion Rand invested in this project. While thousands of donors have contributed, just 100 individuals and foundations have contributed over 95% of this total—the "Club of 100" who have been so instrumental in making this happen.

And of course, the MasterCard Foundation, represented by Rita Roy, made a huge commitment of $50 million to building this institution.

As we look forward to the next ten years, I hope we reflect on the importance of building strong African institutions such as the African Leadership Academy. One thing we're very good at doing in Africa is starting projects. The continent is littered with projects that all had good intentions, but they died after those who started them lost energy, or after those who initially funded them stopped funding them.

Institutions are organizations that are much beyond any one person. They live on, they assume a life of their own, and they continue achieving the vision that has been set out over many generations and over many centuries.

As we look forward to the next ten years, my one wish is that we will continue to build this African institution and all of its affiliates: the African Leadership Network, the African Leadership University, the African Leadership Finance Corporation, the ALX fellowship... What you see here at ALA is really the center of an ecosystem of many other institutions that are being built to ultimately develop 3 million leaders for the continent of Africa over the next 50 years. But it all started with ALA.

As we continue building this broader movement of leadership, the three things that it will require are for us to continue giving opportunity to young people like Joseph, to continue to have faith that it will come to fruition, and that we need to keep doing this in partnership with all of you.

Thank you for a wonderful ten years, and here's to another amazing ten years and 50 years ahead! Thank you.

metadata.speaker: Fred Swaniker
metadata.title: Entrepreneurship, Leadership Development and Education

content:
At the age of six, Joseph Munyambanza found himself here—it's a refugee camp in Uganda. He had fled here together with about 23,000 inhabitants from countries like the Congo, Sudan, Rwanda, and Burundi. He was alone, he was bewildered, and several thousand kilometers from his home.

In this community of 23,000 people, there were only two primary schools and one secondary school. And so, as you can imagine, access to quality education was not very prevalent in the community, and the schools were overcrowded. Very few people had access to high-quality education.

Now, Joseph was spotted by a non-profit organization that was working in the community as someone who had talent, and they sponsored him to go to a school outside of the refugee camp. Joseph felt so bad that he was the only one who had access to high-quality education that he decided he would do something about it.

And so began a program where, on the weekends, he would get together with his peers and they would go and work as laborers on farms nearby, raise money, and use that to sponsor others in the refugee camp to go to schools outside of the camp as well. Soon he was sponsoring 10 young people in his community to go to school. He was 14 years old.

He kept doing this every weekend—they'd go work as laborers, raise more money—and soon, by the age of 17, he was sponsoring 52 children in his refugee camp to go to school.

Now at this point, January or February 2008, we were selecting the first class to join the African Leadership Academy. So we went around the entire continent looking for young people that we believed could transform Africa—people with courage, determination, and passion to really change the continent forever.

But I didn't hear about Joseph in those travels. I actually learned about Joseph when I was speaking at the Harvard Africa Business Forum, something similar to this. Just like what's going to happen after this, there's an afterparty. So I was hanging out at the afterparty, and this scrawny white guy comes up to me and he says, "You know, I didn't even pay to be at this conference, but I snuck into this party because I heard you were going to be here. There's this young man in this refugee camp in Uganda that my organization sponsors—he's amazing." And he went on, and the way he was talking about this guy, he sounded like a saint.

So I said, "No, this is too good to be true."

So I went back to South Africa, looked through the files of all the applicants, and read this guy's story. And yes, it was exactly what Eric had said about him. And so we admitted Joseph into the first class of the African Leadership Academy.

Now, one of the things that happens at the Academy, in addition to educating these young people and training them to be transformative leaders for Africa, is we bring different leaders and speakers onto campus all the time to interact and share their experiences with these young people. One day, a woman came and shared the work that she was doing to help people overcome trauma using theater as the way to do this.

Joseph said, "You know, people in my refugee camp could really use you," and invited her to come and spend a few days with him during his summer holidays at the end of the first year. So she went, saw what he was doing, and fell in love with his project. During Joseph's second year, she helped him to raise about $10,000, and so Joseph built a school in the refugee camp in his second year at ALA and began educating 243 orphans.

June 2010: Joseph graduates from the African Leadership Academy. But unfortunately, he wasn't able to get a scholarship to go on to university. He had been admitted, but didn't have enough funding to go to university. So he went back to his refugee camp and kept working on his projects, educating more young people, educating these orphans.

One of the organizations I started was something called the African Leadership Network. The African Leadership Network is an association of young leaders from across Africa who are a little bit more established than the ones at the African Leadership Academy—people in their 20s, 30s, and 40s. Once again, we bring these leaders together so they can forge relationships with each other and actually do things together. About 70% of the people that we bring are Africans living on the continent, 20% are Africans living in the diaspora, and 10% are non-Africans who are doing interesting things in Africa.

Now, Joseph shared his vision for education and what he was doing in the refugee camp. He had a vision specifically to rent a hostel outside of the refugee camp so that some of the young people from there could get access to high-quality schools outside of the refugee camp. Remember I said that there was only one secondary school in the refugee camp, and it only went up to 10th grade.

So this is what happened when Joseph spoke at the African Leadership Network in 2012:

"We plan to take 110 students into high school, and to do this, we need $13,000 US dollars. I'm sure $13,000 US..."

"Two or three mentors in this room today... Young man from Congo, I'm going to commit the $13,000. This will be from a client by the name of Curtis Jackson, who has a huge initiative to work in Africa, and on his behalf, thank you so much for this opportunity to help."

Now, who here knows who Curtis Jackson is? That's right—50 Cent!

He had been sponsored by 50 Cent, and soon he was able to get an additional 100 young people into school. He was sponsoring now 343 young people to go to school.

After a few more months of doing this, he was able to get a scholarship and ended up attending a university in the US called Westminster College. So Joseph now is in his second year at Westminster College in Missouri. He's continuing to run his program in the refugee camp, and today he controls an organization with a budget of $186,000 and 10 full-time employees.

What I especially am excited about is that he's begun sponsoring some people from his refugee camp to universities. At Westminster, where he is right now, there's a freshman there who came from his refugee camp and was one of the participants in his program. He sent a student to the University of Rochester, including the first girl ever to graduate and go to university from the refugee camp.

And especially dear to me, he sent two students who have come to the African Leadership Academy—Tia and Jean—who also came from his program.

As a result of all this work, Joseph recently was introduced to former UK Prime Minister Gordon Brown, who, as you know, is now the UN Special Envoy on Education. He has also been invited and serves as one of 15 young people on the UN Secretary-General's Special Advisory Council for Youth on Education.

Joseph sent me an email in September telling me about how he had spent his summer holiday. He talked about how he had gone back to the Congo—he hadn't been there for many years—and as a result of connections that he has with Gordon Brown and the UN Secretary-General, he met with the Chief of Staff to the President, the Minister of Education, and his entire cabinet. He identified that there are 7 million children in the Congo who are out of school, and his objective was to see how he could get 1 million of these young people into school.

The first step towards that: at the end of the summer, the Minister of Education of Congo expanded the education budget by 20%, and they are now well on their way to his goal of 1 million.

Now, if this is not a ripple effect, I don't know what is! He went from, within a scope of five years, touching 10 people to 52, to 242, to 343, and now 1 million—and he's only 22 years old.

The example of Joseph really illustrates what I believe is one of the most powerful ripple effects that we can ever have in any society, and that is the impact of leaders.

Now, one might think that, of course, leaders make a difference in every society. But I believe that in Africa, more than anywhere else in the world, just one person, one good leader, can have much more impact in Africa than anywhere else in the world. And here's why.

There's something called institutions that exist in every society. Institutions are the rules and the systems that govern how a society functions. These are things like your constitution, the media, the judiciary, the parliamentary system—all of those things.

The rule that I believe is that the stronger the institutions in a given country, the less effect one single leader can have in that country. And therefore, by the inverse of that, the weaker the institutions in a country, the much, much more powerful effect that just one person can have in that society.

When you look at a developed country like the UK, your parliament—Big Ben—you walk past that place, it's been around for 500 years. You look at the US, it's got very developed systems. So if you become the President of the United States and you think, "Oh, I've arrived, I'm the most powerful man in the world," and you decide, "Okay, I think Americans should get healthcare, I'm going to pass a law to make this possible," you go to the Senate, they say, "No, no, no, you can't do that." You go to Congress, they say, "No, you can't do that."

If you decide that you want to become president for life, there's a 300-year-old constitution that will stop that. There's a very powerful police force that will come and take you out of that Oval Office. If you decide you want to print money and you call Ben Bernanke or Alan Greenspan, the central bank governor, they'll say, "Are you smoking crack?"

You come to Africa, the situation is different. If you are the president of Zimbabwe and you decide that, "You know what, I just want to stay in power forever," there's no constitution that's going to stop you, and you just stay there on and on and on like the Energizer Bunny. If you decide that you want to print money and you call your central bank governor, the guy will say, "Okay, yes sir, how much do you need?" And as a result, hyperinflation ensues in that country.

And so the lack of these institutions in Africa has meant that our leaders have had tremendous impact on us. Just one person, like Robert Mugabe, can destroy an entire country. And this is why I say that leaders in Africa can have much more impact than anywhere else in the world. They are really the ultimate ripple effect in Africa.

This is why myself and my peers were really inspired to develop the African Leadership Academy, when we realized that this was the single biggest thing that was holding us back from achieving our potential as Africans—the quality of the leaders that we have.

We said, "Do we just sit back and hope that one day we get good leaders, or can we create a system, a machine that can actually find young people and develop them—hundreds and thousands of young people like Joseph who each, in their own way..."

When I was growing up, I grew up in different parts of Africa, and everywhere I went, I saw we had different problems: healthcare, infrastructure, poverty, housing, sanitation. It was overwhelming. Where would I start?

But I thought: there's no way in my lifetime that I can try and tackle all these things. But if I can produce a set of leaders—and those leaders, this one will take infrastructure, that one will take politics, this one will take healthcare, this one will take education—each and every one of them in their way will go out and they will become the leaders that can really transform Africa.

As I mentioned, just one leader in Africa can have a very, very powerful effect on that society, and that's really what inspired the African Leadership Academy. Today, we get several thousand applications, and we pick only a hundred people. You might say, "How can a hundred people change Africa?" I say that we don't need a lot of people to transform Africa; we just need a few good leaders.

So when you walk into the walls of the African Leadership Academy, everywhere there's a quote that I like that is all over the place. It's my favorite quote. It says:

"Never doubt that a small group of thoughtful, committed citizens can change the world; indeed, it's the only thing that ever has."

I believe in Africa, I would rewrite that statement to say:

"Never doubt that a small group of thoughtful, committed leaders can change Africa; indeed, it's the only thing that ever will."

Thank you.

metadata.speaker: Patrick Awuah
metadata.title: Education, Leadership Development and Business Ethics

content:
Like many of you here, I am trying to contribute to a Renaissance in Africa. The question of transformation in Africa really is a question of leadership. Africa can only be transformed by enlightened leaders, and it is my contention that the manner in which we educate our leaders is fundamental to progress on this continent.

I want to tell you some stories that explain my view. We all heard about the importance of stories yesterday. An American friend of mine this year volunteered as a nurse in Ghana, and in the period of 3 months she came to a conclusion about the state of leadership in Africa that had taken me over a decade to reach.

Twice she was involved in surgeries where they lost power at the hospital. Emergency generators did not start. There was not a flashlight, not a lantern, not a candle. Pitch black! Patients cut open.

Twice! The first time it was a C-section. Thankfully baby was out; mother and child survived. The second time was a procedure that involved local anesthesia. Anesthetic wears off, patient feels pain, he's crying, he's screaming, he's praying. Pitch black! Not a candle, not a flashlight. And that hospital could have afforded flashlights; they could have afforded to purchase these things. But they didn't. And it happened twice!

Another time she watched in horror as nurses watched a patient die because they refused to give her oxygen that they had. And so 3 months later, just before she returns to the United States, nurses in Accra go on strike. And her recommendation is: take this opportunity to fire everyone. Start all over again. Start all over again!

Now what does this have to do with leadership? You see, the folks at the Ministry of Health, the hospital administrators, the doctors, the nurses—they are among just 5% of their peers who get an education after secondary school. They are the elite. They are our leaders. Their decisions, their actions matter, and when they fail, a nation literally suffers.

So when I speak of leadership, I'm not talking about just political leaders. We've heard a lot about that. I'm talking about the elite—those who've been trained whose job it is to be the guardians of their society: the lawyers, the judges, the policemen, the doctors, the engineers, the civil servants. Those are the leaders, and we need to train them right.

Now my first pointed and memorable experience with leadership in Ghana occurred when I was 16 years old. We had just had a military coup, and soldiers were pervasive in our society. They were a pervasive presence. And one day I go to the airport to meet my father, and as I walk up this grassy slope from the car park to the terminal building, I'm stopped by two soldiers wielding AK-47 assault weapons. And they ask me to join a crowd of people that were running up and down this embankment. Why? Because the path I had taken was considered out of bounds—no signs to this effect!

Now I was 16. I was very worried about what my peers at school might think if they saw me running up and down this hill. I was especially concerned about what the girls might think! And so I started to argue with these men. It's a little reckless, you know. I was 16. I got lucky. A Ghana Airways pilot falls into the same predicament. Because of his uniform, they speak to him differently. They explain to him that they're just following orders. So he takes a radio, talks with their boss, and gets us all released.

What lessons would you take from an experience like this? Several. For me: leadership matters. Those men were following the orders of a superior officer. I learned something about courage—it was important not to look at those guns. And I also learned that it can be helpful to think about girls!

So a few years after this event, I leave Ghana on a scholarship to go to Swarthmore College for my education. It was a breath of fresh air. You know, the faculty there didn't want us to memorize information and repeat back to them as I was used to back in Ghana. They wanted us to think critically. They wanted us to be analytical. They wanted us to be concerned about social issues. In my economics classes, I got high marks for my understanding of basic economics, but I learned something more profound than that, which is that the leaders, the managers of Ghana's economy were making breathtakingly bad decisions that had brought our economy to the brink of collapse. And so here was this lesson again: leadership matters. It matters a great deal.

But I didn't really fully understand what had happened to me at Swarthmore. I had an inkling, but I didn't fully realize it until I went out into the workplace. And I went to work at Microsoft Corporation, and I was part of this team—this thinking, learning team whose job it was to design and implement new software that created value in the world. And it was brilliant to be part of this team. It was brilliant.

And I realized just what had happened to me at Swarthmore. This transformation—the ability to confront problems, complex problems, and to design solutions to those problems, the ability to create—is the most empowering thing that can happen to an individual. And I was part of that.

Now, while I was at Microsoft, the annual revenues of that company grew larger than the GDP of the Republic of Ghana. And by the way, it's continued to... the gap has widened since I left. Now I've already spoken about one of the reasons why this has occurred. I mean, there's the people—they were so hardworking, persistent, creative, empowered. But there were also external factors: free markets, the rule of law, infrastructure. These things were provided by institutions run by the people that I call leaders, and those leaders did not emerge spontaneously. Somebody trained them to do the work that they do.  

Now, while I was at Microsoft, this funny thing happened: I became a parent. And for the first time, Africa mattered more to me than ever before, because I realized that the state of the African continent would matter to my children and their children. That the state of the world depends on what's happening to Africa as far as my kids would be concerned. And at this time, when I was going through what I called my pre-midlife crisis, Africa was a mess. Somalia had disintegrated into anarchy, Rwanda was in the throes of this genocidal war, and it seemed to me that that was the wrong direction, and I needed to be back helping. I couldn't just stay in Seattle and raise my kids in an upper-middle-class neighborhood and feel good about it. This was not the world that I'd want my children to grow up in.  

So I decided to get engaged. And the first thing that I did was to come back to Ghana and talk with a lot of people and really try to understand what the real issues were. And three things kept coming up for every problem: corruption, weak institutions, and the people who run them—the leaders.  

Now I was a little scared, because when you see those three problems, they seem really hard to deal with, and you might say, "Look, don't even try." But for me, I asked the question: Well, where are these leaders coming from? What is it about Ghana that produces leaders that are unethical or unable to solve problems?  

So I went to look at what was happening in our educational system. And it's the same: learning by rote from primary school through graduate school. Very little emphasis on ethics. And the typical graduate from a university in Ghana has a stronger sense of entitlement than a sense of responsibility. This is wrong.  

So I decided to engage this particular problem, because it seems to me that every society—every society must be very intentional about how it trains its leaders, and Ghana was not paying enough attention. And this is true across Sub-Saharan Africa, actually.  

So this is what I'm doing: I'm trying to bring the experience that I had at Swarthmore to Africa. I wish there was a liberal arts college in every African country; I think it would make a huge difference. And what Ashesi University is trying to do is to train a new generation of ethical, entrepreneurial leaders. We're trying to train leaders of exceptional integrity who have the ability to confront complex problems, to ask the right questions, and come up with workable solutions.  

I'll admit that there are times when it seems like Mission Impossible, but we must believe that these kids are smart. That if we involve them in their education, if we have them discuss the real issues that they confront, that our whole society confronts, and if we give them skills that enable them to engage the real world, magic will happen.

Now a month into this project—we had just started classes—a month into it, I come to the office, and I have this email from one of our students. And it said very simply: "I am thinking now." And he signs off, "Thank you."  

It's such a simple statement, but I was moved almost to tears, because I understood what was happening to this young man, and it is an awesome thing to be a part of empowering someone in this way. "I am thinking now."  

This year, we challenged our students to craft an honor code for themselves. There's a very vibrant debate going on on campus now about whether they should have an honor code, and if so, what it should look like. One of the students asked a question that just warmed my heart: "Can we create a perfect society?" Her understanding that a student-crafted honor code constitutes a reach towards perfection is incredible. Now, we cannot achieve perfection, but if we reach for it, then we can achieve excellence. I don't know ultimately what they will do; I don't know whether they will decide to have this honor code. But the conversation that they're having now about what their good society should look like, what their excellent society should look like, is a really good thing.  

Am I out of time?  

Okay. Now I just want to leave that slide up, because it's important that we think about it. I'm very excited about the fact that every student at Ashesi University does community service before they graduate. That for many of them, it has been a life-altering experience. These young future leaders are beginning to understand the real business of leadership, the real privilege of leadership, which is, after all, to serve humanity.  

I am even more thrilled by the fact that last year, our student body elected a woman to be the head of student government. It's the first time in the history of Ghana that a woman has been elected head of student government at any university. It says a lot about her, it says a lot about the culture that's forming on campus, it says a lot about her peers who elected her. She won with 75% of the vote, and it gives me a lot of hope.  

It turns out that Corporate West Africa also appreciates what's happening with our students. We've graduated two classes of students to date, and every single one of them has been placed. And we're getting great reports back from corporate Ghana, from Corporate West Africa. And the things that they're most impressed about is work ethic, you know, that passion for what they're doing, the persistence, their ability to deal with ambiguity, their ability to tackle problems they haven't seen before.  

This is good, because over the past five years, there have been times when I felt this is Mission Impossible, and it's just wonderful to see these glimmers of the promise of what can happen if we train our kids right.

I think that the current and future leaders of Africa have an incredible opportunity to drive a major Renaissance on the continent. It's an incredible opportunity. There aren't very many more opportunities like this in the world. I believe that Africa has reached an inflection point. With the march of democracy and free markets across the continent, we have reached a moment from which can emerge a great society within one generation. It will depend on inspired leadership, and it is my contention that the manner in which we train our leaders will make all the difference.  

Thank you. God bless.

metadata.speaker: Tabitha Karanja
metadata.title: Manufacturing, Beverage Industry, Tax Policy and Local Enterprise Advocacy

content:
And welcome back to Jeff Koinange Live here Citizen Television. On the bench tonight, we're combining a bit of business and politics. Tabitha Karanja is a CEO of Keroche Breweries. They've done a really amazing, remarkable job, but she's recently been in trouble with KRA—owes them like 22 billion Shillings. Let me put that in perspective: it cost 32 billion Shillings to build the Thika Superhighway. This Mombasa Expressway you see here, that cost 66 billion. Tabitha owes them 22 billion.

Tabitha Karanja, welcome to JKL. First of all...

Thank you.

22 billion? What is that? I mean, how... Do I look like I have 22 billion in my bank account? Are you listening? Are you listening? 22 billion, that's what they say.

No, I think they overreacted to me. They overreacted. Uh, it was a very simple request. We requested them after realizing we have arrears of 322 Kenya Shillings. So we just requested for a reasonable, I mean, a realistic payment plan.

So what's the 22 billion?

But then I think when I went on air, because I was scared... It has taken me a month, a month and 4 days, cause I filed that press conference on 4th. Uh, I got scared cause everybody, all the employees are looking up to me to fight for them or to ensure that their jobs are secure. So I told them in that morning, "What do you want us to do? Are you ready we talk to the press and tell them that uh we are almost now going out of your door and the beer in the tank is going to waste, they don't mean to be okay?" And they all clapped. So that's why you saw us that morning very desperate, actually only in the afternoon very desperate to talk to the media. Otherwise, we had tried to reach for himself, Commissioner General. He knows I went even to his office, I waited there. I met his secretary, and the secretary told me he was not in the office. I told him, "Please tell him that I'm looking for an appointment." Since then, calling his office, nobody responds. So we were desperate at the end of it. And then Commissioner of domestic taxes told me, "Tabitha, my hands are tied at the end of it." Then we, as we are Kenyans, we belong here. We are only talking of 322 Kenya Shillings, we just want to be given a payment plan.

32... 332 million?

332... 322 million.

322 million only?

Only. And the reason why we are saying only: before COVID, we were paying over 200 million monthly.

Monthly?

Monthly basis, yes. So after that, I think they overreacted. I don't think there's anybody else who've been done what I think the KRA has done to us. In fact, I'm wondering: what is all this paying two page in newspaper, two page newspaper Standard and Nation, and putting all our issues in their website? So you can imagine all this. Yeah, but uh I think things are okay now. I think we are going to have a meeting with... That's what I can...

Okay, if the KRA says it's been 16 years, right? According to them, you've been paying taxes for all those years?

Yes. Since inception of Keroche Breweries, and they can attest to this, we paid over 30 billion Kenya Shillings. We've been paying. But the reason, because of... I mean, this dispute, if you look at it, is just that we produce a product, we take 10 years, then after 10 years, they knock at our doors and they reclassify the same product. If you sold this product at 80 Shillings, and then they tell you you're supposed to pay at... to buy to sell it at 150, you never sold at 150 because they give you the tax bracket you are to apply then. And this one is in court. We won cases based on that. They've taken to the High Court, we won again to the High Court. They took them to the TAT. The TAT still belongs to KRA, so they rule to their favor after winning the High Court. It's called Low Court, and High Court, and Court of Appeal. Yes, after winning that, now they take it again to the... the same the way and KRA has already won. They give the TAT, the TAT belongs to KRA. So if it belongs to KRA, they can rule it... they can always rule it to their favor.

Sure, yeah.

Yeah.

To set the record straight, is the factory opened or closed right now?

It is closed. It has been closed since 31st, last evening of January this year. So there's no operations, nothing happening.

No operations, and the fear is the beer that is in the tanks, which is worth 500 million Kenya Shillings, if nothing is done, we'll be forced to drain it. Cause the Kenya Power, if you cannot pay them their dues, definitely they switch off the brewery, and the beer cannot stay even a minute without power.

One minute?

Even when it comes to the... If the power goes off, the exchange in the generator is automatic, it just switches.

Switches, yes, cause the beer cannot even go a minute without the... And if that power goes, the beer is... Yeah. So you'd wonder, this is a government institution which has been mandated to support the local enterprises, the local, because there's nowhere they can go, this is their country, this is where we belong. So... But I know now they've called us for a meeting, and I really appreciate to the Commissioner General. Thank you very much, I appreciate. So we'll have a meeting tomorrow, and we just hope this thing will bring everything to a rest.

I was actually about to ask you, if the Commissioner General is listening to you right now, what would you tell him?

He's a good friend of mine, actually, and we were even talking all the way up to December 10th there. But of late now, you see, there's no communication. But I'm happy today cause we got that communication from him, from his office, that we have a meeting tomorrow. So that meeting, I believe it will come... I mean, it will now to agree and we see how we open our plant so that we can save the 250 jobs and the beer that is in the tanks. Yeah, but because now of the closures, the many closures, many disruptions by them since now December, maybe we've worked on less than 20 days the whole of the three months. So we are requesting now for a grace period for the taxes that are in arrears. But going forward, whatever we... I mean, the taxes that fall due, of course, we pay those ones. We pay.

But at one point, you had agreed to pay 500 million Shillings a month to clear the 4 billion Shilling debt. At some point, you had agreed at the 4 billion...

Yeah, we don't owe 4 billion. Who said 4 billion? We don't owe 4 billion. Yeah, we don't owe 4 billion. If there's something they're talking of 500 million, that is an agreement that we agreed after the ADR, you know, the ADR agreement, that is the 9 billion case that is known, right? Is in the public domain. So they decided we get out of court, we come and decide, I mean, discuss it out of court. That is, they call it Alternative Dispute Resolution. And out of that, when they did the in-depth, which they came to Keroche for two weeks, they came out and said uh the literage is what we owe is 500 million. The rest is the 1.1 billion that is for 2002 to 2005, which we had won in the High Court and in the Court of Appeal. And then the other 3... 2.9, which now because we're in... in whatever, it's about the water put in our Viena, which is a case that is also in the public domain, the reclassification and the... the... the reclassification of whatever. So meaning the 3.9, they are letters, and I remember even Commissioner General telling me, "It's your... I mean, you're allowed... you're allowed to go and seek for abandonment so that we can move forward," cause they know all that money, KRA has never collected the... that 3.9, it's in their whatever. That's for about 4 billion. We've never collected that money, it's never in our accounts. So it was just now to assure that we go, we get the abandonment from Treasury, because then they have no power to abandon, only Treasury can do that. When they do that, then we move forward. This amount of money that is neither here nor there is never owed by Keroche, and KRA cannot recover from us because we never sold, we never got to... to our account. So meaning that was the... the aim of us going there, to seek the abandonment of that money.

But there are some who say that, you know, the KRA has some very serious trust issues with Keroche Breweries. They say you are unreliable.

It's not that we are unreliable. I tend to think there are people that continue pushing, maybe without the KRA knowing, they're being pushed by other people to show that the local brand cannot match the international brand. That's what I can say. So always there's an issue. There's an issue to... like to bring down the brand of Keroche Breweries. And as a brand, also... And this brand, that's all. Because what we managed to do, it's beyond even what I think the multinationals have done for those 80 years. Yeah. So what we want now is that level playing ground and for us to be supported in a way that we feel we belong, not that we'll be wishing to be a foreign investor rather than an indigenous businessperson. Yeah, yeah.

But also the KRA accuses you of collecting excise duty, tax, and VAT from your customers through sales.

No, no, it's excise. A beer, that one beer, when you sell to... to the consumer, yes, a liter is 121 Shillings. So in that 322, there's excise. Mhm. So meaning, because it's excise, so that's what they're saying now, we collected and we are not refusing. We collected, willing to pay the 3... and we got these arrears, yes.

And in your meeting tomorrow, what are you going to tell the Commissioner General? You tell them you are willing to pay?

No, no, we've only said we're willing to pay. We just wanted to get that uh realistic, you know, payment plan that is realistic. But for now, because of what we've gone through, you've closed your company since December up to now. So what does that mean? Now we can only get a... a... uh what is it called? We can only go... got a... I mean, given time, yes. Yeah, a grace period. Good, I'm even forgetting! We... we can only be given a grace period so that now after maybe one year, we can now start talking of the... the arrears. But the current taxes, we continue paying.

But you've been in dispute with KRA from, what, 2006? That's 16 years. When is that going to end?

Where... where we were going, it was ending, apart from this difference we have, because we requested this and we don't know how it came. Mhm. Cause I don't want to say it's political, because the way many people are saying it's politics, it's not... it's not political, this. Yeah, yeah. This is business war, and there's a hand there trying to use KRA to... to... to push us out of the market. And uh they always time such a time when the politics is on and people are confused, and there's that divide or the political whatever. So meaning we were even ending this. I remember even Commissioner General telling me the last time I was in his office, and he can attest to that, that even the case that is in... in... in court, we remove it so that now we can come again and do it through the ADR. Yeah, yeah. It's about 3 months when we were talking about that. He's the one who told me, "We need to get... I need to get that case out of court so that we... we take it through the ADR," cause it was bad to be seen the KRA in court with a criminal case with a taxpayer. Yeah, yeah. We talked on that. Yeah. So we were to end, actually. Me, I'm surprised to see what has come up just all of a sudden.

By the way, in your press conference today, it looked like you were looking for some kind of amicable solution between you and the KRA. Is... is that... Did we read it right?

Yeah, yeah, that's what... Because Keroche and KRA, why would they fight? KRA is a tax collector, and Keroche is an... is an entrepreneur where they invest... It's a lot of work to invest like what we managed to do in Keroche. And then we obey the law, we pay the taxes, but falling due, we already know why: because of the COVID. So for us now to... to... to ensure that the effects of the pandemic, economic whatever effect that has been there, these government institutions are the ones to help, and not only in Kenya, it's worldwide, that's what they're doing to ensure that the businesses survive and remain and thrive and get back to where they were. That's now actually the KRA. Even the banks, that's what they've done: they've restructured their loans first, even the second time they've done it, and they're even willing to do the third time just to see the companies... What, these are international banks? What about your own local, your own Kenya where you've been paying taxes all this time? They're the ones wanting now to help you get back to your feet. Yeah, yeah.

By the way, you also appealed to the KRA to reopen your plant. Why should they reopen your plant? Why should they do that when you owe them so much money?

322, yes. 322 is little money to KRA. Between us and them, what we've been paying, it's very little money. If they just open the plant, they'll get it back. And then those employees that are there, why do you need them to get out of the... the company, and yet we are talking of how we are going to build institutions, we are going to build uh factories in the... That's what we are promising the incoming president, whoever will become, that's what they're promising, and it's only 5 months from now. How can you kill one and then you tell people that you'll build? Keroche has taken 25 years to build, so even... even one tenure, it's very hard to build even. And so it's upon us now to ensure that it survives, it moves, it thrives, so that we create even more jobs than what is there. It's about 250 direct, indirect thousands. So what does that tell? If it grows, it will give a thousand employee, direct employees, distribution, Kenya, East Africa, all that. Yeah, yeah, yeah. Keroche can generate 21 billion Kenya Shillings revenue to the exchequer.

When you look at your plant that's closed right now that you built 25 years ago, how does that make you feel?

I feel so bad, because I've never been in such a position, and yet it's real money. I've never been in such a position, and you know, even the worst is for them to write letters to the 36 banks in Kenya. Writing a letter to the 36 banks in Kenya, otherwise maybe there's a bank which could have given that money straight and we pay, we clear with them. But now even the environment they've created between us and the banks is also not good, it's not conducive at all. So you'd wonder, why would you know... There are so many questions you need to ask. Yeah, but we are not asking now because I think we'll get another, that applicable solution with them. I'm sure. Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah.

You just addressed or you mentioned the 36 banks. You want lifting of notices to those banks?

Yeah, yeah, that's what we are requesting. Yeah, we are also requesting that they lift the agencies they put in the... the 36 banks in Kenya, because we... we... we operate in three banks, actually. So for them to take to the other 33, I don't know why they did that.

Is that so that you don't get... There's a bit of... You don't understand, the sabotage, is it?

We don't know. You don't... There are many questions, but for me, we've been very okay, working very nice, uh a lot of support, actually. But when it came to this time, the last three months, it's unbelievable what we've been going through. Yeah, yeah.

You said you're going to meet with KRA and Commissioner General tomorrow. What if your request is turned down? What do you do from there? Where do you go from there if it's turned down?

Yeah, if it's turned down... I don't think he can turn down. He has no alternative. How do you turn down? How do you close... If you close Keroche, what would you be saying? You leave a blog, cause we have only two breweries here: one local, one multinational. You'd better sack... If she can be sacked, then you... you ensure you put your own commission, you know, your own KRA person. Yeah, surely you have no alternative. It's only to open and the company... And we don't need to waste even more time. We need just to open and start and work. When we are doing the... We are losing, both of us, and the government is even losing more. Yeah, yeah.

And losing more?

Yeah.

And you're willing to pay arrears? You mean you're willing to pay everything?

Yeah, and it's the first time you've gotten these arrears. Yeah, it's the... I remember the only arrears I had with Commissioner General who... was it was 10 million in 2008. We could not be able to pay cause we just launched the brewery, and there was so much unethical trade practices, you could not be able to sell your beer. 10 million, and I remember him standing and telling his people, "Even if Keroche pays a Shilling, allow them." We cleared after that. What's Keroche doing? Paying over 2 million... 2 billion Kenya Shillings. I remember him telling me, "In fact, you have built a brand that now I know wherever I'll... I'll be, it's able to generate revenue, 2 billion Kenya Shillings." So that's what even Board is supposed to do. Yeah. My good friend Board is supposed to... to think of how... how in his tenure... What is the tenure of Board? Is it 4 years? Is it 8 years? How many industries... Look around for me. Maybe I read my book upside down, but that's how it should be. How many industries do you leave you've built? Cause this world we are here, we are going, we are living. But what did you do during your tenure? Cause you owe it to the people that put you in that office. Yeah. So when I see Commission writing two pages using the same money I'm struggling, you know, to generate to pay them, and they're using it to pay the two newspapers, I wish they give me so that I can pay my two... uh two months arrears salary I have. You know, it's hurting if... if they agree, mhm, and... and everything goes well tomorrow, going forward, how soon before the factory is opened, before you open?

No, no, no. If they... if they open, you know, everything is on. Of course, now production and all that, it may take a week to take our products back to the market, cause they've not been in the market for the last now 3 months. Uh it will take another one month. So within 2 months, we can be back to the market. But it is really hurting that your brand you'built all this time, you can now be struggling to return it back to the market. Yeah, yeah.

And then at the same time, you've announced that you're running for politics as Senator for Nakuru County, and you've got all these issues that you're dealing with on the business front.

I didn't have them. I didn't have the issues when you announced. Yeah, yeah, I didn't have the issues when I announced. I was very good, I was even looking for the CEO. I'd even announced I'm almost... was getting the CEO so that I leave my... my chair, I leave somebody. I didn't have the issues, and this was people's demand. They wanted me to... to take an elective seat in the Nakuru County.

By the way, this is what you said, this is how you announced your uh your intention to run for Nakuru County Senator. Let me take a... listen.

...Primary School, secondary... County...

I was actually going to ask which party, but you've answered the question: you're going to run under UDA?

Yes, cause that's what the ground says. Yeah, that's what the ground says. Uh I've done my opinion... We did a lot of opinion polls, and uh yeah, we saw the odds, because I was not going to try, I was going to win it. And I've talked to everyone. Even I... I talked to Baba.

Cause you're good friends with Baba.

I talked to him, told him the ground... I know he told me to wait up to February, and I waited. But uh the ground has not changed. And this is Rift Valley, remember Nakuru is Rift Valley. I also talked to my best friend, lawyer called Orengo. I showed him the numbers, and he told me it's a bit... it had when you look at those numbers. But we were still to wait and see. But when I was invited for that meeting, so I... I went, and in front of the people was put the kofia. But I knew later, finally, finally, I waited. Nakuru, those are... it's our new zone, because it's Rift. Yeah, yeah.

By the way, Tabitha, you've never held any political office, no. And there you are on that stage talking to all those people. Yes. How does that... I mean, you think you can do it? You think you can make the switch? We know you're a great businesswoman, you know you've known for your business acumen. But politics, yeah...

You know, you'll not be talking to the crowds all the time, you'll just be performing, doing your job. You'll be performing, doing your job. So what is your job? The same way I've done Keroche for the last 25 years. I've done something, even if I live today, my name will still remain on the wall. So how can I make my name also be remembered in Nakuru County, not only that I was an entrepreneur, that's by giving leadership service. That's what I'm looking for. Yes, switch. And then I've realized, even through doing business, like all what you've been doing is politics. Yeah, yeah. Most of it is about politics.

But it's going to be a very tight race. I know you said you spoke to Baba earlier, but you know, you've chosen UDA because that's what the ground says. But it's going to be a very tight race, you know that, between Azimio and...

Of course, of course, yeah. But you see, it's not about the chama, remember that. It's not about chama, it's about you as a person. Sell your manifesto to the people, and then select, elect you based on that. They'll not elect you because that you're UDA, you're Azimio. Let them elect you on how they believe you can work for them. Yeah, yeah. And you have a track record of those you've done, right? I think it's the same thing you're going to apply now to Nakuru County.

Yes.

You just said the ground has shifted, the ground has said that, you know, it's UDA. It's the ground that's talking, that's what you just said.

Yeah, it's not the individual, it's the ground that's saying. It's not me. You... You can't talk. When you seek for an elective position, it's the people who decide for you. It's the people who will tell you, "This is a vehicle we want if you want us to elect you, there's a vehicle we want you to use." And that is how it is. Maybe, never know, it may change, but for me, I don't care, I don't mind. Now even if it changes, I'll sell my manifesto, and I believe I can be elected even if it changes because of what my investor means to the people. Yeah.

Did you think you would ever switch from business to politics? What did you think of this?

No, no, no. Actually, uh I thought maybe one day I leave office uh to work with the foundation, my foundation and all that, Keroche Foundation and all that. But politics, no. But I was pushed by people, and then as I was pushed by people, I thought the problems that I've been having, if I was in that parliament, I think I could not be going through what I've gone through. Then I thought, I think I've done my part. Uh what about the other people? If I can go and represent the other people in the national, through the Senate, and ensure that nobody will be suffering when it comes to the business or the laws that are put, I mean, done at the Senate or the parliament, whatever, and then they are brought to us without people knowing what those laws mean when they're put to the business. So I thought maybe if I'm there, I can represent the people, the business people, to ensure that the laws, they're favorable to the business, to our business. Yeah.

What about your business, Keroche? Do you think the national leaders can be able to help you resolve your problem, whoever is elected in August? Do you think they'll be able to help you resolve your problems with KRA, which...

Now, whoever is elected in August, which position?

Well, you're in UDA, right? If UDA wins the presidency...

No, I think... I think the problem that the KRA has been having, we just need to have that enable... Somebody will set that enabling environment to do business, and then uh you're on it, you know, you're on it. Like I hear in America, even if a business is struggling or in UK, the government will ensure and they work and ensure and know why are you struggling, cause they never want any business to fall. So I think here, the people who have been put in that line, cause we are many, there are many people who have put in that line, cause we don't... We can't blame His Excellency, of course. You blame the people around who've been put in those offices, the Minister for... who I don't want to mention names and all that. So are they able to make the right decisions at the right time? That is now... So if we have put those right leaders in those offices, we won't be having this problem, and even anybody trying to suppress any upcoming entrepreneur, he will not try, cause he knows the law is put in this country, nobody can. Cause you would wonder, why is Keroche suffering when it's a business that everybody would love, everybody whoever wants to buy that piece of investment, whether it is who, whether it's who. So why wouldn't we see we need it, rather than thinking he's the only one who can manage that, you know what I mean? So we just need to have the good leaders put in those offices, of us that we take the right decision. Yeah.

By the way, um John Mututho, former CEO NACADA, has declared that he's running for the Senate seat in Nakuru, so you have competition.

Yeah, he's almost welcome, actually. I know he tried the last time, he didn't get it. Uh maybe he's got a new manifesto, he'll come and sell it to the people. But I am so confident that I'm the right candidate for the Nakuru County, because I would not be going there for my own gains. I would just be going there to support and ensure that the people of Nakuru... I leave it better than how I found Nakuru, and I was born there. So actually, I'm the only one who understands what Nakuru people need. Yeah, yeah.

All right, let me take a break, come back and talk more about uh your um seeking political seat, because I mean, it must be very stressful for you. Business has been shut down, people sent home, and you still want to run for office. Why? Let me talk about that, and also the loss of your family member. That must have been a very tough, tough loss for you. We'll talk about that when we come back.

We're talking to the CEO of Keroche Breweries, Tabitha Karanja. She's my guest today. She's just declared she's running for the Senate seat in Nakuru County, as are others, and she says she can win despite the issues and the problems and the challenges at Keroche Breweries. Wow, takes a woman to run that kind of... to have that kind of attitude, folks! I tell you.

Keep tweeting @KoinangeJeff, @CitizenTVKenya. The hashtag is #JKLive, #JKLive. Take a break, we'll be back in a moment.
