content:
Personality #10: Strive Masiyiwa
Speaker Full Name: Strive Masiyiwa

Video Title (Exact): Strive Masiyiwa, Founder and Executive Chairman of Econet

YouTube URL: http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aSIQNt6t0bo

Channel Name: Stanford Graduate School of Business

Approximate Duration: 52 minutes 3 seconds

Relevance to Informal Sector African Entrepreneurs: Strive Masiyiwa details his five-year legal battle to dismantle state telecom monopolies and launch Econet, demonstrating how African micro-entrepreneurs can navigate institutional hostility, deploy unconventional grassroots marketing (like bus riders and township street theater to drive EcoCash adoption), and build scalable digital solutions across African markets.

Full Transcript Text:

Transcript Metadata
Speaker: Strive Masiyiwa

Video Title: Strive Masiyiwa, Founder and Executive Chairman of Econet

URL: http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aSIQNt6t0bo

Channel: Stanford Graduate School of Business

Publish Date: December 5, 2017

Country: Zimbabwe / Pan-African

Sector: Telecommunications, Digital Payments, Venture Capital & Philanthropy

Full Transcript Text
Strive Masiyiwa, I want to first start off by saying that you have easily been one of the most instrumental leaders in shaping my journey, and you've even been responsible for my journey here to Stanford Business School. So it's truly an honor to be here today, and I think I speak for many of the people here in this audience that it's truly an honor.  

So I'd like to start with one of the most compelling pieces of advice I've heard from any business leader: You've mentioned that the three most important skills in business are to read, count, and sell. Take us back to the early days of your career and how you cultivated these skills and used them to become a successful entrepreneur.  

Well, first of all, it's indeed a great privilege and honor to be here. Thank you for inviting me, in particular my colleague and dear friend, the chairman of Stanford, Jeff Raikes. Thank you, Jeff. Jeff and I work on the Alliance for a Green Revolution in Africa, and he invited us here to hold our board meeting here. So I've got a number of my colleagues from the board, Judith Rodin, I see there, Josette and Lena. Thank you so much for joining us today.  

Well, you got to be able to read, you got to be able to count, and you got to be able to sell. In reality, that's what we as entrepreneurs do.  

When I was a little boy, my mother, she came up with this idea that I should earn my own pocket money. So she bought me a box of chewing gum, and I started selling them in my school. But I got lost on the way back home because I couldn't read that well, because I was only little! So I quickly learned that you got to be able to sell. I could count, but I couldn't read before! That's probably why I did maths and engineering.  

So let me talk a little bit more about entrepreneurship. It's easy for a lot of us to think of entrepreneurship from a more current context—it's such a hot topic and respected career path here, with thousands of tech startups emerging each year. But let's go back to Zimbabwe in the early '90s when you first had the vision for Econet. What gave you the courage to take on such a daring and uncommon career path?  

Well, by the time I decided to set up Econet in 1993, I had been in business for about six or seven years. So I had a well-established business, because I started in 1986. I had built up a fairly successful construction business. I'm an engineer, and in telecommunications, the whole mobile revolution was something I had been tracking since school, actually. When I was at university, we already knew what was going on, like most engineers do at school. You know, if you want to know what's going to happen in artificial intelligence, talk to the guys at Stanford; they'll tell you what's going to happen in ten years. So we knew this was going to happen, and it was going to be big.  

But 1993 was particularly important in my tracking, because that's when they were introducing the digital standard, which we call GSM. And I immediately knew this is the time to get in. And I thought it was going to be a fairly simple thing, you know. I went to my former employers and I said, "Hey guys, this thing's going to happen. I'd like to do a joint venture with you."

And I used to have a letter—I think someone from intelligence stole it—but I used to have a letter which used to be on my wall written by the head of the telephone company back to me to say, "You know, this is a fad. It's going to disappear. We have more important things to do here, so don't bother us."  

So I went back and I said, "Okay, since you don't want to be bothered, let me do it."  

They said, "No, you can't do that, because then you would violate our monopoly."  

I said, "So how can you have a monopoly in something you don't do?"  

So I did the smartest thing, which was hire a lawyer! Right? I went to a lawyer and I said, "You know, do they really have a monopoly?"  

He says, "No, they don't. But if you really want to take them on, there's an easier thing to do: Just steal a tank and go park it in front of the president's office. That's it! Much quicker, because that's how he's going to react!"  

I think somebody did it to him about three weeks ago!

So anyway, I took them to court, and I hired a lawyer from New York, an amazing American lawyer called Judith O'Neill. And she was a specialist in telecommunications law, but she couldn't practice in our jurisdiction. And she read the law and she said to me, "You know, you've got a point. I'll help you with this."

So she actually used to come to Harare and advise my legal team on this battle. And it took us five years. Wow.

So at the time, you were trying to bring in a service when 75% of Africans had not heard a telephone ringing. So you were trying to solve a problem that Africans did not yet know they had. How did you gain the boldness and the conviction to take on such a problem at the time?

You know, when I worked as a telephone engineer... imagine, we used to take out adverts, the government used to, saying to people, "You talk too much on the phone!" Dad used to say, "Don't jabber-jabber so much to the customers!"

I mean, together, when you work for the telephone company in any African country, one of the great... whenever you walk down the street, people would come up to you and say, "You know, can you help me get a telephone line?" It was just a badge of honor. And a lot of my friends made money out of it; it was called corruption, yeah!

But it could take officially 14 years to get a telephone in most African countries. Our teledensity was 0.07%. So it was literally impossible for anyone to have a telephone line.

And when we went to the Constitutional Court—we took this thing through the lower courts—and of course, to be honest, by the time we got to the Constitutional Court, I was Public Enemy Number One! I mean, it wasn't funny. I used to get arrested.

So, but when we finally get to the Constitutional Court, we had to get evidence for our court to even consider. It's not very different from your own Supreme Court, and we were to face a nine-member bench. The matter was no longer about the monopoly; we had taken it as a natural freedom of expression.

And so we said, "Look, 75% of the people of this country have never heard a telephone ringing." That was the headline, and that captured headlines across the entire African continent: "75% of our people have never heard a telephone ringing."

And people were calling in: "So where did you get this statistic from?"

And I showed them where we got it. We had to gather this research, which is very important. As an entrepreneur, you've got to get your data. So the court pulled down the monopoly.

And for me, it was really... we were just trying to respond to a need. The revolution for me in telecommunications in Africa, when we look back now, that is just over 20 years ago, 75% of the African people have a telephone now—not just ringing, but their own one! Because our teledensity now is 75% continentally. Some countries like Botswana, well, you know, they're 120%, 130%. I don't know how they do that! In Nigeria, I know how they do it, because it's the robes, you see, so they have one phone here...

But it's a remarkable revolution for our industry.

It seems like every step of the way, building trustworthy partnerships were fundamental to your success—whether it was gaining the trust of agents who enable mobile money to work, or the trust of the hundreds of young people who first spread the message of Econet during the early days. How did you get people to trust you?

You know, I think the key is by not being transactional in relationships. And it goes broader than just your relationship with customers. Getting people to accept mobile money rather than mobile phones was the most counterintuitive thing we ever had to do, because you're talking to people who don't have money, or very little money, and they also had no bank accounts. So we had to persuade them that they could give us their money.

In the case of Zimbabwe, they had faced 500,000% hyperinflation. They knew if you put money in the bank, the next day you didn't have it. And we had to launch mobile money during that time.

So I used to say to my people, when we were discussing how do you take mobile money across, how do we get people to accept it: It's just like trying to get people to drink... How did they do that? Coca-Cola! A black drink in a bottle! But they did it, right? To build this incredible company, Coca-Cola! I mean, that must have been the most difficult thing, to get somebody to drink that black stuff!

Well, we got people to open bank accounts—millions of them! And one of the ways we used to do it, which you're familiar, many of you, with what we call matatus, right? In Africa, the little kombis. So we went to the universities, and we hired the university students, and we wanted them to ride on matatus. So they ride two-by-two in matatus.

But you know how noisy and lively African buses are, right? We talk to each other. So you get onto the bus, and you start... they're supposed to strike a conversation about mobile money: "I'm sending money to my cousin on the other side of town." The whole bus stops! And they talk! They get off the next bus stop, they get onto the next one. And they had to do this, and we had a calculation that said we needed them to talk to 1.5 million people to get to our tipping point. There was no marketing; that was it! Those guys on the buses talking and getting onto the next one.

And people didn't realize the same guys coming on the bus and having an argument about... And we also set street comedy, where someone would say, "You've stolen my money!" and they start a mock fight in the middle of a township. And people will always gather when there's a fight, right? So they then explain that, "Actually, you can't steal my money, because it's in my phone!" And we got people to go out and register. And so these are just techniques that our people worked on.

Amazing. Here at the Stanford Business School, we celebrate failure. We even go as far as to say it's necessary for growth and success. And to look at a leader such as yourself, it can be extremely tempting to view you as absent of failure. Given that entrepreneurship, one of the hardest parts is managing your own psychology, can you talk to us about how you've navigated failure and self-doubt?

Well, I wouldn't stand and say I've ever celebrated failure! I've run into it now and again. Probably the most spectacular was my entry into Nigeria. Now that was pretty spectacular. You know, we went in just after the end of military rule in Nigeria, this would be I guess '99, 2000. And because one in five black people in the world is a Nigerian, this is some market! And we were trying to get in.

And we went in, and of course, we had to build a consortium. Nigeria was particularly difficult. Today, you've got billions of dollars going into Nigeria. But if you look back in 2000, 2001, there was no mobile industry in Nigeria. No one was putting money into Nigeria. I remember going around the banks in South Africa and investors, and they said, "Are you mad? You want to go to Nigeria?"

So, we have to be in Nigeria. If you're going to be in business in Africa, you have to be in Nigeria, period. So we went in and we built a consortium of Nigerian high-net-worth businesses and business leaders to bid for a license. And the government had set up an auction system, and they became the most expensive—even to this day—licenses ever issued in Sub-Saharan Africa. In Tunisia, somebody paid more for it, but we paid in 2001 $285 million for a license.

And a year into the business, one of my partners walked in and put a bill on the table for one of the state governors, and said, "You know, you got to pay us each $4 million, or we throw you out of the country." So I got thrown out of the country, and lost... you know, pretty much got kicked out of that investment.

It took me ten years of international arbitration to win back our investment that we had lost. And along the way, I had that governor jailed! Spent 13 years in a British prison, after making the mistake of going to Dubai and got picked up by Interpol. I mean, it's a known fact that I was a witness against him for corruption.

So, you know, there was bittersweet... very difficult time for us, but there were a lot of entrepreneurial lessons. And after five years, we went back into Nigeria, and the fastest-growing parts of our businesses are in Nigeria today. So we learned a lot. That was really, really difficult, and there were no celebrations except when I got the arbitral award, which is the biggest in African history. So there was a nice end to it.

You've been sought out by many leaders, such as Barack Obama. But who do you look to for inspiration? Are there any up-and-coming young leaders on the continent that inspire you about the future of Africa?

Absolutely. You know, when I started that Facebook page... I didn't know that my daughter, who was at college in the US, was sharing things I was sending her with her friends. So she started saying to me, "You know, my friends think you should talk about this, that's what my friends said." "Well, you know, we share everything."

So we then got to start working on this Facebook page, and the most interesting part for me is reading the comments. I just get absolutely inspired by the comments of young Africans from virtually every corner of the continent who are running businesses in extraordinary situations that even I couldn't have imagined, and they're making a success of it. So I really get inspired by what our young entrepreneurs are doing, and I am in constant conversations with them on Facebook. I even know some of them, you know. I go into meetings and I say, "Where's Austin?" and stuff like this, and they come because they're doing amazing things.

And surely you got people like Juliana Rotich, the young Kenyan woman who built Ushahidi. We got Fred... Is Fred here, too? Fred Swaniker, the African Leadership Academy. Many of you know Fred is an alumnus of Stanford. I mean, these are the guys who are going to totally transform our continent and the world, to be honest.

So, but you know, it's not so much... and it's a great privilege, of course, when you can have a conversation with people like President Obama, who I knew before he was president. And I always remind him that, "You know, I'm eight months older!" This helps you to get a stability. And then it's such a great success, but in Africa, "Demaris, I'm senior brother!"

So, no, but we are... really, it's people I work with over the years. People like Dr. Judith Rodin, she's here. She's the former president of the Rockefeller Foundation. She's been an amazing mentor to me over the last ten years, particularly in understanding philanthropy. Because many of us as entrepreneurs, when we set out to go into philanthropy, we actually don't know how it works. And you need to learn to be talking to people like Dr. Rodin to understand. So it's a lot of people that I work with over a very, very long time that I turn to when I face challenges.

Shifting to philanthropy a bit, in addition to your success as an entrepreneur, you've funded the education of over 40,000 children across Zimbabwe and Africa. How must it feel to have come so far from humble beginnings, and what has motivated you to give back in such an extraordinary way?

Well, first of all, I'm really excited this week, because we just got an announcement that we got our... the Rhodes... of our program this year, and we got one last year. And I think that's our third or fourth now.

So, and it began like a lot of things. I don't think my wife and I sat down and said, "You know, let's give back," because to be honest with you, we started when we didn't have any money! So there's almost nothing to give back if you think of it that way. There was a crisis in Africa at the time, which was HIV/AIDS. People were dying on a scale you cannot imagine. If in my small business I was burying members of my workforce every week, you know... We actually thought we're all going to die! That's how it felt living in Africa in 1990, '91, because of the HIV crisis.

And what made the crisis so difficult were these children. What would we do with the children? I knew what happens when children don't go to school. We had Liberia to tell us about that: child soldiers, all sorts of challenges. You could rip apart a country if these kids did not go to school.

So for us, it was responding to that. And we came up with this model which my wife then said she was going to run full-time. It was basically: if we can find a relative to the child, rather than try to institutionalize any children, let's find their relatives and tell their relatives we will meet the economic side. We'll pay for school fees, we'll give you some food, we'll help with clothing, and so forth.

So it began as a little program really around our own employees, and we probably had 50 when my wife kind of began to do it on a full-time basis. And she'd come from work, and she would just really just make sure these kids were looked after. And one day, you know, it just walked in and said, "Actually, you know, there's 5,000 that we now help, and we've extended beyond the company because people keep bringing these kids to us."

So we built it from there. And as of this year, twenty-odd years into it, we've assisted 250,000 that went through our system of education. We began to... wherever we went, the first thing we told our management teams, if we went to Botswana or Zambia, any country: "You've got to set up the program. You've got to support it." So we support it across every single country where we operate.

And then we select from those kids the really high performers. What do you do if he's 16 and you got a genius on your hands? You say, "Go home"? We just treat them like our own kids. We help them apply for scholarships to Stanford and Harvard and wherever. So we have 354 in the United States this year of our kids, and we've got some in China, some in the UK, and so forth, and we help them along. And so it's been a great program to see.

You've mentioned that entrepreneurship is not just about making money, but about being an agent for change. There's many people here in this audience who have large dreams of going into the world and being catalysts for transformative change. What do you think we should know, and most importantly today, what is your call to action for us?

First of all, don't wait until you've made your billion! Okay? I know everyone at Stanford ends up making a billion once they're entrepreneurs, right? I mean, that's why you come to Stanford, right? Right! So look, you're almost guaranteed to be successful, so start straight away! Why do you have to wait? As you register your company, register your foundation, register your philanthropy! And it's actually good for you.

In our house, we actually never discuss business; we discuss the things we're doing around philanthropy with my kids. And it's very difficult with my kids, because they're more interested in the philanthropy side than... Maybe during holidays, they prefer to go work for their mother; very few volunteer to go and sell in one of my shops!

But the reality is these things, in today's society, we have to start straight away. There's no reason for you to wait. You've got to find a cause. If you don't find a cause, you'll find that making money is itself quite empty. You kind of get into your cause now. What is it you're interested in? Is it the environment? Is it climate change? Is it... There is something that should capture your interest every day.

And for me, I can't wait at the end of my day to escape into discussing the issues of philanthropy. That's why I'm here. We are here to discuss smallholder farmers in Africa. So make it an integral part of what you are doing.

But if there's an even more excellent way, as they say, why not just do the philanthropy? Because if you feel you can make a change with that, rather than going off to run a for-profit, do it! That's my counsel.

Final question before we open it up to some of our business students here for questions: What do you think are some of the most pressing global problems that we should be thinking about today?

Wow. You know, we always think, don't we, that we would like to hand our children fewer problems than were handed to us. You know, our parents kind of handed over a world where they said, "Well, we've achieved... the Soviet Union is gone, because we lived through the Cold War." Not so sure we're handing over a great world to you at the moment. I'm sorry about that! You got a few problems that you're going to have to deal with.

Because top of mind for me is climate change, because it doesn't give us... what is it? We don't have a Planet B. Somebody said we don't get another shot at it if we don't get into it now. So it's up there.

From an African perspective, it's jobs. One would argue it's global, but for your generation, it's bigger than decolonization ever was as a challenge. We have a continent where the average age is 19. We are 1.2 billion; by some estimates, we'll be 4 billion by the turn of this century, in the lives of most of you. If we don't create jobs, we end up with Boko Haram and Al-Shabaab. It's as simple as that, and they can sweep all the way down to the south.

So the security nexus is linked to the jobs. We have to create hope. You know, when I think of the people trying to cross the Mediterranean... sometimes you read reports of five hundred drownings a week in the Mediterranean. We almost forget that they had to cross the Sahara first to get to the Mediterranean, and yet we have a continent with so much resources, so much capacity.

So it's an extraordinary charge for us where we are still able to do something, but an even greater challenge for our children. But it's also global. I think the stability of the world, the future of the world, will to a great extent be shaped by our response to this. So we have to pick up every tool, everything that we can, to try and take on some of these challenges. The rest, we're at Stanford, you know them—amazing!

So now we'll take some questions from the audience.

I was just wondering, on either a personal or professional level, sort of what keeps you up at night? What do you wake up in the morning really concerned about, thinking about?

You know, I never stay up at night! President Obama said to me, "What keeps you up at night?" I said, "Nothing! I'm not running the world, you are!"

Is it okay suppose you woke up in the middle of the night? So, okay: jobs. How do we create employment? That really is a challenge to me. How do we get our young people... So I am persuaded that the answer lies in part with entrepreneurship, okay? If I can't create somebody a job, maybe I can help them create their jobs, inspire them to go out and do something. But I have an exciting job to do, which does give me a lot of energy in the morning.

We have a question right up here.

Thank you so much for this opportunity. I mean, I've always dreamed to come very close to you. My name is Brian and I'm from Zimbabwe. So my question was: I understand after you finished your undergraduate in Germany or somewhere in Europe, I'm no longer sure, you went back to Zimbabwe to work, you know, in Africa, and then start to build your ideas from the continent. What advice would you give to someone who is graduating right now, or maybe to this specific graduating in 2020: Do you think it's best for us, if we dream of changing our continent through entrepreneurship, to first start working and gain some skills, or to go and work maybe in specific sectors that we think we would want to change in the future?

Yeah, thank you. That's quite multifaceted. I think, you know, there's no simple answer to this. I wish I could say that, but what I can say to you: The sooner you... if you have an intention to get home and work there, the sooner you go, the better. It's actually very difficult if you kind of spent 5, 10 years, you've got a family, you've got roots, and so forth. That's harder to do.

I just picked up my bag and I went home, okay? And, you know, it was easy. I think it would have been much harder if it had been ten years later. But having said that, I know a lot of friends who came after they had spent some time building up experience and so forth, and did very well.

But I also go as far as to say that I'll never condemn somebody who doesn't come, okay? They are contributing. Africans living and working in the Diaspora are contributing as much to Africa today as anybody who's there, and I'm very proud of what they do. We can't accommodate a lot of these guys even if we wanted to. But they are sending money home, they are keeping people in school. The burden they carry for such a small group of people is extraordinary. So that's why I say there's no simple answer. I wish I could say there was. All the above will work out.

But I wouldn't send you to a country at war. There might be an issue. I had to leave Zimbabwe 18 years ago; haven't been back even for one day, okay? So, you know, there are always issues that one needs to take into consideration.

Hello, Strive. Hi, my name is Tunde. I'm from Nigeria.

I figured Tunde! There are just some names, you know: Tunde from Nigeria, Tendai from Zimbabwe. I mean, you never get a Tendai from Kenya! Anyways, thank you.

Kind of piggybacking on your point, I feel about initiatives like what Africans in the Diaspora can kind of do to support development or goals in Africa, more sort of entrepreneurship rather than what you mentioned in terms of like philanthropy or supporting folks back home, so like investments and stuff like that. Because from what you said, not only do we have like people here, we have like tremendous talent that work for tough companies and stuff like that.

And there's a lot of conversation around this issue today: How can we encourage... if we call it the Diaspora, which means we include people like LeBron James, by the way—he's an African in the Diaspora! In Africa, we think of all black people around the world as part of the African Diaspora. But you know, Africa is not just black people; we have a wonderful diversity on our continent.

But on a serious note, there's a lot of conversation around encouraging those who are living and working outside Africa to invest in creating businesses and supporting entrepreneurship, even investing through local stock exchanges and so forth, trying to mobilize capital. I'm a great supporter of that, but I haven't seen anything that I could say to you, "This is the perfect solution." Thank you.

Hi, Strive. My name is Ruth, I'm from Ghana. I was wondering, as chairman of AGRA, what do you think is the future of smallholder farming in Africa? And in thinking about that, how do you think we're going to meet food security challenges?

You should listen to the radio interview that Jeff and I did this morning at 7 o'clock! Jeff Raikes, please, Jeff, stand up! He's the chairman of your esteemed university, but has been a member of the AGRA board for many, many years, and helped set it up. And we spent, goodness, an hour and a half, and you really got to listen to what Jeff had to say, because I was just the backup, you know. I'm a city boy; I'm not a farmer.

But I've learned a few things, and amongst them, of course, you know, 70% of our food production in Africa is done by women smallholder farmers, and they are aging. It's a paradox for us: We've got millions of young people without jobs, but they're not interested in agriculture, and rightly so—it's not sustainable. What we got to do is to put in place a policy framework that modernizes the way we do agriculture, looks at agriculture as an industry, sustains the incomes of smallholder farmers, increases their incomes.

And this is what we are trying to do from the perspective of AGRA. We are investing and catalyzing in small businesses. We've created over a hundred seed companies in Africa, and these seed companies now produce a third of all the certified seed produced on the African continent. It's phenomenal! In ten years, they produce enough seed to feed 15 million people every year. So we're trying to help 30 million smallholder households.

The smallholder farmer is the absolute bedrock of Africa. There's no nation—China, Europe, the United States—that ever got going without sorting out their agriculture. So to the extent that... we got to put in place the right framework from a policy perspective, and that's what we work to try and encourage governments to do: Ensure that there is sustained domestic investment, both from governments, from entrepreneurs, and create a stable environment for farmers' markets, ensuring they get access to seeds, and there's a whole value chain around it. So there's a lot of space in agriculture.

Hi, Mr. Masiyiwa. I'm Elmer from Angola. Here at the GSB, we think a lot about managerial practices that we're supposed to implement to increase the likelihood of success. But those are mostly premised on the existence of certain factors, such as the enforceability of the rule of law or the existence of a highly qualified labor market. People that have succeeded in developing economies in spite of those obstacles are usually associated with the ruling regime. I think it's fair to say that you are not one of those people, but you still succeeded. So how did you do that? And for those of us that are still working on our first billion or million or thousands, what sort of advice would you give?

You know, somebody asked Richard Branson, "How do I become a billionaire?" And he said, "Start buying..." He says, "How do I become a millionaire?" He says, "You know, start with a billion and buy an airline!"

I understand where you want to go. You know, it's one of my challenges when I'm advising young entrepreneurs from different African countries, because, you know, there are different types of governments, there are different situations on the ground. And how do I advise someone from Togo and someone in South Africa, Zimbabwe, Zambia, you know? Because I can't... So what I try to do is to teach principles that will make you a success as an entrepreneur irrespective of the conditions.

And one of my mantras is to say: The entrepreneur must train like a soldier. We fight in the conditions, not the conditions! Because we really can't wake up in the morning and say, "Today it's raining, I'm not fighting!"

So the challenges are there, but the thing is, Africa is full of entrepreneurs. Entrepreneurship is alive and well in Africa. It is just building the support systems to ensure that these ventures can grow in scale. So I hope that as some of you get skills from here, you can take them home to be able to help others to scale.

All right. My name is Terry, I'm from Rwanda. I took that as advice, but I tried to look into that. The problem is part of data in Africa is in the air; it's not somewhere you can actually find data. And even when there is data, it's so hard to break through the government censorship actually to get that data. So what do you think about how can you break through that?

And I also have an insight question about your program. How do you make it more attractive to students to come back to Africa?

I have a better offer for you: Go and start your own business! It's a better offer than Microsoft or Intel or anybody! Once you decide to go down that route, none of those are good offers. So that's my challenge for you.

I have a program which is fascinating, which we take young American graduates every year—this year we had 30—and we send them to Africa for three to six months, and they work for African companies. They don't work for governments, it's not Peace Corps; you got to go and you got to work for companies like mine. And guess what? They don't want to go home either! So there's something going on there, my friend. You got to come!

Afternoon. My name is Daphne. I'm from Zimbabwe, and fortunately, I'm one of your Capernaum scholars. I graduated from Spelman College this past May, so I have a background in biochemistry, and I am interested in addressing health problems in developing countries, mostly particularly in diagnostics, because I feel like those diseases such as malaria, HIV, tuberculosis have been neglected mostly. And I'm interested in someday owning my own biotechnology company in Zimbabwe to address matters in Zimbabwe, because it's very, very important for us to have such facilities that allow us to try and solve our own problems using our own resources. What advice would you give a young person like myself with no background in business, but interested in making such changes to our continent, to the place that we come from?

Wow, that's great! We have a program with Morehouse College, so Andrew Young came to me and said, "Why don't you have a program just for Morehouse?" So that's okay, so we did a deal where it said we would send ten students to Morehouse. But I forgot that was only men, so we ended up doing the identical program at Spelman, and that's where the Andrew Young program she talks about comes.

So it's always meeting these amazing young people there, and this is the future of Africa. Look, the most important thing for you... the challenges for you are there, but they are no different from any generation anywhere else in the world, okay? To the extent that you can come home, come home, and we will help you and we will get you started in the business that you want to get into.

And really, we want to say that about... I mean, your country Zimbabwe, which is also my country, has just gone through an extraordinary change that the whole world witnessed, and so there's a lot of sense of hope. So I'll see you there for Christmas next year!

So I know there's still tons of questions in the audience, but you'll have to post it to his Facebook page because we're out of time now. But I think that we all agree that it's been phenomenal, and let me give another round of applause!

metadata.speaker: Bethlehem Tilahun Alemu

How do we do it? Absolutely fair question. The reason that we've talked a lot I think or come to a lot of focus on entrepreneurship through unemployment is this sort of sense of you guys trying to take big issues like unemployment into your own hands and create a solution. Then you see people doing amazing stuff like James Eder and you go, "Gee, you know, I could do that and create 40 jobs myself," obviously. But what we do know, not everybody has been put in a situation where they have the means to fail fast or fail forward or fail in setting up a business. Okay? And trust me, I've set up a business before, and it wasn't great.

And then, you know, you look at something like Ariana who's just completely amazing, and you go... and Branson as well. So what does it take to do that?

So what we've been doing is we've had a couple of Google Hangouts with Doug Richard, who in the UK is one of those... those of you who know the program The Dragons' Den, used to be on Dragons' Den. Doug is an entrepreneur himself and a brilliant one. And as I told you yesterday, his mom just died, so he will be carrying on after the summit with these Google Hangout how-to sessions. So I do urge all of you... sometimes the One Young World team in London will be in touch with you and ask you to participate visually in one of the little boxes on the Google Hangout. We can't have all of you in there obviously, but I would say to you, do keep your eyes open when Louise and the gang are posting how-tos with people like Doug, because there is such good... some of those sessions, honestly, it's like going to university and getting half an hour with someone who's really magic. And the stuff is there. Equally, Mr. Nunn's dialogues online. I know one of the Google Hangouts that he did on agriculture and agribusiness was just phenomenal stuff that you can't learn anywhere else.

So to bring that live to you today, I'm going to bring back to the stage returning ambassador, returning counselor Carol Stone. Carol is an entrepreneur herself, quite apart from being the most well-connected... Hello Carol!

When Carol was first a counselor with Bishop Desmond Tutu when we were in Zurich, the pair of them ran onto the stage, and David said to me, "If Desmond Tutu and Carol Stone had a baby, how much energy would that be? How delightful!"

So Carol is going to run the session with Bethlehem Alemu, who you met earlier, who's African Entrepreneur of the Year. Carol, thank you very much indeed.

Well, first of all, this is all about how to be an entrepreneur. Who here wants to be an entrepreneur? Good, a good number! Well, you can be. You can be one now when you're young, you can be one middle-aged, you can be one a bit later on. That's a wonderful thing. You've got an idea, you've got an inspiration, you can do it.

Now, I started work at 18. I was a secretary. I worked from 9:00 in the morning till 5:00 at night and thought that would be my life. And for a lot of the time, it was my life. But then towards the end of that working life, I did actually establish an opinion market research company, asking people what they thought about issues of the day. And in fact, it was that very company that first asked what young people wanted to discuss at One Young World, so I was very, very proud of it. I was 65. That was six years ago; I'm now 71. So I started very late! And what's more, I got married for the first time at 57, but that's not on the agenda!

So I'm saying you can do it when you want to, but of course, I'd rather you start perhaps younger than that. But for someone who did start much younger, that Kate mentioned, we've already heard from this morning, really is proof that there's huge potential for investment in Africa, which is a wonderful thing. And she is the CEO and founder of the ethical footwear company soleRebels, and she's created lots of jobs in her home country of Ethiopia. Forbes magazine said she was a woman to watch. For us, she's a woman to hear. A welcome to Bethlehem Alemu!

There she is! Welcome. Thank you.

Well, we heard from Bethlehem this morning, and she sort of rather skated over how she actually got the business off the ground. She said that one or two banks refused her, but she got people around her and she started it. So I want to know just a little bit more. If I... you were about 25, were you?

Yes, mid-20s.

Much, much younger than me, 40 years earlier! She suddenly decided she wanted to... First of all, how on earth did you decide shoes?

That's a really good question, and I get that question all the time. And I'm going to explain it again. Why shoes is... the way I grew up, I've been watching people doing things by hand, which really interested me to mobilize the community in the business. One of the things that people do when I grew up, when I see, is spinning, which is a culture that we had, and weaving—people create a lot of fabrics from it.

So we had another culture, which is recycled tire shoes. People were wearing that recycled tire shoe for different reasons. First, it was cheap to buy. The second one is it was durable—you can wear them every time, they can last for a year or two. So I see those two opportunities working together. So I use the talent that I have around me, and I use the idea of recycled tires. So I came up with an idea of producing products from that.

And how did you actually get those people around you? Did you suddenly, when you couldn't get anything from the first banks, how did you get that funding?

Actually, I didn't get any funding when I started my company. And I want to make sure that everybody here who wants to be an entrepreneur, to do not go back because people refuse you. What I would like to say is, if you have any idea and if you believe in yourself, your idea can be bigger even if people say, "Well, this is not the idea that I'm going to support." But you believing in yourself and being passionate about what you do is the big bonus for you, because nobody is responsible for your life but you.

So I grew up in Ethiopia, but I have seen a lot of people working every day to make it through, to go through in different places and to make it through for a day. I see people struggling to have food in their mouths, versus there is a lot of people who are supposed to support the community. So if you want to be an entrepreneur, have a clear vision in what you are about to do. And then there is a lot of challenges, of course. You're going to come up with the challenges to solve your own problems.

Well, David Jones, our co-founder of One Young World, wrote a book a short while ago called Who Cares Wins, meaning that people don't mind, young people, anyone doesn't mind a business making profit, but they do want them to give something back to society. Now, I think you formed a crèche, haven't you, for children?

Yes.

Already? How do you take that? Did you automatically have a social conscience?

Yes, when we started the company, because we said we're going to empower our own people, we invest in the people themselves. So to be a social entrepreneur, you have to blend the idea of social community service inside your business. So when you do that, it's working together and then it's going to be easier. It's going to be hard once you form the company to be able to be a socially conscious company. It's a little bit tough. But it's already blended in, and I always say that soleRebels, from the beginning, in our DNA, we're a fair trade company.

So to get a fair trade organization certificate, it's just to have a transparency between us and our customers, because these days people are saying, "We're a fair trade company." How are you proving that? What's your criteria to be a fair trade company? So that's what we do.

So to the people who had their hands up, what hope or inspiration can you give them? Would you say probably half of them will succeed? If they fail, certainly try again. But what was the moment when you thought, "This company is going to succeed"? Was it the first order? Was it somebody first saying what wonderful shoes? What was it? And what sizes do you do? Because I take a size 10.

We can go to size 44. We can go to size 15. So we can really... you can order online if you want custom-made products also.

So what was that moment when you thought, "This is going to be a successful company"? The first order, the first time someone wrote about it—what was it?

Well, the challenge is that even if you have a big idea, even if you shake the world, being in Ethiopia, being in Africa, is the biggest challenge that I see. If I was born in the States or somewhere outside Africa, can you imagine where my company is going to be? So the market that people build for us is down there. So you have to break into the market, because when people see businesses, they always want to see somebody else behind them, right?

So we have to break into that. Your idea, really big idea, and you have to be able to manage and register your trademarks, things like that, in the right way. Because the formula is the same for me and somebody from the United States, because it's a competition, right? It's a global business. So it doesn't give me any opportunity if I don't compete with other companies in the right way.

Okay, then let's take it back just a bit from the practical. How much do you have to actually persevere? Did you have setbacks? Did you have setbacks before you had success?

A lot! Every day, actually. The challenges come every day. But one of the barriers was the market—to win the market, to win customers. That's a big challenge. Even if you have a big product, good product, sustainable product, to win the market, you have to really work hard.

People say you have to do 10,000 hours to be the best in the market, whatever you're doing. But in my mind, I did 40,000 hours because I spend more time in my company and to really see what's going on in the market, how I'm winning the market, what customers are looking for from their brand, and how am I going to create a job opportunity inside my community and outside my country also. Because soleRebels is a global business today.

We managed to hire more than 20 people outside Ethiopia, which is a big bonus for us, because whenever we open soleRebels stores, we hire local people. For example, we opened a branded store in Taiwan—six stores. So we don't bring in Ethiopian people to manage the stores; we hire local people, which is Taiwanese. When we open a store in Switzerland, we hire local people there too. So in South Korea, everywhere. So we do have 140 people working for soleRebels, but bigger than that, we do have 20 international workers for soleRebels.

And just for the practical side, I mean, if you're going to write a business plan first, if you're going to take it to a bank, if you're going to go to a private investor, what would you give as...

I did not go to the bank, but I did go to an organization who have a specific program for women who want to start a business, but I didn't get any support. But that pushed me really to the end that I'm going to do it by myself, and I'm going to use whatever support and whatever ideas that I can get around me.

And my thinking is, if you're running a business, you don't have to run it as a charity. If it is a business, you have to really win the market. You have to be strong, and then you have to control your own destination. Don't let people control you, because it's your idea. Even if people invest in your company, make sure that you're in control of your own destiny.

Well, you say it's your own idea. What about the problem of, in television for example, where I've been some of my life, people can pinch a program idea and put that program on? What about intellectual property? What about someone pinching your ideas of shoes?

That's a really good question. After I launched my brand, there are a lot of companies coming to Ethiopia to invest, which is really good because they open a factory and they start their business and then hire local people. The problem starts when they steal your intellectual property. Even if they are coming, even if they are a foreign company, they cannot win... that doesn't mean that they win the market because of different reasons—because of infrastructure, probably because of the product that they're producing, because people were doing the same thing for the last 20 years, they're just following in a different form.

So you make sure that your idea is your own by registering your trademark and what you do. That's really important, because if people see if you don't know what to do about your intellectual property, people are going to steal it—your name. That means they're going to take your face off, they're going to put it on their face to sell your product. And it's not fair to do that.

What happened was, like a month before, somebody, a competitor from my country who's working in the same industry, stole my intellectual property, registered my domain name, forwarded it to his website. Whenever people type in solerebels.com, it's going to his website. He's selling his product. Do you think that's fair? No!

If somebody really does that on soleRebels, on me, what's going on on the ground for startups and other entrepreneurs? So you make sure that you secure your intellectual property. I do have this kind of really good audience and then stage to talk about it. There is a lot of people who are entrepreneurs, who are doing good in their territory, but they cannot really have this opportunity to talk about it. So wherever you are, if you're in Ethiopia or if you're in South Africa or if you're in the UK, you should have that done.

Thank you. I would have assumed that you'd gone right for business and that you were a single woman. That's not the case?

No, I'm not! I'm married and I have three children.

You can have it all! And in a way, I suppose it spurs you on rather than holds you back?

It's going well, I guess. But sometimes when I travel like this, it's a little bit hard. But my family and my husband have been really supporting me from start to now, and I wish they continue to support me to go forward.

Before we go to questions and answers for the second half, what about the future? What's your next ambition for the company?

Yeah, my next ambition is to be an Apple of Africa.

Is that possible?

Yes, to be an Apple of Africa. Apple is a big company in the world, right? So imagine soleRebels being an Apple of Africa. So that being said, it's not just only an ambition, but we're taking the right points to make that happen. One of the things that we want to do is we do have more than 10 branded stores today, but between 5 to 10 years, we want to have 100 stores all over the world, branded stores by the name of soleRebels. And then we're going to hire 5,000 people inside Ethiopia and another 300 people around the world. That's the plan for soleRebels in the future.

Thank you. Thank you so much. I think we'll now go to questions and answers, because from that number of hands up, there are probably still quite a few questions to ask. I'll take two or three at a time. Someone who's caught my eye in a red shirt down there is James Eder, who started Student Beans. Come up on the stage with your microphone for a moment, James, and tell us what you've done.

Hi everyone, again. I know you've already heard from me for a few minutes, but to really make a point, what I'd just love to do is just ask for one volunteer, please, to put up your hand—just one volunteer to come to the front. I saw you first, just the lady. Can we have a round of applause for the volunteer, please? Thank you very much. Round of applause, a bit louder! It's not easy to come up here. Thank you.

So what I'd like to do is I'd like to give you this book, which I mentioned earlier, some jelly beans, and also my business card. Let me introduce... I'm James.

Your name is?

Isa.

Great, thank you very much. Go and sit down. Round of applause again for the volunteer!

So the reason why I wanted to do that, because it's not about me, it's about you in the room, and it's about taking opportunities you're presented with every single day. Now, that was an opportunity. It was a real opportunity for everyone in the room. I gave you my business card. I'm happy to mentor you, to provide you some free mentoring. But the reason why I did that: why didn't you volunteer?

So I'd like to leave a quote and then hand back or be involved in the Q&A:

"Watch your thoughts, they become words. Watch your words, they become actions. Watch your actions, they become habits. Watch your habits, they become character. Watch your character, it becomes your destiny."
— Frank Outlaw

I just think it's so important—the opportunities that are presented every day, it's whether you take them or not. So thank you very much.

Excellent. If anyone can remember all that, I should be surprised, but I think the gist of it was very, very good advice. Thank you very much indeed, James.

Okay, questions. If you could say who you are and if you're an entrepreneur already, let me know. And where you're from, of course.

Hi, I'm Dion from Montserrat in the Caribbean. I have a question. I own a small business with my mother, it's fast food. My question is: How did your first opportunity come about for you to expand outside of Ethiopia, and how did you go about it?

That's a really good question, because whenever people want to start a business, probably they want to start from local areas, right? But it's different for me. I did not start soleRebels from local, from Ethiopia. I am manufacturing in Ethiopia, actually. I am selling my products in different countries. Why? There are a lot of products coming to Ethiopia from outside, there are no products going out from Ethiopia, and we don't build our name as a competitor out there.

So I really like to challenge myself to break into different boxes. One of the boxes is that we are competitors. Now I am able to compete. I am not here because I have an idea, "I'm going to do this, I'm going to do that next year." But I have done it. I have done it from scratch and I penetrated the market. You could do the same, but make sure that your idea and how you develop your company makes sense for the others.

Thank you. I'm going to take two or three at a time just because I want to get as many as I can. Who are you, where are you from?

Hello, my name is Matthew Duby, I'm from the UK. I just want to ask you directly: What made you make the jump from a stable job into becoming an entrepreneur? Because it's something that I'm looking to do, and it's just what stimulated you to make that jump?

I'll just answer it very quickly. I thought, you never know what might happen, let me take a risk, let's take a chance. We prepared for failure. And so somebody said to me market research would be good for you. So I actually formed a limited company within a PLC, and it was very, very hard work—lots of times crying at weekends, "I can't do this, I'm exhausted, I wish I'd never tried it." But at the end of the day, what I always feel, I'm glad I had a go. Even had I failed, I'd be glad I had a go rather than not try. I sold my company two years ago, or all the shares I had within it, I paid off my mortgage, which is a wonderful feeling, and I'm very, very pleased I had a go. So it was just thinking: do it now, don't wait for the perfect time.

Thank you very much.

Hi, I'm Caleb. Congratulations for the great achievement. My two questions mainly: 1) How do you break into the steep competition against leading brands? 2) How do you go about sourcing for cheaper capital when there are high interest rates?

Yes, thank you. How do you get market outside Ethiopia, right? That's your first question. How do you break against the big brands in the various markets?

Actually, I did not break any big brand. I am another brand who's growing really fast, because my products are really different than the other products, and my message for people is delivered through the products. What I'm selling is not just a product, but I am sharing an experience. People come and see different opportunities in soleRebels. For example, we don't produce one product at a time; we produce more than 150 products in a day, different ones. So when people see that, they believe that it's something different, something new for the market. That's how I get to the market.

The second question is, how did you scale up your business, right? If I put it in one word, I scaled up my business because I do have really good relationships with people who are working with me, and I do have really good partners who have a background in retail marketing and those things. So I really work collaboratively with other people who know the market, who know the industry too. So that's how I get to the market.

Absolutely. To build on that, people do business with people, and exactly like you said, it's the network of people in the room. If you think you're building connections now, that's how you get in and work with bigger organizations and small as well.

I agree with that. As a networker myself, I think when you're here now, do take advantage. You're so lucky to be here and meeting these people. You may come back another year, but make sure you've got people's phone numbers, their emails, their Twitter accounts, whatever you want to know. Keep in touch with them. Remember where you met them, what they looked like—"had a yellow jumper"—so you remember them, whatever it is. Because you may well need them, and if you nurture people, it helps you throughout your life.

Next question.

Hi, my name is Yasin, I'm Sudanese. My question is... well, Sudan is a very beautiful country, but it's also a country that's in constant conflict. It's a country where you have a lot of talented people who are sitting at home. Entrepreneurship is blocked, actively blocked to an extent. Small and mid-sized companies do not always survive. So within such a context, how can we as young people, as entrepreneurs, change such a landscape?

Let me take the man in the yellow jumper as well.

Hi, John George Chawa from Zambia. My question... because from just the time you started explaining, I've gathered a lot of facts which are as clear as daylight. So my question is, how can I upgrade because I'm a social entrepreneur? What I do is to see change in my community in terms of prevention of HIV and AIDS. There are so many problems that I would like to help in my community, but I've got some personal problems. So how can I marry the two—social entrepreneurship and business entrepreneurship?

Thank you. Which one are you going to take first?

Yes, thank you for your questions. I don't know what's going on in Sudan, but people are going to be responsible for whatever they want to do because that's their dream. So in whatever situation... I didn't have a lot of people supporting me from the government, right? I didn't have a lot of people supporting me from organizations, and I don't think that's really important. What's important is your idea and what you want to do about it, and it's about your dream. If you're going to do it, of course we are all going to take risks. Life is a risk, we always take risks. So I would say to you, if you have any idea to develop any business in Sudan, I think it can be done, and you can do it the way I do it. You don't have to conflict with governments and things like that. If people see the change that you are bringing, then they start supporting you. So you'd better start it if you have any ideas to do.

To your question, I don't know what kind of business that you want to do, but I know that you want to empower your community and you want to deliver some kind of message for people to keep themselves from HIV. Is that what you're saying? So I don't know how to create a business starting from an organization to the business. What I know is, start a business and support your community—that can work. You can have some idea and then you can start your business, but you can say you're supporting your community by teaching about HIV/AIDS. I think that's the way to go.

I'm so sorry, we've got so many questions in so little time. I think I'll take one gent over here.

I'm Clinton from South Africa. It's more of a statement as compared to a question.

Good, we like those!

I think the African delegates that are here don't really appreciate what we have at our doorstep at the moment, with corporates looking at us as the final frontier. Before they set up onshore in our continent, here's what we want: partner with our entrepreneurs, give women equity before you set up onshore, and address youth unemployment. So we use this as a negotiating tool before we actually let them set enterprise onto our continent.

Thank you very much. Let the gentleman behind you... Was that a question or a comment?

It's a question. I'm an entrepreneur from Botswana, my name is Dea. I wanted to ask you if you are a first-generation entrepreneur, and if yes, how does it feel to be a first black woman entrepreneur?

I am the first generation in entrepreneurship in my family. My family completely never did business, and they don't have any idea about business. So I am the first generation. And it's really tough to be able to have your own idea and start from scratch sitting in Ethiopia, and using different components like technology, things like that, to scale up your idea and to implement it. It's really tough, but I always believe in myself and my team also: we can do this, and you can do that too.

I'll take the lady here in the purple.

Hi, my name is Saj, I'm from Bahrain. Me and my mom, we own a small business, a handmade business actually. My question is very simple: I have an idea, but I don't know how to implement it to be an entrepreneur. So my question to you is, what are the basic steps or the strategy you took to actually be who you are right now?

Can you make a short answer?

That's a really good question. When I started the business, I felt the same, but I understood that if I empower the workers that I have, if I pay the right amount of money for the talent that they have, and then if I give sustainability for my workers—it's not like they're going to work today, and if something happens, we're going to fire them tomorrow—you're going to have to train your people to be on your side and to believe in what you're doing. That's how I built my team. So I think that helps.

Can I just add one very quick thing to that? It was just around having the vision, but also breaking down what's the first thing that you can do to make a difference to start. Because people put it very much in a big picture, but just see if there's one action that you can do to take that next step, and then the next one, and it builds up.

Thank you very much indeed.

Hi, I am Tan, a social entrepreneur from South Africa. Business has moved from geographical limits onto the internet, and the reality on our continent is that there isn't infrastructure for ICT to support businesses that move onto the internet. What is your advice for people on the African continent, especially young black Africans in townships and underdeveloped areas, for them to move in and compete on the same scale that Europeans and other foreigners are competing in on the net?

Sometimes when you don't have a lot of opportunity, you create the opportunity yourself. Why I'm saying that is, soleRebels is a pioneer of a lot of things. soleRebels is a pioneer of building a brand from scratch and scaling it up to a global level. soleRebels is a brand that started selling products online. How? Because there are companies who can do that, so you can outsource what you need to other companies who can develop that for you. So it doesn't have to be in Ethiopia, it can be done somewhere else.

Thank you very much.

Hi, my name is Kate and I'm an entrepreneur from the United Kingdom. I started my business at the beginning of this year, and we build commercial-scale urban farms that grow sustainable fruit and fish in cities. In the past 10 months, probably everything that could have gone wrong has gone wrong at some point. I wondered, for both of you, what was the worst thing that's gone wrong for you in your business and what you learned from it?

I went to a trade fair in Atlanta with my product to show what I'm doing, and one person came and said, "This is really nice, so I'm going to write you an order." So he wrote an order. He didn't pay. So I was really happy to get orders from somebody from Atlanta. So I took that order, I processed the order, and then I sent the product to him. And he didn't want to pay. So I called his office. Somebody answered the phone: "Is everything okay in Ethiopia?" I was like, "Can you pay my money?" So those are the things that you face every day.

And another thing: somebody ordered... we had a relationship for two years, and for some reason, this company or this person ordered $80,000 worth of shoe products to sell in the UK. So we processed the order, we sent the order to him. The guy completely disappeared after he received the goods. At that time, shall I shut down my company? Because I am a startup, I cannot afford to lose $80,000 worth of products! And sometimes people hit you like that to destroy you, but it doesn't matter, you keep going. There is a lot of catastrophe from somewhere, but you keep going.

My only one is on the very first year I started the company, I took on a woman I thought would be good. She was absolutely vile, bossy, and terrible. I had to keep her for 3 months, because she could stay for the 3 months. She stayed, it was terrible. I'll never do it again!

So thank you very much. Thanks to James Eder for coming in from off stage, which was wonderful. Thank you Bethlehem, and good luck for all you're doing. Well done! Thank you very much, and thank you to you, Carol, as well for sharing.

content:
Personality #18: Magatte Wade
Speaker Full Name: Magatte Wade

Video Title (Exact): Poverty, Inc. - Magatte Wade on Entrepreneurship

YouTube URL: http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h8LIbmJzo6I

Channel Name: John W. Hammond Institute for Free Enterprise

Approximate Duration: 45 minutes 18 seconds

Relevance to Informal Sector African Entrepreneurs: Magatte Wade details how over-regulation, bureaucratic red tape, and hostile business environments force millions of African micro-entrepreneurs into informal survivalism, advocating for market-based reforms, value-added manufacturing, brand creation, and high-quality SME job generation as the true path to African prosperity.

Full Transcript Text:

Transcript Metadata
Speaker: Magatte Wade

Video Title: Poverty, Inc. - Magatte Wade on Entrepreneurship

URL: http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h8LIbmJzo6I

Channel: John W. Hammond Institute for Free Enterprise

Publish Date: May 8, 2017

Country: Senegal / Pan-African

Sector: Consumer Goods, Skincare Manufacturing, Economic Freedom & Enterprise Advocacy

Full Transcript Text
My name is Magatte, and I was born in Senegal on the West Coast of Africa. Oftentimes people ask me, "How did you get into entrepreneurship?" For me, entrepreneurship is on a very personal plane, because other than being an entrepreneur, I have two issues basically that almost keep me haunted.

One of them is the fact that my people are dying at a regular rate. Imagine the workplace, imagine all the seats in this room, and we put young people like you in it. Now let's take all the people in a small fisherman's boat, a pirogue, and we push that boat from the coast where I'm from into the Atlantic Ocean, trying to move up to Europe. As you can imagine, most of those boats don't make it to their destination, and most people end up drowning. Imagine people your age and younger dying every single day because they are trying to reach Europe, hoping to help their family back home, and they end up at the bottom of the ocean serving as fish food.

That's pretty gruesome, isn't it? Well, that's my real story. I have friends, I bring friends who have relatives who are victims on a regular basis. Or a plane gets somewhere in Europe, and all of a sudden a body drops from the sky because somebody squeezed themselves into the landing gear or the cargo section. If they freeze to death up there because of the altitude, when the landing gear opens, they fall off the plane.

That is the sad reality of migration. When people talk about migrants, I have lived with these stories for as long as I can remember having a brain and being able to understand what's going on. In my case, we call them economic migrants. Economic migrants are those people who leave their place of origin, their country, to go to another country in search of jobs.

The second reason that haunts me is the fact that my culture is dying. Why? Because Africans, and people from the developing world in general—people who have been part of dominated cultures—share this dynamic. When people feel that their traditional identity and culture are not respected globally, they tend to push down their own culture while accepting Western culture because it is the accepted, dominant culture.

In my case, I was born in Senegal, raised by my grandmother after my parents moved to France, and after business school in France, I decided to move to the United States. I worked in Silicon Valley during the dot-com heyday, working for companies like Google before most people even knew what those companies were about. What I learned in Silicon Valley created a deep internal crisis for me. Here I was living this amazing life, but every day I opened the newspaper, there was some nasty story about Africa, and a lot of it was related to poverty.

I remember driving down Highway 1 near Big Sur, emotional and crying, and I almost crashed into the ocean. At that moment, I made a deal with God: "From now on, I want everything that I do forward to be related to getting Africa into shape. I don't know what it's going to be, but you have to know that I am committed to it."

Being in Silicon Valley, I learned the magic of entrepreneurship—creating something out of nothing—and developed a deep appreciation for brand philosophy. A brand is a container for culture. I realized that if I wanted my culture to be preserved, it needed to be embedded in products that people all over the world love and respect. Look at brands like Hollister: it's a pure fabrication of a surfer lifestyle, yet young people all around the world buy into that culture.

I decided to use the power of branding to tell the world the story of my culture, get them to love it, and build companies that create high-quality jobs back home so my people don't have to risk their lives crossing the ocean to find work.

My first company, Tiossan, was a beverage company using native Senegalese hibiscus and botanical recipes. My second company, SkinIsSkin, is a skincare company. We practice impact sourcing—buying raw ingredients like shea butter directly from women's cooperatives in Senegal, putting over 4,000 women to work. But we need to go beyond just sourcing raw materials; we need to move up the value chain. Instead of just harvesting raw shea butter for pennies, we must manufacture the finished creams, lotions, and packaged products in Africa. That is where the real value, wealth, and high-paying jobs are created.

When people talk about poverty, poverty is a simple concept: people are poor because they have no money. Why do they have no money? Because they have no income. Where does income come from? A job! Where do jobs come from? Businesses! And where do new jobs come from? Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) and entrepreneurs!

If we agree that jobs come from entrepreneurs and businesses, shouldn't we focus on making sure there is a good business climate for entrepreneurs to start and grow companies?

Yet when you look at the World Bank's Doing Business index—which measures ten indicators of how easy or difficult it is to start and run a business—almost all African countries sit at the very bottom of the ranking! Almost nobody talks about this, but it is the root cause of systemic poverty.

Let me give you real examples of how bad regulations kill businesses. In the US, if an employee wants to quit, they give two weeks' notice. If a business needs to let an employee go, they give severance or notice. In Senegal, if an employee wants to leave or if you need to lay someone off, the law requires three months' written notice! If they worked for you for six years, you owe them six months of pay. If they worked twelve years, you owe a full year of salary!

Now imagine you are a young person wanting to start a small business. How can you take the risk of hiring five people when firing one underperforming worker could bankrupt your entire company? The result? Nobody hires formally, or businesses refuse to start in the first place!

Another example: in some African countries, the minimum capital required just to open a corporate bank account used to be $1,000! $1,000 is more than the annual income of many citizens! It is a series of absurd, anti-business regulations that choke enterprise at all levels.

And then people wonder why there are no formal jobs, why 80% to 90% of the economy is forced into informal survivalism, why young people get desperate, get on pirogues, and die at sea!

The difference between a young person in America making $15 an hour and a young person in Senegal making $1 an hour for the exact same effort is not talent, ambition, or intelligence. The only difference is the legal and economic framework of the country in which they were born! Poor people live in badly regulated places.

To fix poverty, we must fix the business climate. We need legal reforms that allow local entrepreneurs to flourish.

When it comes to my own business, I practice conscious capitalism and the stakeholder model. Every business decision must be a win-win for six key stakeholders:

Our employees

Our customers

Our suppliers

The environment

The local community

Our shareholders

Some people ask about microfinance and micro-lending platforms like Kiva. Microfinance was a wonderful first step to help people float, but microfinance primarily funds necessity entrepreneurs—people who sell vegetables on the side of the road because there are no jobs. There is a huge difference between a necessity entrepreneur selling fruits to survive, and an opportunity entrepreneur building a manufacturing plant, a tech platform, or a brand that hires hundreds of people. What Africa desperately needs is funding and business climate reforms for the missing middle—the Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) that drive real economic transformation.

If you care about eradicating poverty, if you care about human dignity, remember that entrepreneurs and enterprise are the true magic that creates prosperity. Do whatever you can to break down the barriers and make it easier for entrepreneurs to do their magic!

Thank you very much.
